q: A 0.50 g sample of pure iron-56 (mass number 56, atomic number 26) is placed in a mass spectrometer at 298 K. Assuming every atom in the sample is the ⁵⁶₂₆Fe isotope, how many protons does each individual nucleus contain?
why: The atomic number Z equals the number of protons. For ⁵⁶₂₆Fe, Z=26 so each nucleus has 26 protons; the remaining 56−26=30 nucleons are neutrons. Mass number (56) counts protons plus neutrons, not protons alone.

q: A neutral sulfur atom (Z=16) is in its ground state at standard conditions (298 K, 1 atm). Following the Aufbau principle, Hund's rule, and the Pauli exclusion principle, which electron configuration correctly represents this atom?
why: Sulfur has 16 electrons filled by Aufbau order: 1s² (2) + 2s² (4) + 2p⁶ (10) + 3s² (12) + 3p⁴ (16). The 3p subshell holds 4 of its possible 6 electrons. [Ne]3s²3p⁴ is equivalent shorthand.

q: A neutral oxygen atom (Z=8) at 298 K is excited by spectroscopy. Using its ground-state configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁴ and applying Hund's rule to the 2p orbitals, how many unpaired electrons are present in the ground state?
why: Hund's rule fills the three 2p orbitals singly before pairing. With 4 p-electrons, the configuration is (↑↓)(↑)(↑), giving 2 unpaired electrons. Forgetting Hund's rule and pairing first would incorrectly suggest 0 unpaired.

q: Copper (Z=29) is one of the well-known anomalous transition metals. At 298 K and 1 atm, a neutral Cu atom exhibits a configuration that maximizes stability through subshell filling. Which configuration represents the ground state of Cu?
why: Cu and Cr are anomalies: a fully filled d¹⁰ (and half-filled d⁵) subshell is more stable than expected, so one 4s electron is promoted to 3d. The result is [Ar]4s¹3d¹⁰ rather than the naive [Ar]4s²3d⁹.

q: A hydrogen lamp emits a photon of wavelength 656 nm (frequency 4.57×10¹⁴ Hz). Using Planck's relationship, which equation correctly relates the photon's energy E to its frequency f, where h is Planck's constant (6.63×10⁻³⁴ J·s)?
why: Planck's relation E = hf gives photon energy from frequency. For 4.57×10¹⁴ Hz: E = (6.63×10⁻³⁴)(4.57×10¹⁴) ≈ 3.03×10⁻¹⁹ J. E = mc² applies to rest mass energy and E = ½mv² applies to classical kinetic energy.

q: Consider an isolated atom whose third principal energy level (n=3) is being analyzed. Using the formula 2n² for maximum electron capacity per shell, what is the maximum number of electrons that can occupy n=3 across the 3s, 3p, and 3d subshells combined?
why: Maximum electrons per shell = 2n². For n=3: 2(3)² = 18. This breaks down as 3s (2) + 3p (6) + 3d (10) = 18. Confusing 2n² with 2n+1 or only counting 3s and 3p gives the common errors of 8 or 9.

q: A chloride anion Cl⁻ (formed from neutral Cl, Z=17) is dissolved in 0.10 M aqueous solution. Each Cl⁻ ion has gained one electron compared with the neutral atom. How many electrons are present in a single Cl⁻ ion?
why: Neutral Cl has Z = 17 protons and 17 electrons. Adding one electron to form Cl⁻ gives 18 electrons, isoelectronic with Ar. The mass number 35 counts protons + neutrons, not electrons; subtracting an electron would give 16 (Cl⁺).

q: A hydrogen atom relaxes from n=2 to n=1, releasing a photon of approximately 121.6 nm (1.64×10⁻¹⁸ J). Based on the Rydberg formula and the regions of the electromagnetic spectrum, in which region does this n=2→n=1 transition emit?
why: All transitions ending at n=1 are the Lyman series, which lies in the UV. Transitions ending at n=2 (Balmer) are visible; those ending at n=3 (Paschen) are IR. The n=2→n=1 wavelength of 121.6 nm confirms UV.

q: Four neutral atoms — Na (Z=11), K (Z=19), Mg (Z=12), and Cl (Z=17) — are compared in their ground states at 298 K. Using periodic trends in atomic radius (down a group, radius increases; across a period, radius decreases), which atom has the largest atomic radius?
why: Atomic radius increases down a group (more shells) and decreases left-to-right across a period (greater Zeff). K is in period 4 group 1, the lowest-leftmost of these four, giving it the largest radius (~227 pm). Cl, far right in period 3, is the smallest.

q: Period 3 elements Na, Mg, Al, and Si are compared by first ionization energy at 298 K. Mg has a fully filled 3s² subshell (extra stability). Rank the four atoms from lowest to highest first ionization energy.
why: IE generally rises across a period, but Mg's filled 3s² is unusually stable, making Al's first IE LOWER than Mg's (removing Al's 3p¹ is easier). Hence Na < Al < Mg < Si. Forgetting the s²→p¹ dip gives the strict-trend distractor.

q: When forming polar covalent bonds, electronegativity differences drive bond polarity. Among the elements O (3.44), F (3.98), Cl (3.16), and He (no Pauling value because it does not bond), which has the highest Pauling electronegativity?
why: Fluorine has the highest Pauling electronegativity (3.98) of any element because it sits at the upper right of the periodic table (excluding noble gases). He has no Pauling value because it forms essentially no compounds, so it is not the answer.

q: Electron affinity of Cl is −349 kJ/mol while F is only −328 kJ/mol, despite F sitting above Cl in group 17. Why is chlorine's electron affinity MORE negative (more exothermic) than fluorine's, contrary to the usual increasing-up-the-group trend?
opts: Cl is more electronegative than F
F is so small that adding an electron causes strong electron-electron repulsion in its compact 2p shell
Cl has fewer occupied shells than F
F actually has a more negative EA; the data above is wrong
Cl has a higher Zeff than F
why: Fluorine's 2p shell is unusually compact, so adding a 9th electron causes large electron-electron repulsion that offsets the favorable nuclear attraction. Chlorine's 3p shell is more diffuse, so the incoming electron experiences less repulsion, giving Cl the more negative EA.

q: An isoelectronic series Na⁺, Mg²⁺, F⁻, and O²⁻ all share 10 electrons (the Ne configuration) but differ in nuclear charge Z. Which species has the LARGEST ionic radius?
opts: All four have the same radius because they have the same electron count
why: In an isoelectronic series, the ion with the SMALLEST nuclear charge (Z) holds the 10 electrons most loosely, giving the largest radius. O²⁻ (Z=8) < F⁻ (Z=9) < Na⁺ (Z=11) < Mg²⁺ (Z=12), so O²⁻ is largest.

q: Period 2 atoms N (Z=7), O (Z=8), F (Z=9), and Ne (Z=10) are compared in their ground states at 298 K. As Zeff increases left to right across a period, atomic radius shrinks. Which of these has the SMALLEST atomic (covalent) radius?
why: Across period 2, increasing Zeff pulls electrons closer, so radius decreases. Ne, at the far right, has the highest Zeff and the smallest radius among these. Note: Ne's atomic radius is van der Waals-defined, but for periodic-trend questions it is treated as smallest in period 2.

q: Consider gas-phase atoms Na, Mg, Cl, and Ar at 298 K. Their first ionization energies (kJ/mol) are 496, 738, 1251, and 1521 respectively. Based on the periodic trend that IE rises across a period and noble gases have full octets, which has the highest first ionization energy?
why: Argon has a complete octet ([Ne]3s²3p⁶) and the highest Zeff in period 3, making it extremely difficult to ionize. Within period 3, IE rises Na < Mg < Cl < Ar, so Ar (1521 kJ/mol) has the largest first IE.

q: Metallic character increases going down a group and decreases going left to right across a period. Comparing Na, K, Mg, and Al — all of which form metallic solids at 298 K — which is the MOST metallic?
why: Metallic character increases down a group (lower IE, easier electron loss) and decreases across a period. K sits lower-left than the other three, with the lowest IE (419 kJ/mol), giving it the strongest metallic character.

q: Bond polarity is approximated by the difference in Pauling electronegativity (ΔEN) between bonded atoms; ΔEN > ~0.5 indicates a polar covalent bond. Among C-H (ΔEN = 0.4), O-H (ΔEN = 1.4), N-H (ΔEN = 0.9), and C-Cl (ΔEN = 0.5), which bond is the MOST polar?
why: Greater ΔEN means a more polar bond. O-H has ΔEN = 1.4, the largest of the choices, making it the most polar (and the basis for water's strong hydrogen bonding). At ΔEN ≥ ~1.7 the bond is generally considered ionic.

q: Solid sodium chloride melts at 801°C and conducts electricity when molten or dissolved in water. The electronegativity difference between Na (0.93) and Cl (3.16) is 2.23. What kind of bonding holds NaCl(s) together?
opts: Ionic bonds (electrostatic attraction between Na⁺ and Cl⁻)
why: ΔEN ≥ ~1.7 generally signals ionic bonding. Na (ΔEN 0.93) loses an electron to Cl (3.16), giving Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions held in a 3D lattice by Coulomb attraction. The high melting point and conductivity of the melt confirm ionic character.

q: Four molecules — CO₂, H₂O, CCl₄, and BF₃ — each contain polar covalent bonds (ΔEN > 0.4). However, only some are polar OVERALL because symmetry can cause bond dipoles to cancel. Which molecule has polar bonds AND a net molecular dipole moment?
why: A molecule is polar only if bond dipoles do not cancel by symmetry. H₂O is bent (104.5°) so its two O-H dipoles sum to a net dipole. CO₂ (linear), CCl₄ (Td), and BF₃ (trigonal planar) are symmetric, so individual bond dipoles cancel.

q: In hydrogen cyanide (H-C≡N), the central carbon forms one single bond to H and a triple bond to N. Counting one electron domain for the H-C bond and one for the C≡N triple bond (a triple bond counts as one domain), what is the hybridization of carbon in HCN?
why: Hybridization follows the number of electron domains: 2 = sp, 3 = sp², 4 = sp³. Carbon in HCN has two domains (H and N), giving sp hybridization with two unhybridized p-orbitals forming the two π-bonds of the triple bond.

q: Pure liquid HF at 20°C boils at 19.5°C, dramatically higher than HCl (−85°C) despite HF's smaller mass. The H-F bond has ΔEN = 1.9 and F has lone pairs. What is the dominant intermolecular force between two HF molecules?
opts: Hydrogen bonding (H bound to F donates to lone pair on F)
why: Hydrogen bonding requires H bonded to N, O, or F interacting with a lone pair on N, O, or F. HF satisfies both criteria, giving very strong H-bonds responsible for HF's anomalously high boiling point relative to HCl, HBr, and HI.

q: At 0°C and 1 atm, the density of ice (0.917 g/mL) is LESS than that of liquid water (0.9998 g/mL), so ice floats. This is unusual because most solids are denser than their liquids. What structural feature of ice causes this density inversion?
opts: Trapped air bubbles in the ice
An open hexagonal lattice in which each H₂O hydrogen-bonds to four others, leaving void space
Higher surface tension of ice compared to liquid water
Lower molar mass of ice molecules
Stronger London dispersion forces in ice
why: In ice, each water molecule H-bonds to exactly four neighbors in a tetrahedral, hexagonal lattice that holds molecules farther apart than the more disordered liquid. The resulting open structure makes ice ~9% less dense than liquid water.

q: You are drawing the Lewis structure of carbon dioxide (CO₂), a linear triatomic gas at 298 K and 1 atm. Carbon (group 14) contributes 4 valence electrons and each oxygen (group 16) contributes 6. What is the total number of valence electrons used in the CO₂ Lewis structure?
why: Total valence e⁻ = 4 (C) + 2(6) (O) = 16. These distribute as two C=O double bonds (8 bonding e⁻) plus two lone pairs on each O (8 lone-pair e⁻), satisfying octets on all three atoms.

q: The nitrate ion NO₃⁻ has 24 valence electrons distributed across three resonance structures, each with one N=O double bond and two N-O single bonds. Using the formal charge formula FC = V − N − B/2, what is the formal charge on the central N atom in any one resonance structure?
why: For N: V = 5 valence electrons, N (lone pair e⁻) = 0, B (bonding e⁻) = 8 (one double + two single = 4 bonds = 8 e⁻). FC = 5 − 0 − 8/2 = 5 − 4 = +1. Each single-bonded O carries −1 and the double-bonded O carries 0, summing to the −1 overall charge.

q: Ammonia (NH₃) is a trigonal pyramidal molecule with N as the central atom. Nitrogen contributes 5 valence electrons; three are used in N-H bonds. How many lone pairs reside on the central nitrogen atom in NH₃?
why: N has 5 valence electrons. Three are used in three N-H bonds, leaving 2 nonbonding electrons = 1 lone pair. This lone pair is responsible for NH₃'s pyramidal shape and its Brønsted basicity.

q: Compounds such as SF₆ (six S-F bonds) and PCl₅ (five P-Cl bonds) place more than 8 electrons around the central atom. Octet expansion requires accessible empty d-orbitals on the central atom, available only for period 3 and beyond. Which of the following CAN expand its octet?
why: Octet expansion requires available d-orbitals, which appear starting in period 3. Sulfur (period 3) can use its 3d orbitals to host >8 valence electrons (e.g., SF₆ with 12). Period 2 elements C, N, O, F have no 2d subshell and cannot expand.

q: The sulfate ion SO₄²⁻ has S as the central atom bonded to four oxygen atoms. Sulfur contributes 6 valence electrons, each oxygen contributes 6, and the 2− charge adds 2 more. What is the total number of valence electrons in the Lewis structure of SO₄²⁻?
why: Total valence e⁻ = 6 (S) + 4(6) (O) + 2 (extra electrons from 2− charge) = 32. These distribute over four S-O bonds and lone pairs on each oxygen, with formal charges minimized in resonance structures featuring two S=O double bonds.

q: Ammonia (NH₃) has a central N atom with 4 electron domains: 3 N-H bonding pairs and 1 lone pair. VSEPR predicts the ELECTRON-domain geometry as tetrahedral, but the MOLECULAR geometry refers to atom positions only. What is the molecular geometry of NH₃?
why: Four electron domains with 1 lone pair give an AX₃E geometry: trigonal pyramidal molecular shape (electron geometry tetrahedral). The lone pair pushes the three H atoms below the N, lowering H-N-H from 109.5° to ~107°.

q: Sulfur hexafluoride (SF₆) is a colorless, dense gas used as an electrical insulator. Its central S atom forms 6 S-F bonds with no lone pairs (6 electron domains). What is the molecular geometry predicted by VSEPR theory?
why: Six bonding domains with zero lone pairs is AX₆: octahedral geometry, with all F-S-F angles 90° (or 180° for trans pairs). Square planar (AX₄E₂) requires 6 domains with 2 lone pairs, not zero.

q: Sulfur tetrafluoride (SF₄) has 5 electron domains around the central sulfur: 4 bonding pairs (S-F) and 1 lone pair. The lone pair occupies an equatorial position (less repulsion). What is the molecular geometry of SF₄?
why: AX₄E with 5 total domains gives a seesaw shape (electron geometry trigonal bipyramidal). The equatorial lone pair leaves two axial F's and two equatorial F's, producing the characteristic seesaw. T-shaped (AX₃E₂) requires 2 lone pairs, not 1.

q: Liquid water at 25°C has a bent molecular geometry due to two bonding pairs and two lone pairs around oxygen (4 domains, electron geometry tetrahedral). Lone-pair–lone-pair repulsion compresses the H-O-H angle below the ideal tetrahedral 109.5°. What is the experimental H-O-H bond angle in H₂O?
why: AX₂E₂ ideal angle is 109.5°, but two lone pairs on O squeeze the H-O-H angle further than NH₃'s 107° (one lone pair). The experimental value is 104.5°. 109.5° ignores lone-pair repulsion; 107° is the NH₃ value.

q: Xenon tetrafluoride (XeF₄) has 6 electron domains around the central Xe: 4 bonding pairs and 2 lone pairs. The two lone pairs occupy opposite (trans) axial positions to minimize repulsion. What is the molecular geometry of XeF₄?
why: AX₄E₂ with 6 domains gives square planar: the two lone pairs sit trans (180° apart) on the axes, leaving the four F's in one plane at 90° to one another. Octahedral (AX₆) has no lone pairs; seesaw applies to 5-domain AX₄E.

q: A student weighs out 36.0 g of liquid water (molar mass 18.0 g/mol) at 298 K. Using the relation moles = mass / molar mass, how many moles of H₂O does this sample contain?
why: n = mass / molar mass = 36.0 g / 18.0 g·mol⁻¹ = 2.00 mol. Inverting (18/36 = 0.5) is a common slip; multiplying instead of dividing gives 648, etc. Always check that the units cancel to mol.

q: A 6.00 g graphite sample (molar mass C = 12.0 g/mol) corresponds to 0.500 mol of carbon atoms. Using Avogadro's number Nₐ = 6.02×10²³ atoms/mol, how many carbon atoms are present?
why: Atoms = moles × Nₐ = 0.500 × 6.02×10²³ ≈ 3.0×10²³. Forgetting to multiply by 0.5 (just using Nₐ) gives 6×10²³; doubling instead of halving gives 1.2×10²⁴.

q: An ideal gas at standard temperature and pressure (STP, defined as 273.15 K and 1 atm) follows PV = nRT. For 1.00 mol of gas, V = nRT/P = (1)(0.0821)(273)/(1). What is the molar volume of an ideal gas at STP?
why: V = (1 mol)(0.0821 L·atm·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹)(273 K)/(1 atm) = 22.4 L. 24.0 L applies at 25°C/1 bar (some textbooks); 11.2 L is the half-mole answer; 44.8 L is for 2 mol.

q: A balloon contains 2.00 mol of helium gas at STP (273 K, 1 atm). Using the molar volume of an ideal gas at STP (22.4 L/mol), what volume does the helium occupy?
why: V = n × 22.4 L/mol = 2.00 × 22.4 = 44.8 L. Forgetting to multiply by 2 mol leaves 22.4; multiplying by 4 mistakenly gives 89.6.

q: A small dry ice sample contains 0.250 mol of CO₂ (molar mass 44.0 g/mol) at room temperature. Using mass = moles × molar mass, what is the mass of this sample in grams?
why: Mass = 0.250 mol × 44.0 g/mol = 11.0 g. Using 1 mol instead of 0.25 gives 44.0 g; doubling gives 22.0 g; multiplying by 4 gives 176 g.

q: A 4.40 g sample of CO₂ (molar mass 44.0 g/mol) is sealed in a flask. Convert to moles, then to molecules using Nₐ = 6.02×10²³ molecules/mol. How many CO₂ molecules are in the sample?
why: n = 4.40 / 44.0 = 0.100 mol. Molecules = 0.100 × 6.02×10²³ = 6.02×10²². Skipping the mole conversion and applying Nₐ directly gives 6.02×10²³; counting atoms (not molecules) in 0.1 mol of CO₂ would give 1.8×10²³.

q: Combustion analysis of an unknown carbohydrate yields mass percentages of 40.0% C, 6.7% H, and 53.3% O. Assuming a 100 g sample (40.0 g C, 6.7 g H, 53.3 g O) and dividing each by atomic mass to find moles, what is the empirical formula?
why: Moles: C 40.0/12 = 3.33; H 6.7/1 = 6.7; O 53.3/16 = 3.33. Dividing by smallest (3.33) gives 1:2:1 → CH₂O. C₆H₁₂O₆ (glucose) is the molecular formula but not the empirical formula; the empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio.

q: A 0.500 mol sample of liquid water at 25°C contains both H and O atoms. Each H₂O molecule has 3 atoms (2 H + 1 O). Using Nₐ = 6.02×10²³ molecules/mol, how many TOTAL atoms (H plus O) are in the sample?
why: Molecules = 0.500 × 6.02×10²³ = 3.01×10²³. Each molecule has 3 atoms, so total atoms = 3 × 3.01×10²³ = 9.03×10²³. Forgetting the ×3 for atoms-per-molecule gives 3.01×10²³ (just molecules).

q: For the Haber process N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g), 28.0 g of N₂ (molar mass 28.0 g/mol) is mixed with 9.0 g of H₂ (molar mass 2.0 g/mol) at 500 K. Convert each to moles and compare to the 1:3 stoichiometric ratio. Which is the limiting reactant?
why: n(N₂) = 28/28 = 1.0 mol; n(H₂) = 9/2 = 4.5 mol. Stoichiometry needs 3 mol H₂ per 1 mol N₂, so 1.0 mol N₂ requires only 3.0 mol H₂. Excess H₂ is present, so N₂ runs out first and is limiting.

q: A combustion vessel at 600 K is charged with 4.00 mol H₂ and 1.00 mol O₂ for the reaction 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(g). Stoichiometry requires 2 mol H₂ per 1 mol O₂. Which reagent is the limiting reactant?
why: Required H₂ for 1.00 mol O₂ = 2 × 1 = 2 mol; H₂ available = 4 mol (excess). Required O₂ for 4 mol H₂ = 4/2 = 2 mol O₂, but only 1 mol is available. Therefore O₂ runs out first and limits product formation to 2 mol H₂O.

q: A synthesis predicts a theoretical yield of 50.0 g product, but only 42.5 g is isolated after recrystallization. Percent yield is defined as (actual / theoretical) × 100%. What is the percent yield of this reaction?
why: % yield = (42.5 / 50.0) × 100% = 85%. Inverting the ratio (50/42.5 ≈ 1.18) gives the >100% distractor. Yields above 100% suggest impurities or measurement error and are not physically meaningful for this problem.

q: Continuing the Haber reaction N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃ from earlier (28.0 g N₂ + 9.0 g H₂, with N₂ limiting at 1.00 mol), how many grams of NH₃ (molar mass 17.0 g/mol) are theoretically produced?
why: From 1 mol N₂, the 1:2 ratio gives 2 mol NH₃. Mass = 2.00 mol × 17.0 g/mol = 34.0 g. Using a 1:1 ratio mistakenly gives 17 g; tripling N₂'s mass gives 51 g.

q: In the same Haber problem (1.00 mol N₂ limiting; 4.5 mol H₂ initially), N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃ uses 3 mol H₂ per 1 mol N₂. After complete reaction, how many moles of H₂ remain UNREACTED?
why: H₂ consumed = 3 × 1.00 = 3.0 mol. H₂ remaining = 4.5 − 3.0 = 1.5 mol. Forgetting the 3:1 ratio gives 3.5 mol; subtracting the wrong way gives a negative or 0.5 result.

q: A chemist dissolves 0.500 mol of NaCl in enough water to make a final solution volume of 250 mL at 25°C. Using molarity M = moles solute / liters solution, what is the molar concentration of NaCl?
why: Convert 250 mL to 0.250 L. M = 0.500 mol / 0.250 L = 2.00 M. Using mL instead of L (0.500/250) gives 0.002 M; halving instead of doubling gives 0.125; failing to convert at all gives 125.

q: A laboratory dilution starts with 100 mL of 6.00 M HCl stock and dilutes it to a final concentration of 0.500 M. Using M₁V₁ = M₂V₂, what final volume V₂ (in mL) is required?
why: V₂ = M₁V₁/M₂ = (6.00)(100)/(0.500) = 1200 mL. Forgetting to invert the ratio gives 600 mL (using 6/0.5 = 12 then × 50). Always check: more dilute solution should have a LARGER volume.

q: A 1.00 m aqueous solution of KCl (which dissociates completely into K⁺ and Cl⁻, so van't Hoff factor i = 2) is prepared. Pure water freezes at 0.00°C with Kf = 1.86°C·kg/mol. Using ΔTf = i·Kf·m, what is the freezing point of this solution?
why: ΔTf = (2)(1.86)(1.00) = 3.72°C. New Tf = 0.00 − 3.72 = −3.72°C. Forgetting i = 2 (treating KCl as a nonelectrolyte) gives −1.86°C; using i = 3 gives −5.58.

q: A 0.100 M aqueous glucose solution (a nonelectrolyte, i = 1) is held at 300 K. Using van't Hoff's osmotic-pressure equation π = iMRT with R = 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K), what is the osmotic pressure π?
why: π = (1)(0.100)(0.0821)(300) = 2.46 atm. Forgetting to multiply by 0.10 (using just RT) gives 24.6; using R = 8.21 (wrong unit) gives 246; using i = 2 erroneously gives 4.93.

q: Four 1.00 m aqueous solutions are prepared at 25°C: glucose (i = 1), urea (i = 1), NaCl (i = 2), and CaCl₂ (i = 3). Freezing-point depression follows ΔTf = i·Kf·m. Which solution freezes at the LOWEST temperature?
opts: All freeze at the same temperature
why: ΔTf is proportional to i. CaCl₂ → Ca²⁺ + 2Cl⁻ gives i = 3, the largest of the choices, so it depresses Tf the most. Glucose and urea (i = 1) depress least; NaCl (i = 2) is intermediate.

q: An ethanol/water mixture is prepared from 46.0 g ethanol (MW = 46.0 g/mol) and 72.0 g water (MW = 18.0 g/mol) at 25°C. Mole fraction X(ethanol) = n(EtOH) / [n(EtOH) + n(H₂O)]. What is X(ethanol)?
why: n(EtOH) = 46/46 = 1.00 mol; n(H₂O) = 72/18 = 4.00 mol. X(EtOH) = 1.00 / (1.00 + 4.00) = 0.20. Using mass fraction (46/118 ≈ 0.39) is the classic distractor; ignoring water count gives 1.0.

q: Henry's law states C = kH·P; gas solubility in a liquid depends on partial pressure and temperature. Carbonated water loses CO₂ when warmed because gas solubility decreases with temperature. Under which conditions is gas solubility GREATEST in water?
opts: Pressure does not matter, only temperature
why: Henry's law gives C ∝ P (more pressure forces more gas in), and gas dissolution is exothermic so cooler T shifts equilibrium toward dissolution. Therefore high P and low T maximize solubility — exactly why soda is bottled cold and pressurized.

q: A 0.20 m aqueous KCl solution (i = 2 for full dissociation) has Kb = 0.52°C·kg/mol. Pure water boils at 100.00°C at 1 atm. Using ΔTb = i·Kb·m, what is the boiling point of this solution?
why: ΔTb = (2)(0.52)(0.20) = 0.208°C ≈ 0.21°C. New Tb = 100.00 + 0.21 = 100.21°C. Ignoring i = 2 gives 100.10; using i = 3 gives 100.31; the 1 m result (100.52) is the wrong-molality distractor.

q: A rigid 5.00 L tank is filled with 2.00 mol of N₂ gas at 27°C (300 K). Using the ideal-gas law PV = nRT with R = 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K), what is the pressure inside the tank?
why: P = nRT/V = (2.00)(0.0821)(300)/(5.00) = 9.85 atm. Using T = 27 K (forgetting to convert °C → K) gives ~0.89 atm; halving for 1 mol gives 4.93; doubling gives 19.7.

q: A sealed rigid container holds an ideal gas at 1.00 atm and 273 K. The container is heated to 546 K (volume held constant). Using Gay-Lussac's law P₁/T₁ = P₂/T₂, what is the new pressure?
why: P₂ = P₁ × T₂/T₁ = 1.00 × (546/273) = 2.00 atm. Doubling temperature (in K) doubles pressure at fixed V and n. Inverting the ratio gives 0.50 atm; using °C instead of K gives nonsense.

q: A piston initially holds 10.0 L of an ideal gas at 1.00 atm and 298 K. The piston is compressed isothermally (constant T) to 2.00 L. Using Boyle's law P₁V₁ = P₂V₂, what is the new pressure?
why: P₂ = P₁V₁/V₂ = (1.00 × 10.0)/2.00 = 5.00 atm. Inverting the ratio gives 0.20 atm; multiplying instead of dividing gives 20 atm. Compressing the gas raises pressure inversely with volume.

q: A 10.0 L vessel at 300 K contains a mixture of 2.00 mol N₂ and 3.00 mol Ar; the total pressure is 5.00 atm. Using Dalton's law P_i = X_i · P_total with mole fraction X(N₂) = 2/(2+3) = 0.40, what is the partial pressure of N₂?
why: X(N₂) = 2/5 = 0.40, so P(N₂) = 0.40 × 5.00 atm = 2.00 atm. Using mass ratio or swapping to Ar's mole fraction (0.60 → 3.00 atm) is the common error. The two partial pressures must sum to 5.00 atm.

q: Two ideal gases He (MW = 4.0 g/mol) and O₂ (MW = 32.0 g/mol) effuse from identical pinholes at the same temperature. Graham's law gives rate(A)/rate(B) = √(MW_B / MW_A). What is the ratio of effusion rates rate(He) : rate(O₂)?
why: rate(He)/rate(O₂) = √(32/4) = √8 ≈ 2.83. Forgetting the square root (using 32/4 = 8) gives 8:1; using the mass ratio without inversion gives 1:8. Lighter gases effuse faster.

q: Real gases deviate from ideal-gas behavior when intermolecular attractions matter (low T) and when the gas's own molecular volume is significant (high P). At which combination of conditions do real gases deviate MOST from PV = nRT?
why: Low T allows attractive forces to slow molecules and reduce pressure below ideal; high P shrinks the available free volume so molecular size matters. The two effects combine at low T, high P (e.g., near liquefaction), maximizing deviation.

q: A 2.46 L flask is filled with an ideal gas at 27°C (300 K) and 2.00 atm. Using PV = nRT with R = 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K), how many moles of gas are present in the flask?
why: n = PV/RT = (2.00)(2.46)/[(0.0821)(300)] = 4.92/24.63 ≈ 0.200 mol. Using 27 K instead of 300 K gives a huge wrong answer; halving correctly gives 0.10 mol (a one-step error).

q: Equal moles of Ne, Ar, Kr, and Xe are placed in separate flasks at the same temperature, 298 K. The kinetic theory of gases gives average translational kinetic energy as KE_avg = (3/2)kT per molecule, depending only on T. Which sample has the highest average KE per molecule?
opts: All four are equal because T is the same
why: Average KE = (3/2)kT depends ONLY on temperature, not mass. At identical T, all four gases have the same average KE per molecule. Lighter Ne moves FASTER (higher v_rms) but with the SAME average KE, since KE = ½mv² and m·v² is conserved across species at equal T.

q: A 100.0 g block of iron (specific heat capacity c = 0.450 J/(g·°C)) is heated from 25°C to 85°C, a ΔT of 60°C. Using q = m·c·ΔT, how much heat (in joules) is absorbed by the iron?
why: q = (100.0)(0.450)(60) = 2700 J. Dropping a factor of 10 (forgetting one of the multipliers) gives 270; multiplying by 100 instead of 60 gives 27000. Always include all three terms with correct units.

q: Use Hess's law to combine: (1) C(s) + ½O₂(g) → CO(g), ΔH₁ = −110 kJ/mol; (2) CO(g) + ½O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH₂ = −283 kJ/mol. Adding (1) and (2) gives C(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g). What is ΔH for this overall reaction?
why: Hess's law: ΔH_overall = ΔH₁ + ΔH₂ = (−110) + (−283) = −393 kJ/mol. Subtracting instead of adding gives −173; reversing one reaction's sign gives wrong sign. The two-step path equals the direct path because enthalpy is a state function.

q: The standard enthalpy of formation of liquid water is ΔH_f° = −286 kJ/mol at 298 K, corresponding to H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → H₂O(l). What is the enthalpy change for forming 2.00 mol of H₂O(l) from its elements at 298 K?
why: ΔH = n × ΔH_f° = 2.00 × (−286) = −572 kJ. Halving instead of doubling gives −143; flipping sign gives +572. Formation reactions release energy when ΔH_f° < 0, so 2 mol releases twice the heat.

q: Combustion of 1 mol CH₄ has ΔH_rxn = −100 kJ/mol (a hypothetical exothermic reaction). If you reverse the reaction (the products become reactants and vice versa), the magnitude of ΔH stays the same but the sign flips. What is ΔH for the reverse reaction?
why: Reversing a reaction reverses the sign of ΔH (Hess's law). ΔH_reverse = −ΔH_forward = −(−100) = +100 kJ/mol. The reverse of an exothermic reaction is endothermic with the same magnitude.

q: Combustion of glucose: C₆H₁₂O₆(s) + 6O₂(g) → 6CO₂(g) + 6H₂O(l), ΔH_combustion = −2800 kJ/mol at 298 K. A bomb calorimeter burns 0.500 mol of glucose to completion. How much heat is released?
why: Heat released = n × ΔH = 0.500 × (−2800) = −1400 kJ (1400 kJ given off). Ignoring the 0.5 factor gives −2800; doubling instead of halving gives −5600; flipping sign gives +1400.

q: Consider 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l) at 298 K. Three moles of gas (2 + 1) become 2 moles of liquid; gases have far higher entropy than liquids and the moles of gas decrease. What is the sign of ΔS for this reaction?
why: Going from 3 mol of gas to 2 mol of liquid drastically reduces positional disorder. ΔS < 0. The reaction is still spontaneous because ΔH is very negative; the −TΔS penalty is overcome at moderate T.

q: Pure ice melts at 0°C (273.15 K) and 1 atm: H₂O(s) → H₂O(l). The molecules in liquid water have more positional and translational freedom than in the rigid ice lattice. What is the sign of ΔS_system for melting?
why: Melting moves from an ordered solid to a more disordered liquid, so ΔS_system > 0. ΔS_fusion of water is +22 J/(K·mol). At equilibrium (0°C), ΔG = 0 and ΔH_fusion = TΔS_fusion.

q: Three phases of water are compared at 1 atm and their respective phase temperatures: H₂O(s) at 0°C, H₂O(l) at 50°C, and H₂O(g) at 110°C. Molar entropy generally rises with increased molecular freedom (S_solid < S_liquid < S_gas). Which phase has the HIGHEST molar entropy?
why: Gas-phase molecules have far more translational and rotational freedom than liquids or solids. Standard molar entropies: S°(ice) ≈ 41, S°(liquid) ≈ 70, S°(gas) ≈ 189 J/(K·mol). H₂O(g) wins by a wide margin.

q: Compare four reactions at 298 K. Entropy increases when (a) gas moles increase, (b) liquids/solids become gases, or (c) ions/atoms become disordered. Which reaction has the MOST POSITIVE ΔS?
why: Option B creates a new mole of gas (O₂) from liquid hydrogen peroxide — generating gas from liquid is the strongest entropy increase. Reactions A (gas→liquid), C (3 mol gas→2 mol gas), and D (gas→solid) all DECREASE entropy.

q: A reaction has ΔH = −50 kJ/mol (exothermic) and ΔS = +120 J/(K·mol) (entropy increases). Using ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, both terms favor spontaneity at any T > 0 K. At what temperatures is this reaction spontaneous?
why: When ΔH < 0 and ΔS > 0, ΔG = (negative) − T(positive) is negative for every T > 0 K. Both enthalpy and entropy drive the reaction forward, so it is spontaneous at all (positive) temperatures.

q: At exactly 0°C (273.15 K) and 1 atm, ice and liquid water are in phase equilibrium: H₂O(s) ⇌ H₂O(l). Phase equilibria require ΔG = 0 because no net change occurs. What is ΔG for ice melting at exactly 0°C?
why: At a phase transition (here 273.15 K, 1 atm), system is at equilibrium, so ΔG = 0. Above 0°C, ΔG < 0 for melting; below 0°C, ΔG > 0. At equilibrium, ΔH_fusion = TΔS_fusion exactly.

q: A reaction has ΔH = −40.0 kJ/mol and ΔS = −100 J/(K·mol). Both ΔH and ΔS are negative. Using ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, the reaction is spontaneous (ΔG < 0) only when |TΔS| < |ΔH|. Below what temperature is the reaction spontaneous?
why: Set ΔG = 0: T = ΔH/ΔS = (−40000 J)/(−100 J/K) = 400 K. Below 400 K, the −TΔS term (positive) is smaller than |ΔH|, so ΔG < 0. Watch units: convert kJ to J before dividing, otherwise you get 0.4 K (a common error).

q: For an electrochemical cell, ΔG° and E°_cell are linked by ΔG° = −nFE°_cell, where n is moles of electrons and F = 96485 C/mol. If a galvanic cell has E°_cell = 0.000 V at 298 K, what is ΔG°?
why: ΔG° = −nFE° = −n × 96485 × 0 = 0. When E° = 0 V the cell does no electrical work and the reaction sits at standard equilibrium with K = 1. Both ΔG° and E° are zero simultaneously.

q: The standard Gibbs free-energy change is related to the equilibrium constant by ΔG° = −RT ln K, where R = 8.314 J/(K·mol) and T = 298 K. If a reaction has K = 1.00 at 298 K (products and reactants equally favored), what is ΔG°?
why: ln(1) = 0, so ΔG° = −RT(0) = 0. K = 1 means standard products and reactants are equally favored; no net driving force at standard conditions. ΔG > 0 corresponds to K < 1; ΔG < 0 corresponds to K > 1.

q: An elementary-style rate law is determined experimentally to be rate = k[A]²[B] at 298 K. The initial concentrations are doubled in [A] and halved in [B]. Using the rate law, by what factor does the new rate compare to the original?
why: Rate ∝ [A]² × [B]. Doubling [A] multiplies rate by 2² = 4; halving [B] multiplies by ½. Net factor = 4 × 0.5 = 2. Forgetting the squared term gives 0.5; ignoring [B] gives 4.

q: A first-order reaction has rate constant k = 0.0693 min⁻¹ at 298 K. The half-life of a first-order reaction is given by t₁/₂ = ln(2)/k = 0.693/k. What is the half-life in minutes?
why: t₁/₂ = 0.693/0.0693 = 10.0 min. Inverting (0.0693/0.693) gives 0.1 min; using 1/k without the ln(2) factor gives 14.4 min. Half-life of a first-order reaction is INDEPENDENT of starting concentration.

q: A common rule of thumb (consistent with the Arrhenius equation k = A·exp(−Ea/RT) for typical Ea ~ 50 kJ/mol) is that doubling temperature can change k dramatically. If T rises from 298 K to 596 K, by approximately what factor does k typically change for a moderate-Ea reaction?
why: k = A·exp(−Ea/RT) is exponential in 1/T, so even modest T changes give large k changes. A common rule says rates roughly DOUBLE for every 10°C rise; doubling T to 596 K is far beyond that and routinely yields >10× rate increases.

q: A zero-order reaction has rate = k (independent of concentration). Integrating gives [A]_t = [A]_0 − kt. When [A] is plotted on the y-axis and time t on the x-axis, what shape does the plot take?
opts: A straight line with negative slope (slope = −k)
A straight line with positive slope
why: [A] = [A]₀ − kt is linear in t with slope −k (intercept [A]₀). Exponential decay is the first-order plot of [A] vs t; ln[A] vs t is linear for first order; 1/[A] vs t is linear for second order.

q: A second-order reaction has rate law rate = k[A]² with rate measured in M/s and concentration in M. Solving for k's units: k = rate/[A]² = (M/s)/M². What are the units of k for a second-order rate law?
why: k = (M·s⁻¹)/(M²) = M⁻¹·s⁻¹ for 2nd order. General rule: units of k = M^(1−n)·s⁻¹ where n is reaction order. So 0-order: M·s⁻¹; 1st: s⁻¹; 2nd: M⁻¹·s⁻¹; 3rd: M⁻²·s⁻¹.

q: A catalyst is added to a reaction at 298 K. Catalysts work by providing an alternative pathway with a different activation energy, but they do NOT change thermodynamic state functions. Which quantity does a catalyst directly affect?
why: A catalyst lowers Ea (for both forward and reverse paths equally), speeding up the approach to equilibrium without changing ΔH, ΔS, ΔG, or K. The position of equilibrium is unchanged; only kinetics improves.

q: For a reversible reaction, the energy diagram shows Ea(forward) = 50 kJ/mol and Ea(reverse) = 80 kJ/mol. Since ΔH = Ea(forward) − Ea(reverse), the reaction's overall enthalpy change can be calculated. What is ΔH for the forward reaction?
why: ΔH = Ea(fwd) − Ea(rev) = 50 − 80 = −30 kJ/mol. Negative ΔH means the forward reaction is exothermic: the products sit lower in energy than reactants by 30 kJ/mol. Adding the two Ea's (130) is the wrong operation.

q: A platinum catalyst is added to an equilibrium mixture of N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ at 700 K. The catalyst lowers Ea equally for both forward and reverse reactions, accelerating approach to equilibrium without altering K. Which way does the equilibrium position shift?
opts: Shifts left toward N₂ and H₂
why: Catalysts speed both directions equally; K is unchanged so the equilibrium position does NOT shift. The system simply reaches equilibrium faster. Only changes in T can change K.

q: Write the equilibrium constant expression for the Haber reaction N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) at 500 K. Recall: products in numerator, reactants in denominator, each raised to the power of its stoichiometric coefficient. What is Kc?
why: Kc = [products]^coeffs / [reactants]^coeffs = [NH₃]² / ([N₂][H₂]³). Forgetting the cube on H₂ gives option A; inverting the expression gives option C. Coefficients become exponents, not multipliers.

q: For the heterogeneous decomposition CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g) at 1100 K, pure solids and pure liquids are excluded from K because their activities equal 1. Only gas-phase or aqueous species appear. What is the correct Kc expression?
why: Pure solids CaCO₃ and CaO have activity = 1, so they drop out of the expression. Only the gas CO₂ remains: Kc = [CO₂]. The vapor pressure of CO₂ over the solid mixture at fixed T is therefore constant.

q: For the gaseous reaction A(g) ⇌ B(g) at 400 K with K = 5.0, the reaction quotient Q is computed from current concentrations. If Q < K, the system has too few products and must shift toward products to reach equilibrium. Which direction does the reaction shift?
why: Q < K means insufficient products; the reaction shifts forward (right) to make more products and raise Q toward K. Conversely Q > K shifts left, and Q = K means equilibrium.

q: The reaction 2A(g) ⇌ B(g) has K_forward = 4.0 at 350 K. Reversing the reaction inverts K; halving the coefficients takes the square root of K. For the REVERSE reaction B ⇌ 2A (same coefficients, opposite direction), what is the new K?
why: K_reverse = 1/K_forward = 1/4.0 = 0.25. Squaring would correspond to doubling coefficients; taking square root would correspond to halving coefficients. Equilibrium constants are never negative.

q: The Haber synthesis N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) is exothermic (ΔH = −92 kJ/mol). Le Chatelier's principle treats heat as a 'product' for exothermic reactions. If the temperature is raised from 500 K to 700 K, which way does equilibrium shift?
why: For exothermic reactions, heat is a 'product'; adding heat (raising T) drives the system toward reactants (left). Industrially, the Haber process compromises with moderate T because higher T lowers yield but raises rate.

q: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), there are 4 mol of gas on the left and 2 mol on the right. Le Chatelier: raising pressure shifts equilibrium toward the side with FEWER gas moles. If pressure is increased from 1 atm to 100 atm at 700 K, which way does equilibrium shift?
opts: Shifts left (toward N₂ + H₂, 4 mol gas)
why: Higher P favors fewer gas moles. The right side has 2 mol vs 4 mol on the left, so equilibrium shifts right toward NH₃. K_p stays constant (only T changes K), but the position shifts. This is why industrial Haber runs at high pressure.

q: An equilibrium mixture of N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) sits in a sealed rigid 10.0 L vessel. Argon (an inert gas) is injected into the vessel at constant volume. Argon does not participate in the reaction and partial pressures of N₂, H₂, NH₃ are unchanged. What happens to the equilibrium?
why: Adding inert gas at constant V leaves partial pressures (and concentrations) of all reactive species unchanged. Q is unchanged and equilibrium does not shift. Only changes that alter [reactant] or [product] (or T) shift equilibrium.

q: A weak acid HA dissociates in water: HA(aq) ⇌ H⁺(aq) + A⁻(aq). Initial [HA] = 0.10 M and Ka = 1.0×10⁻⁵ at 298 K. Setting up an ICE table with x = [H⁺] formed and using the small-x approximation Ka ≈ x²/0.10, what is the approximate [H⁺] at equilibrium?
why: x² = Ka × C = (1.0×10⁻⁵)(0.10) = 1.0×10⁻⁶. x = √(1.0×10⁻⁶) = 1.0×10⁻³ M = [H⁺]. Forgetting the square root gives 10⁻⁶; setting [H⁺] = Ka gives 10⁻⁵.

q: In a weak-acid ICE table at 298 K, we often use the simplification 'C − x ≈ C', where C is the initial concentration and x is the amount dissociated. The 5% rule states this approximation introduces acceptable error only when x is below a critical fraction of C. Under what condition is the 5% rule valid?
why: If x is less than 5% of initial C, then C − x ≈ C introduces less than 5% error in [HA] and the simplification is acceptable. For x ≥ 5% of C (typical when Ka is 'large' or C is 'small'), solve the quadratic instead.

q: Acetic acid is dissolved in water at 25°C: CH₃COOH ⇌ H⁺ + CH₃COO⁻ with Ka = 1.8×10⁻⁵ and initial [CH₃COOH] = 0.10 M. Setting up the ICE table with the small-x approximation x²/0.10 ≈ 1.8×10⁻⁵, what is [H⁺] at equilibrium?
A 0.001 M (1×10⁻³ M) solution of HCl, a strong acid, fully dissociates in water at 25°C so [H⁺] = 1×10⁻³ M. Using pH = −log[H⁺], what is the pH of this solution?
why: pH = −log(1×10⁻³) = 3. Confusing the molarity with [H⁺] log gives pH = 1; using the wrong sign or pOH gives 11. Strong acids fully dissociate so [H⁺] equals the formal HCl concentration (above the autoionization regime).

q: A blood-like sample at 25°C is measured to have pH = 8.3. Using the relation pH + pOH = 14.00 in pure water at 25°C (since Kw = 1.0×10⁻¹⁴), what is the pOH of this sample?
why: pOH = 14.00 − pH = 14.00 − 8.3 = 5.7. Adding instead of subtracting gives 22.3; setting pOH = pH gives 8.3. The relation only holds at 25°C where Kw = 1.0×10⁻¹⁴.

q: Acetic acid has Ka = 1.8×10⁻⁵ at 25°C. The conjugate base, acetate ion (CH₃COO⁻), has Kb such that Ka × Kb = Kw = 1.0×10⁻¹⁴. What is Kb for acetate?
why: Kb = Kw / Ka = (1.0×10⁻¹⁴) / (1.8×10⁻⁵) = 5.56×10⁻¹⁰. Forgetting Kw and just inverting Ka gives 5.6×10⁴ (wrong magnitude); confusing exponents gives 5.6×10⁻⁹.

q: For a conjugate acid-base pair at 25°C in water, the relation Ka × Kb = Kw (where Kw = 1.0×10⁻¹⁴) leads to a logarithmic identity. Taking −log of both sides gives pKa + pKb = pKw. What numerical value does pKa + pKb sum to at 25°C?
why: −log(Ka·Kb) = −log(Kw) = −log(10⁻¹⁴) = 14. Therefore pKa + pKb = 14 at 25°C. The same identity holds for pH + pOH = 14 in any aqueous solution at 25°C.

q: A blood plasma sample at 37°C has pH = 4.50 (an unusually acidic test sample). Using the inverse relation [H⁺] = 10^(−pH), what is the hydrogen-ion concentration in mol/L?
why: [H⁺] = 10^(−4.50) = 10^(−5) × 10^(0.50) = 1.0×10⁻⁵ × 3.16 ≈ 3.2×10⁻⁵ M. Rounding the half-decade incorrectly toward 10⁻⁴ or 10⁻⁵ alone is the common error; pH 4.50 lies BETWEEN these orders of magnitude.

q: The seven common strong acids on the DAT list are HCl, HBr, HI, HNO₃, H₂SO₄, HClO₃, and HClO₄. Anything not on this list is treated as weak. Among HCl, HBr, HF, and HClO₄, which is the WEAK acid?
why: HF is NOT on the strong-acid list; despite being a hydrohalic acid, the strong H-F bond keeps it from full dissociation in water (Ka ≈ 6.6×10⁻⁴). HCl, HBr, and HClO₄ all fully dissociate and are strong acids.

q: A 0.10 M aqueous solution of acetic acid (CH₃COOH, Ka = 1.8×10⁻⁵) at 25°C reaches equilibrium. Using the small-x approximation x² ≈ Ka × C, find [H⁺], then take pH = −log[H⁺]. What is the pH?
why: x² = (1.8×10⁻⁵)(0.10) = 1.8×10⁻⁶; x = 1.34×10⁻³ M = [H⁺]. pH = −log(1.34×10⁻³) ≈ 2.87. pH = 1.0 would only apply to a strong acid; pH = 4.74 is the pKa, not the pH of 0.10 M acid.

q: DAT general chemistry expects students to memorize the standard list of strong acids that fully dissociate in water at 25°C: HCl, HBr, HI, HNO₃, H₂SO₄, HClO₃, and HClO₄. How many strong acids appear on this standard DAT list?
why: The seven strong acids are HCl, HBr, HI, HNO₃, H₂SO₄, HClO₃, and HClO₄. Memorizing this list lets you immediately identify any other acid (HF, acetic, formic, HCN, H₃PO₄, etc.) as weak by elimination.

q: Four salts are dissolved separately in water at 25°C to give 0.10 M solutions. NaCH₃COO produces Na⁺ (neutral) and CH₃COO⁻ (conjugate base of weak acetic acid, hydrolyzes to give OH⁻). NH₄Cl gives an acidic solution; NaCl and KNO₃ give neutral solutions. Which salt produces a BASIC solution?
why: Conjugate base of a weak acid (acetate from acetic) hydrolyzes water: CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COOH + OH⁻, raising pH. NH₄Cl gives the conjugate acid of a weak base (acidic). Salts of strong acid + strong base (NaCl, KNO₃) are neutral.

q: The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation is pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]). When the log term equals zero (i.e., the ratio [A⁻]/[HA] is unity), pH equals pKa. This is the optimum buffering condition. Under what concentration condition is pH = pKa?
opts: At the equivalence point of titration
why: log(1) = 0, so pH = pKa whenever [A⁻] = [HA]. This is also the half-equivalence point of a weak-acid titration and the point of maximum buffering capacity.

q: A buffer is prepared with 0.20 M acetic acid (HA) and 0.10 M sodium acetate (A⁻) at 25°C; pKa(acetic) = 4.74. Using Henderson-Hasselbalch pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]), what is the pH of this buffer?
why: log(0.10/0.20) = log(0.5) = −0.30. pH = 4.74 + (−0.30) = 4.44. Since [HA] > [A⁻], pH must be below pKa. Inverting the ratio gives 5.04 (a sign error).

q: A buffer initially contains 0.10 mol/L HA and 0.10 mol/L A⁻ (pKa = 5.00, pH = 5.00). 0.010 mol/L of strong acid (H⁺) is added. The H⁺ converts A⁻ to HA: new [A⁻] = 0.090 M, new [HA] = 0.110 M. Using Henderson-Hasselbalch, what is the new pH?
why: log(0.090/0.110) = log(0.818) = −0.087. pH = 5.00 + (−0.087) ≈ 4.91. The buffer absorbs H⁺ with only a small drop. Without buffer, adding 0.01 M H⁺ to neutral water would crash pH to 2.

q: You need to prepare a buffer holding pH ≈ 4.7 for an enzyme assay at 25°C. Optimal buffer choice has pKa within ±1 unit of the target pH. Choose from acetate (pKa 4.74), phosphate (pKa 7.20), bicarbonate (pKa 6.35), and ammonia (pKa 9.25). Which is best?
why: Best buffer has pKa closest to the desired pH. Acetate's pKa = 4.74 is within 0.04 units of pH 4.7 — essentially perfect. The other choices (pKa 6.35, 7.20, 9.25) are too high and would not buffer effectively at pH 4.7.

q: 25.0 mL of 0.100 M acetic acid (weak acid, Ka = 1.8×10⁻⁵) is titrated with 0.100 M NaOH (strong base) to the equivalence point at 25°C. At equivalence the only species present is the conjugate base CH₃COO⁻, which hydrolyzes to give a basic solution. What is the pH at equivalence?
why: At equivalence, all HA has been converted to A⁻. A⁻ is a weak base that hydrolyzes water: A⁻ + H₂O ⇌ HA + OH⁻, so the solution is basic (pH > 7). For weak acid + strong base, equivalence pH is always > 7.

q: During titration of a weak acid HA with strong base NaOH, the half-equivalence point is reached when exactly half the HA has been neutralized so [HA] = [A⁻]. Plugging this into Henderson-Hasselbalch makes log(1) = 0. What is the pH at half-equivalence?
why: At half-equivalence, [HA] = [A⁻], so pH = pKa + log(1) = pKa + 0 = pKa. This makes the half-equivalence point a key way to determine pKa experimentally — read pH directly off the titration curve at half the equivalence volume.

q: Sulfurous acid H₂SO₃ is a diprotic weak acid with Ka₁ ≈ 1.4×10⁻² and Ka₂ ≈ 6.3×10⁻⁸. When titrated with NaOH, each successive H⁺ is neutralized, producing one equivalence point per acidic proton. How many distinct equivalence points appear in the titration of H₂SO₃ with NaOH?
why: Diprotic acids show two equivalence points (one for each H⁺): the first removes H⁺ from H₂SO₃ to form HSO₃⁻, the second removes H⁺ from HSO₃⁻ to form SO₃²⁻. Each pKa corresponds to a half-equivalence and each titrated H⁺ to an equivalence.

q: Barium sulfate dissolves slightly: BaSO₄(s) ⇌ Ba²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) with Ksp = 1.0×10⁻¹⁰ at 25°C. Letting molar solubility = s, then [Ba²⁺] = [SO₄²⁻] = s and Ksp = s². What is the molar solubility s of BaSO₄ in pure water?
why: s² = 1.0×10⁻¹⁰, so s = √(1.0×10⁻¹⁰) = 1.0×10⁻⁵ M. Forgetting the square root gives 10⁻¹⁰. Each ion is at concentration s = 10⁻⁵ M.

q: AgCl is dissolved in 0.10 M NaCl at 25°C; Ksp(AgCl) = 1.8×10⁻¹⁰. By the common-ion effect, [Cl⁻] ≈ 0.10 M is fixed by NaCl. Setting Ksp = [Ag⁺][Cl⁻] and solving for [Ag⁺] = molar solubility s, what is the solubility of AgCl in this solution?
why: s = Ksp / [Cl⁻] = (1.8×10⁻¹⁰) / 0.10 = 1.8×10⁻⁹ M. Solubility in pure water would be √Ksp ≈ 1.34×10⁻⁵; the common-ion 0.10 M Cl⁻ suppresses dissolution by ~10⁴×.

q: Silver chromate dissociates as Ag₂CrO₄(s) ⇌ 2Ag⁺(aq) + CrO₄²⁻(aq). Letting molar solubility = s, the ion concentrations become [Ag⁺] = 2s and [CrO₄²⁻] = s. Building the Ksp expression with stoichiometric coefficients as exponents, what is Ksp in terms of s?
why: Ksp = [Ag⁺]²[CrO₄²⁻] = (2s)²(s) = 4s²·s = 4s³. Forgetting the coefficient 2 in (2s)² gives s³; the 27s⁴ form applies to MX₃ (one M³⁺ and three X⁻) salts.

q: In a galvanic (voltaic) cell, spontaneous redox occurs and electrical work is delivered to the external circuit. Reduction occurs at the cathode (cations gain electrons), and the cathode is the positive terminal in a galvanic cell. Which statement correctly describes the galvanic cathode?
why: Mnemonic: 'red cat' — REDuction at the CAThode. In a GALVANIC cell, the cathode is positive (cations migrate toward it). In an ELECTROLYTIC cell the cathode is negative; reduction still happens there but the polarity flips.

q: A standard Daniell cell is constructed: Zn|Zn²⁺(1 M) || Cu²⁺(1 M)|Cu at 25°C. Standard reduction potentials: Zn²⁺/Zn E° = −0.76 V, Cu²⁺/Cu E° = +0.34 V. Cu (higher E°_red) is the cathode; Zn is the anode. Using E°_cell = E°_cathode − E°_anode, what is E°_cell?
why: E°_cell = E°(cathode) − E°(anode) = (+0.34) − (−0.76) = +1.10 V. Adding the magnitudes (0.34 + 0.76 = 1.10) is equivalent here because subtracting a negative is adding. Positive E° means spontaneous galvanic operation.

q: In a Zn/Cu galvanic cell at 25°C, oxidation produces electrons at the Zn anode that travel through the external wire to the Cu cathode where reduction occurs. Cations migrate through the salt bridge to balance charge. In which direction do electrons flow externally?
opts: No external flow; only ions move
why: Electrons always travel from anode to cathode through the external wire (the anode is the source of electrons because oxidation occurs there). In the salt bridge, cations move toward the cathode and anions move toward the anode to maintain charge neutrality.

q: Standard reduction potentials at 25°C: F₂ + 2e⁻ → 2F⁻ (+2.87 V), Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻ (+1.36 V), Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na (−2.71 V), Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Zn (−0.76 V). The strongest oxidizing agent has the most positive E°_red. Which is the strongest oxidizer?
why: Most positive E°_red ⇒ greatest tendency to be reduced ⇒ strongest oxidizer. F₂ at +2.87 V is the strongest oxidizing agent of any neutral species — it readily strips electrons from almost any reductant.

q: Standard reduction potentials at 25°C: Li⁺/Li (−3.04 V), Na⁺/Na (−2.71 V), Zn²⁺/Zn (−0.76 V). The strongest REDUCING agent (best electron donor) has the most NEGATIVE E°_red, since the reverse oxidation is most spontaneous. Which is the best reducer?
why: Most negative E°_red ⇒ reverse oxidation has most positive E°_ox ⇒ strongest reducing agent. Li at −3.04 V is the strongest reducer among common metals, which is why lithium is used in high-voltage batteries despite its reactivity challenges.

q: Cu metal is added to a 0.10 M AgNO₃ solution at 25°C. Standard reduction potentials: Ag⁺/Ag = +0.80 V, Cu²⁺/Cu = +0.34 V. The candidate reaction is Cu(s) + 2Ag⁺(aq) → Cu²⁺(aq) + 2Ag(s); E°_cell = E°(Ag⁺/Ag) − E°(Cu²⁺/Cu). Will this reaction proceed spontaneously?
why: E°_cell = (+0.80) − (+0.34) = +0.46 V. Positive E°_cell means the reaction is spontaneous as written: Cu reduces Ag⁺. ΔG° = −nFE° = −2(96485)(0.46) ≈ −89 kJ, well below zero.

q: A Zn/Cu galvanic cell (E°_cell = +1.10 V, n = 2) operates at 25°C with [Cu²⁺] = 0.010 M and [Zn²⁺] = 1.00 M. Q = [Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺] = 100. Use the Nernst equation E = E° − (0.0592/n) log Q. What is the cell potential E?
why: E = 1.10 − (0.0592/2)·log(100) = 1.10 − (0.0296)(2) = 1.10 − 0.0592 ≈ 1.04 V. Lower [Cu²⁺] reduces the driving force, so E < E°. Using n = 1 instead of 2 gives 0.98; flipping Q's numerator/denominator gives 1.16.

q: A galvanic cell discharges over time at 25°C until the reaction reaches equilibrium and Q approaches K. Using the Nernst equation E = E° − (0.0592/n) log Q, and noting that at equilibrium ΔG = 0 corresponds to E = 0, what is the cell potential when Q = K?
why: At equilibrium Q = K and ΔG = 0, so the cell does no further work: E = 0. Equivalently, E° = (0.0592/n) log K, so when Q = K the Nernst expression gives E = E° − E° = 0. A 'dead battery' is at this point.

q: Uranium-238 (²³⁸₉₂U) undergoes alpha decay, emitting an α particle (⁴₂He nucleus). Alpha decay reduces mass number by 4 and atomic number by 2. The resulting daughter nuclide is determined by ²³⁸₉₂U → α + ⁴⁻ᵐZ. Which is the daughter?
why: Alpha decay: A decreases by 4 (238 → 234), Z decreases by 2 (92 → 90). Z = 90 is thorium, so the daughter is ²³⁴₉₀Th. Forgetting to change Z gives ²³⁴U; β decay (Z+1) gives ²³⁴Pa instead.

q: A radioactive isotope follows first-order decay with half-life t₁/₂. After n half-lives, the fraction of the original sample remaining is (1/2)ⁿ. What fraction remains after exactly 3 half-lives?
why: Fraction remaining = (1/2)³ = 1/8. After 1 half-life: 1/2. After 2: 1/4. After 3: 1/8. Confusing 'after n half-lives' with '1/n' gives 1/3; squaring instead of cubing gives 1/4.

q: Carbon-14 (¹⁴₆C) decays to nitrogen-14 (¹⁴₇N) with a half-life of 5730 years. The mass number stays at 14, but the atomic number rises from 6 to 7. This is achieved by converting a neutron into a proton plus a beta particle. What kind of decay is this?
why: β⁻ decay: a neutron becomes a proton (Z increases by 1) plus an emitted electron (β⁻), with A unchanged. ¹⁴C → ¹⁴N + β⁻ + ν̄ fits exactly. β⁺ would DECREASE Z; α decreases Z by 2; γ doesn't change A or Z.

q: Three forms of ionizing radiation differ greatly in penetration: α particles (helium nuclei, stopped by paper), β particles (high-speed electrons/positrons, stopped by aluminum foil), and γ rays (high-energy photons, requiring lead/concrete shielding). Which is the MOST penetrating?
why: γ rays are massless, chargeless, high-energy photons that interact only weakly with matter, requiring thick lead or concrete to attenuate them. α particles are stopped by paper; β by a few mm of aluminum. Order of penetration: γ >> β >> α.

q: A student places 18.0 g of ice initially at -20°C (253 K) into an open container and heats it at constant 1 atm until it becomes superheated steam at 130°C (403 K). Using c_ice = 2.09 J/g·°C, c_water = 4.18 J/g·°C, c_steam = 2.03 J/g·°C, ΔH_fus = 334 J/g, and ΔH_vap = 2260 J/g, what is the total heat absorbed?
why: Sum five steps: q = m·c·ΔT for each phase plus m·ΔH for each transition. Numerically: 18(2.09)(20) + 18(334) + 18(4.18)(100) + 18(2260) + 18(2.03)(30) ≈ 0.75 + 6.01 + 7.52 + 40.7 + 1.10 ≈ 56 kJ. The vaporization step dominates because breaking all hydrogen bonds requires far more energy than warming or fusion.

q: A 50.0 g sample of pure benzene is heated steadily at 1 atm and its temperature is recorded. The graph rises from 60°C, then stays exactly at 80.1°C for several minutes while heat continues to flow in, and only afterward begins climbing again. What does the flat plateau represent?
opts: A phase change occurring at constant temperature
Loss of mass from the system
why: During a phase transition, all incoming heat goes to overcoming intermolecular forces (q = m·ΔH_vap), not to raising kinetic energy, so T is invariant. Once the last molecule of liquid converts to vapor, the temperature can rise again. The plateau length is proportional to the latent heat ΔH_vap of the substance.

q: For water at 1 atm, ΔH_fus = 6.01 kJ/mol while ΔH_vap = 40.7 kJ/mol — vaporization requires roughly 6.8× more energy than fusion. What is the molecular reason for this large difference?
opts: The mass of the sample changes between the two transitions
Vaporization must break essentially all hydrogen bonds, while fusion only loosens the lattice without fully separating molecules
Fusion is exothermic while vaporization is endothermic
The two enthalpies refer to different substances
Only vaporization involves a change in entropy
why: Going solid→liquid only disrupts the long-range crystalline order; molecules remain in close contact with most IMFs intact. Going liquid→gas separates molecules to ~1000× greater distances, requiring complete rupture of hydrogen bonds. Hence ΔH_vap >> ΔH_fus for hydrogen-bonded liquids like H₂O.

q: Methane (CH₄) is the simplest alkane. Its central carbon is bonded to four hydrogen atoms with H-C-H bond angles of 109.5°, giving a perfectly tetrahedral geometry as predicted by VSEPR. What hybridization of the carbon orbitals accounts for these four equivalent σ bonds?
why: Steric number = bonds + lone pairs = 4 + 0 = 4, which corresponds to sp³ hybridization (mixing one 2s and three 2p orbitals). The four sp³ hybrid orbitals point to the corners of a tetrahedron at 109.5°, matching the observed geometry of CH₄.

q: Ammonia (NH₃) has a trigonal pyramidal molecular geometry with H-N-H bond angles of 107°, slightly compressed from the ideal tetrahedral angle. The central nitrogen carries one lone pair in addition to its three N-H σ bonds. What is its hybridization?
why: Steric number = 3 bonds + 1 lone pair = 4, requiring sp³ hybridization. The lone pair occupies one sp³ orbital and exerts greater repulsion than bonding pairs, compressing the H-N-H angle from 109.5° to about 107°.

q: Carbon dioxide (O=C=O) is a linear molecule (180°) found in the atmosphere at ~420 ppm. The central carbon participates in two double bonds with no lone pairs of its own. What hybridization is required at carbon to accommodate two σ bonds and two π bonds in this geometry?
why: Steric number at C = 2 σ bonds + 0 lone pairs = 2, giving sp hybridization. The two sp orbitals form σ bonds at 180° to the oxygens, while the two unhybridized 2p orbitals form the two π bonds (one with each oxygen).

q: Acetylene (H−C≡C−H) is the linear hydrocarbon used in welding torches that produces flames near 3100°C in oxygen. Counting the C≡C triple bond and both C−H bonds, how many π bonds are present in one molecule of acetylene?
why: Each triple bond consists of one σ + two π bonds, while each single bond is purely σ. Acetylene therefore has 3 σ bonds (2 C-H + 1 C-C σ) and 2 π bonds, both within the C≡C unit. The carbons are sp hybridized, leaving two perpendicular 2p orbitals to overlap into the two π bonds.

q: Xenon tetrafluoride (XeF₄) is a square planar molecule with F-Xe-F angles of 90°. The central xenon has four Xe-F σ bonds and two lone pairs that occupy axial positions to minimize lone-pair/lone-pair repulsion. What hybridization is assigned to the xenon?
why: Steric number at Xe = 4 bonds + 2 lone pairs = 6, requiring sp³d² hybridization (octahedral electron geometry). The two lone pairs sit trans to each other (axial), leaving the four fluorines in a square plane with 90° bond angles.

q: Liquid water at 25°C has an unusually high boiling point (100°C) and high heat capacity (4.18 J/g·°C) for such a small, light molecule (MW = 18 g/mol). Considering the O-H bonds and the lone pairs on oxygen, what is the dominant intermolecular force between two H₂O molecules?
why: Hydrogen bonding occurs when H is covalently bound to N, O, or F and interacts with a lone pair on another N/O/F atom. Each water molecule can donate 2 H-bonds and accept 2, forming an extensive 3D network — this gives water its anomalously high boiling point relative to H₂S, H₂Se, or H₂Te.

q: When comparing argon (Ar), hydrogen chloride (HCl), and water (H₂O) in the gas phase at 25°C and 1 atm, only one type of intermolecular force is shared by all three substances despite their differing polarities. Which force is universally present in every molecule and atom?
why: London dispersion forces arise from instantaneous, transient dipoles created by electron-cloud fluctuations and exist in every species. Polar molecules also have dipole-dipole forces, and only N/O/F-bound hydrogens give H-bonds, but dispersion is the universal floor.

q: At 1 atm, four substances have boiling points to identify: He (4 g/mol), CH₄ (16 g/mol, nonpolar), HCl (36.5 g/mol, polar), and H₂O (18 g/mol, H-bonding). Rank them from lowest to highest normal boiling point.
why: He (-269°C) and CH₄ (-161°C) only have weak London forces, with He smallest. HCl (-85°C) adds a dipole-dipole component. H₂O (100°C) has hydrogen bonding, which dominates and pushes its BP far above the heavier HCl, giving He < CH₄ < HCl < H₂O.

q: Hydrogen fluoride (HF, MW = 20) boils at 19.5°C, while hydrogen chloride (HCl, MW = 36.5) boils at -85°C. HCl is nearly twice as massive — by simple London-force reasoning it 'should' boil higher. Why does HF actually boil over 100°C higher than HCl?
opts: HF forms strong hydrogen bonds (F-H···F); HCl does not because Cl is too large/diffuse
HCl is ionic in the liquid state
Their boiling points are actually equal at 1 atm
HF has much greater London dispersion than HCl
why: Hydrogen bonding requires H bonded to N, O, or F. F's small size and high electronegativity give a very strong, localized H-bond network in HF; Cl's larger and less electronegative atom does not meet the H-bond criterion. The H-bond energy easily outweighs the London advantage HCl gets from its higher mass.

q: Four pure liquids are in identical sealed flasks at 25°C: pentane (C₅H₁₂, BP 36°C), diethyl ether ((C₂H₅)₂O, BP 35°C), ethylene glycol (HOCH₂CH₂OH, BP 197°C), and acetone ((CH₃)₂CO, BP 56°C). Which liquid will exhibit the LOWEST equilibrium vapor pressure at 25°C?
opts: All four have the same vapor pressure
why: Vapor pressure varies inversely with intermolecular force strength: stronger IMFs hold molecules in the liquid more effectively. Ethylene glycol has TWO -OH groups per molecule, enabling a dense H-bond network, so its boiling point is highest (197°C) and its vapor pressure at 25°C is lowest of the four.

q: A 100.0 g sample of liquid water in an insulated coffee-cup calorimeter is heated from 20.0°C to 45.0°C using a small immersion heater. Given the specific heat capacity of water c = 4.18 J/g·°C, how much heat (q) was absorbed by the water?
why: Apply q = m·c·ΔT with m = 100.0 g, c = 4.18 J/g·°C, ΔT = 25.0°C. q = 100 × 4.18 × 25 = 10,450 J ≈ 10.45 kJ. A common error is forgetting to multiply by mass, which gives the much smaller 1045 J distractor.

q: A 200.0 g iron block (c_Fe = 0.45 J/g·°C) and a 50.0 g sample of water (c_H₂O = 4.18 J/g·°C) each receive exactly 1000 J of heat from identical heaters. Assuming no heat loss, which sample undergoes the larger temperature increase?
opts: Both rise by exactly the same amount
Cannot tell without knowing initial T
why: From q = m·c·ΔT, ΔT = q/(m·c). For iron: ΔT = 1000/(200·0.45) = 11.1°C; for water: ΔT = 1000/(50·4.18) = 4.78°C. Iron's much smaller heat capacity (m·c product) means the same energy raises its temperature more than twice as much.

q: A 200.0 g block of iron at 100.0°C (c_Fe = 0.45 J/g·°C) is dropped into 100.0 g of water at 20.0°C (c_H₂O = 4.18 J/g·°C) in a perfectly insulated calorimeter. Assuming no heat loss to the container, what is the final equilibrium temperature?
why: Set heat lost by Fe = heat gained by H₂O: m_Fe·c_Fe·(T_f - 100) + m_w·c_w·(T_f - 20) = 0. → 90(T_f-100) + 418(T_f-20) = 0 → 508 T_f = 17,360 → T_f ≈ 34.2°C. Water's much larger m·c product pulls the final temperature toward water's initial value.

q: Combustion of 1.0 g of methane in an open container releases 55.6 kJ of heat to the surroundings, warming a beaker of water. From the perspective of the reacting methane (the system), what is the sign of q for this exothermic process?
why: By IUPAC convention, q > 0 means heat flows INTO the system and q < 0 means heat flows OUT of the system. An exothermic reaction releases heat from system to surroundings, so q_system is negative. Equivalently, ΔH < 0 for exothermic reactions at constant pressure.

q: A 0.500 g sample of benzoic acid is combusted in a sealed bomb calorimeter (constant volume) with heat capacity C_cal = 5.00 kJ/°C. The combustion releases 2.50 kJ of heat, all absorbed by the calorimeter assembly. What temperature change ΔT does the calorimeter experience?
why: For a bomb calorimeter, q_rxn = -C_cal·ΔT. Solving for ΔT: ΔT = q_absorbed/C_cal = 2.50 kJ / 5.00 kJ/°C = 0.500°C. Note that constant-volume calorimetry uses the calorimeter constant C_cal directly, not m·c, since C_cal already lumps in all components.

q: Argon (Z = 18) has the noble-gas configuration [Ne] 3s² 3p⁶ with 18 electrons. Among the following common ions, identify the one that is BOTH isoelectronic with Ar AND carries a +2 charge.
why: Isoelectronic with Ar means 18 electrons. Ca has Z = 20 and protons = 20; Ca²⁺ has lost 2 electrons → 18 e⁻, matching Ar. K⁺ and S²⁻ are also 18-electron species but carry +1 and -2 charges respectively, failing the +2 requirement.

q: Chromium (Z = 24) is one of two well-known first-row transition metals (the other being Cu) that violate the Aufbau rule. Instead of the predicted [Ar] 4s² 3d⁴ configuration, its actual ground-state configuration places only one electron in the 4s orbital. What is the correct ground-state electron configuration of neutral Cr?
why: A half-filled 3d⁵ subshell has extra exchange-energy stability, so promoting one 4s electron to 3d gives the lower-energy configuration [Ar] 4s¹ 3d⁵. This makes Cr's six valence electrons all unpaired (one in 4s, five in 3d).

q: Compare the second ionization energies (IE₂, the energy to remove an electron from M⁺) of Na (Z=11), Mg (Z=12), Al (Z=13), and K (Z=19). The first IE removes a valence electron, but the second IE may need to penetrate a noble-gas core. Which of these elements has the LARGEST IE₂?
why: Na⁺ has the [Ne] noble-gas configuration; removing a 2p electron requires breaking a closed shell, costing ≈4560 kJ/mol. Mg⁺ and Al⁺ still have valence electrons (3s, 3p), so their IE₂ values (1450, 1820 kJ/mol) are far smaller. K⁺ is also closed-shell ([Ar]), but its 3p electrons are farther out than Na's 2p, giving K a smaller IE₂ than Na.

q: Compare the carbon-carbon bond lengths in ethane (H₃C-CH₃, single bond), ethene (H₂C=CH₂, double bond), ethyne (HC≡CH, triple bond), and benzene (delocalized, bond order 1.5). Higher bond order means more shared electron density and stronger attraction. Which compound has the SHORTEST C-C bond?
why: Bond length decreases as bond order increases because more electron density between the nuclei pulls them closer. Triple bond (3) < benzene (1.5) < double (2) ordering of bond order: actually 3 > 2 > 1.5 > 1, so ethyne (~120 pm) < ethene (~134 pm) < benzene (~140 pm) < ethane (~154 pm).

q: Sulfur trioxide (SO₃) is trigonal planar with one S=O double bond and two S-O single bonds in any single Lewis structure. The actual molecule has three equivalent S-O bonds of bond order 4/3 ≈ 1.33. How many equivalent resonance structures contribute to the SO₃ resonance hybrid?
why: Each resonance structure places the S=O double bond at a different one of the three oxygens. Since there are three equivalent positions for the double bond, there are exactly 3 resonance structures. Averaging gives a bond order of (1+1+2)/3 = 4/3 per S-O bond.

q: A pharmacist measures out 4.50 g of pure water (H₂O, MW = 18.0 g/mol). Avogadro's number is 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹. How many individual hydrogen atoms are present in this sample?
why: Moles H₂O = 4.50/18.0 = 0.250 mol. Each H₂O contains 2 H atoms, so mol H = 0.500. Atoms H = 0.500 × 6.022×10²³ ≈ 3.0 × 10²³. The factor-of-2 stoichiometric step (H per H₂O) is the most common error point.

q: An ideal gas sample is initially at P₁ = 2.00 atm, T₁ = 300 K (27°C), and V₁ = 5.00 L in a sealed cylinder. The cylinder is heated to T₂ = 600 K (327°C) and the gas is allowed to expand against a piston to V₂ = 10.0 L. What is the final pressure P₂?
why: Use combined gas law: P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂ → P₂ = P₁(V₁/V₂)(T₂/T₁) = 2.00 × (5/10) × (600/300) = 2.00 × 0.5 × 2 = 2.00 atm. The doubling of T exactly cancels the doubling of V, so pressure is unchanged.

q: A chemist observes that a particular reaction proceeds spontaneously at every temperature she tries — both at 100 K and at 1000 K. Recall that ΔG = ΔH - TΔS, and spontaneity requires ΔG < 0. Which combination of signs of ΔH and ΔS guarantees spontaneity at all temperatures?
why: ΔG = ΔH - TΔS must be negative for all T > 0. If ΔH < 0 (exothermic, favors spontaneity) AND ΔS > 0 (entropy increases, -TΔS contributes another negative term), then ΔG is negative regardless of T. The other sign combinations are temperature-dependent or never spontaneous.

q: A second-order reaction A → products has rate law: rate = k[A]² with k = 0.500 M⁻¹·s⁻¹. The initial concentration is [A]₀ = 0.200 M. Using the half-life expression t₁/₂ = 1/(k[A]₀) for second-order kinetics, calculate the time required for [A] to fall to 0.100 M.
why: For a second-order reaction, t₁/₂ = 1/(k·[A]₀) = 1/(0.500 × 0.200) = 1/0.100 = 10 s. Note that unlike first-order, the second-order half-life DEPENDS on [A]₀, so subsequent half-lives get progressively longer.

q: For the gas-phase equilibrium 2 NO₂(g) ⇌ N₂O₄(g) at 298 K, the equilibrium constant in terms of concentrations is K_c = 4.7 M⁻¹. Using K_p = K_c·(RT)^Δn with R = 0.0821 L·atm/mol·K and Δn = (1 − 2) = -1, calculate K_p at 298 K.
why: Δn = mol gas products - mol gas reactants = 1 - 2 = -1. K_p = K_c·(RT)^Δn = 4.7 × (0.0821 × 298)^(-1) = 4.7 / 24.5 ≈ 0.19. Negative Δn means K_p < K_c whenever RT > 1, as it always is at room temperature.

q: The endothermic dissociation PCl₅(g) ⇌ PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g) has ΔH > 0. A sealed reaction vessel containing this equilibrium at 500 K is then cooled to 350 K with no change in volume. According to Le Châtelier's principle, in which direction does the equilibrium shift?
why: For an endothermic reaction, heat acts as a 'reactant' on the left side. Cooling removes heat (a reactant), so the equilibrium shifts in the direction that releases heat — the reverse (exothermic) direction. K also decreases as T drops for endothermic reactions (van't Hoff).

q: A 25.0 mL aliquot of 0.100 M acetic acid (CH₃COOH, K_a = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵) is titrated with 0.100 M NaOH. At the half-equivalence point, exactly half the acid has been converted to its conjugate base, so [HA] = [A⁻]. What is the pH of the solution at this point?
why: At half-equivalence, the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation pH = pK_a + log([A⁻]/[HA]) reduces to pH = pK_a since [A⁻] = [HA] makes log(1) = 0. pK_a = -log(1.8×10⁻⁵) = 4.74, so pH = 4.74.

q: The Daniell cell Zn|Zn²⁺(1 M)‖Cu²⁺(1 M)|Cu has a standard cell potential E°cell = +1.10 V at 25°C, with n = 2 electrons transferred per mole of reaction. Using ΔG° = -n·F·E°cell with F = 96,485 C/mol, calculate ΔG° in kJ/mol.
why: ΔG° = -n·F·E°cell = -(2)(96,485 C/mol)(1.10 V) = -212,267 J/mol ≈ -212 kJ/mol. The negative sign confirms spontaneity, consistent with E°cell > 0. Sign errors and forgetting the factor of n are the main error modes.

q: A 100.0 mg sample of a radioactive isotope is monitored over time and the remaining mass is measured as 12.5 mg. Using the relation m_t = m_0·(1/2)^n where n is the number of half-lives elapsed, determine n.

Silver chromate (Ag₂CrO₄) dissolves slightly in pure water according to Ag₂CrO₄(s) ⇌ 2 Ag⁺(aq) + CrO₄²⁻(aq). Given K_sp = 1.1 × 10⁻¹² at 25°C, calculate the molar solubility s (mol/L) of Ag₂CrO₄ in pure water.
why: If s = solubility, then [Ag⁺] = 2s and [CrO₄²⁻] = s, so K_sp = (2s)²(s) = 4s³. Solving: s³ = K_sp/4 = 2.75×10⁻¹³, s = (2.75×10⁻¹³)^(1/3) ≈ 6.5×10⁻⁵ M. Forgetting the (2s)² stoichiometric factor gives the much smaller 1.0×10⁻⁶ trap.

q: A particular chlorine isotope is written in standard notation as ³⁵₁₇Cl, where the subscript 17 is the atomic number Z and the superscript 35 is the mass number A. The number of neutrons N in any nuclide is given by N = A − Z. How many neutrons are present in this isotope?
why: Mass number A = protons + neutrons, so neutrons = A − Z = 35 − 17 = 18. Cl-35 has 17 protons (defining it as chlorine), 18 neutrons, and 17 electrons in the neutral atom.

q: A particular isotope of carbon contains 6 protons in its nucleus and 8 neutrons. This isotope is radioactive and used in carbon dating with a half-life of 5,730 years. Recall that mass number A = protons + neutrons. What is the mass number of this isotope?
why: Mass number A = Z + N = 6 + 8 = 14. The isotope is ¹⁴C, the radiocarbon used in dating organic remains. Its 6 protons identify it as carbon; its 8 (rather than 6) neutrons make it neutron-rich and unstable.

q: Phosphorus has atomic number Z = 15 and is found in phosphate groups of DNA and ATP. Following the Aufbau principle (1s 2s 2p 3s 3p ...), Hund's rule, and the Pauli exclusion principle, what is the ground-state electron configuration of neutral P?
why: Total of 15 electrons: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p³, abbreviated as [Ne] 3s² 3p³. The three 3p electrons each occupy a separate p orbital with parallel spins (Hund's rule), giving 3 unpaired electrons.

q: Neutral iron (Fe, Z = 26) has a ground-state electron configuration of [Ar] 4s² 3d⁶. The six 3d electrons distribute across five degenerate 3d orbitals according to Hund's rule (maximize parallel spins before pairing). How many unpaired electrons does Fe have?
why: Distribute 6 d-electrons in 5 orbitals: ↑↓ ↑ ↑ ↑ ↑. After all five are singly occupied (5 unpaired), the 6th electron pairs with one of them, leaving 4 unpaired electrons. The 4s² electrons are all paired and contribute 0 unpaired.

q: Neutral sulfur (S, Z = 16) has 16 protons and 16 electrons. The sulfide ion S²⁻ is formed when neutral S accepts two additional electrons to complete its valence shell, achieving the [Ar] noble-gas configuration. How many electrons are in S²⁻?
why: Neutral S has 16 e⁻. The 2- charge means S has gained 2 electrons, so total = 16 + 2 = 18 electrons. S²⁻ is isoelectronic with argon (Ar, Z = 18) and has the closed-shell configuration [Ne] 3s² 3p⁶.

q: Nitrogen (Z = 7) has the ground-state configuration 1s² 2s² 2p³, with the three 2p electrons singly occupying the p_x, p_y, and p_z orbitals (Hund's rule, parallel spins). Using m_l = -1, 0, +1 for the 2p orbitals filled in order, what set (n, l, m_l, m_s) describes the LAST (highest-energy) electron added?
why: Hund's rule fills the 2p orbitals in order m_l = -1, 0, +1, all with the same spin (+½ by convention). The 7th electron is the third 2p electron, occupying m_l = +1 with m_s = +½. n = 2 (second shell), l = 1 (p subshell).

q: An element X in the fourth period has the ground-state electron configuration [Ar] 4s² 3d¹⁰ 4p³. Counting electrons: 18 (Ar core) + 2 + 10 + 3 = 33. Identify element X by its atomic number.
why: Total electrons = 18 + 2 + 10 + 3 = 33, so Z = 33, which is arsenic (As). The 4p³ valence configuration places As in group 15 (pnictogens) of the periodic table, just below P.

q: In the hydrogen emission spectrum, the Lyman series corresponds to electronic transitions from upper levels n ≥ 2 down to n = 1, with the largest energy gap (and shortest wavelength) of any series. Photons in this series have wavelengths between 91 and 122 nm. In which region of the electromagnetic spectrum does the Lyman series fall?
why: The Lyman series wavelengths (91–122 nm) fall in the ultraviolet range (10–400 nm). The Balmer series (n→2) is in the visible region; Paschen and beyond (n→3, n→4) emit in the infrared. Higher-energy transitions correspond to shorter wavelengths.

q: Naturally occurring chlorine consists of two isotopes: ³⁵Cl with mass 34.97 amu at 75.0% abundance and ³⁷Cl with mass 36.97 amu at 25.0% abundance. Using the weighted-average formula AW = Σ(fᵢ · mᵢ), what is the average atomic mass of Cl reported on the periodic table?
why: Average atomic mass = (0.750 × 35) + (0.250 × 37) = 26.25 + 9.25 = 35.5 amu. The 75/25 abundance ratio places Cl's average mass closer to 35 (the more abundant) but not exactly at 35.

q: Copper (Cu, Z = 29) is one of the well-known anomalies in the Aufbau filling order. Rather than [Ar] 4s² 3d⁹, Cu's ground-state configuration is [Ar] 4s¹ 3d¹⁰ because a fully filled 3d¹⁰ subshell is exceptionally stable. How many electrons are in the 3d subshell of neutral Cu?
why: Cu's actual ground-state configuration is [Ar] 4s¹ 3d¹⁰, with a fully-filled d-subshell. Verify: 18 (Ar) + 1 + 10 = 29 ✓. The full d¹⁰ shell gives extra exchange-energy stability that beats the predicted 4s² 3d⁹.

q: Atomic radius decreases left-to-right across a period because the increasing effective nuclear charge (Z_eff) pulls the same shell of valence electrons inward. Among the second-period elements Be (Z=4), B (Z=5), C (Z=6), and N (Z=7), all in the n = 2 shell, which has the SMALLEST atomic radius?
why: All four are in row 2, so the same n applies, and the radius depends on Z_eff. As Z increases (4 → 7) without adding shells, Z_eff increases and the radius shrinks. N (largest Z) therefore has the smallest atomic radius among the four.

q: Electronegativity (EN) generally increases left-to-right and bottom-to-top on the periodic table, peaking in the upper-right corner (excluding noble gases). Pauling's scale assigns F = 4.0, O = 3.4, N = 3.0, C = 2.6. Among C, N, O, and F, which element has the HIGHEST electronegativity?
why: Fluorine has the highest electronegativity of any element on the Pauling scale (4.0). Its small radius and 7 valence electrons give it an enormous attraction for an additional electron in any covalent bond. Order: F > O > N > C.

q: Consider the iso-electronic series N³⁻, O²⁻, F⁻, and Na⁺ — each species has exactly 10 electrons (Ne configuration). However, the proton counts differ: 7, 8, 9, and 11 respectively. With more protons attracting the same 10 electrons, the radius shrinks. Which species is the LARGEST?
opts: All four are the same size
why: In an isoelectronic series, ionic radius decreases as nuclear charge (Z) increases because more protons pull the 10 e⁻ cloud tighter. N³⁻ has the fewest protons (Z = 7) and therefore the weakest pull, giving it the largest radius. Order: N³⁻ > O²⁻ > F⁻ > Na⁺.

q: Argon (Z = 18, IE₁ = 1521 kJ/mol) has a higher first ionization energy than its left-neighbor chlorine (Z = 17, IE₁ = 1251 kJ/mol), even though Ar has more electrons. What is the chemical reason for this trend?
opts: Ar has more total electrons (mass effect)
Ar has a stable, fully-filled 3p⁶ octet; removing an electron disrupts a closed shell
Ar has a larger atomic radius than Cl
Cl is a metal and Ar is a nonmetal
There is no actual difference in IE₁
why: Argon's [Ne] 3s² 3p⁶ configuration is exceptionally stable; ionizing it disrupts the noble-gas octet, requiring extra energy. Cl, missing one electron from this octet, gives up an electron more easily. Ionization energy generally increases left-to-right but spikes at noble gases.
