q: Electron affinity (EA) measures the energy released when a gas-phase atom gains an electron — the more negative EA, the more favorable the addition. Among the halogens F (-328 kJ/mol), Cl (-349), Br (-325), and I (-295), which has the MOST negative electron affinity?
why: Despite F being smaller and seeming to attract electrons more strongly, its 2p subshell is so compact that adding an electron causes significant electron-electron repulsion, slightly destabilizing F⁻. Cl⁻ (3p subshell) avoids this crowding, giving Cl the most negative EA among the halogens.

q: First ionization energy (IE₁) generally decreases down a group because the outermost electron sits in a larger, higher-n orbital that is farther from the nucleus and more shielded by inner shells. Among the alkali metals Li (520 kJ/mol), Na (496), K (419), and Rb (403), which has the LOWEST IE₁?
why: Going down group 1 (Li → Na → K → Rb), the valence ns electron occupies a progressively larger orbital and is shielded by more inner-shell electrons. The valence electron in Rb (5s¹) is the easiest to remove, giving Rb the lowest IE₁ of the four.

q: Comparing the first ionization energies of N (Z = 7, [He] 2s² 2p³) and O (Z = 8, [He] 2s² 2p⁴), the periodic trend predicts O > N because O has higher Z_eff. However, experimental values give IE₁(N) = 1402 kJ/mol and IE₁(O) = 1314 kJ/mol — N is HIGHER. Why?
opts: Nitrogen, because removing an electron disrupts its half-filled 2p³ stability
Oxygen, because it has higher Z_eff
Cannot be determined without more data
Nitrogen has a larger atomic radius
why: Nitrogen's half-filled 2p³ subshell has extra exchange-energy stability, so removing one electron costs more than the trend predicts. Oxygen's 2p⁴ has a paired electron in one p orbital; removing it relieves some pair repulsion, lowering IE₁ below the simple trend.

q: A bond between two atoms with electronegativity difference ΔEN is classified using the rules: ΔEN < 0.4 nonpolar covalent, 0.4 ≤ ΔEN < 1.7 polar covalent, ΔEN ≥ 1.7 ionic. The H-Cl bond has ΔEN = |3.0 - 2.1| = 0.9. What classification corresponds to ΔEN = 0.5?
why: ΔEN = 0.5 falls in the polar covalent range (0.4–1.7). One atom pulls bonding electron density partially toward itself (creating δ+/δ- partial charges), but no full electron transfer occurs as in ionic bonding. Examples: C-O (0.9), C-N (0.5), N-H (0.9).

q: Pure copper metal Cu(s) at 25°C and 1 atm has a face-centered cubic lattice in which each Cu atom contributes its 4s¹ valence electron to a delocalized 'sea' of electrons that moves freely throughout the solid, conferring high electrical conductivity. What type of bonding holds the lattice together?
why: Metallic bonding involves a lattice of metal cations held together by a delocalized sea of valence electrons. This explains characteristic metal properties: high electrical/thermal conductivity, malleability, ductility, and metallic luster. Cu is a textbook example.

q: The polarity of a covalent bond is set by the electronegativity difference ΔEN. Pauling values: H = 2.1, F = 4.0, Cl = 3.0, Br = 2.8, I = 2.5. Calculate ΔEN for each H-X bond and identify the MOST polar.
why: ΔEN values: H-F = 1.9, H-Cl = 0.9, H-Br = 0.7, H-I = 0.4. Largest ΔEN = most polar bond, so H-F is the most polar. Within the halide series, polarity decreases down the group as halogen EN drops.

q: Carbon tetrachloride (CCl₄) contains four C-Cl polar bonds (ΔEN ≈ 0.5). The molecule is tetrahedral with bond angles of 109.5°. Considering the vector sum of the four bond dipoles arranged tetrahedrally, what is the net molecular polarity of CCl₄?
why: Although each C-Cl bond is polar, the four bond dipoles point symmetrically toward the corners of a tetrahedron and cancel exactly by vector addition. The net molecular dipole moment is zero, making CCl₄ nonpolar despite having polar bonds.

q: Single-bond dissociation energies (kJ/mol) at 25°C: C-C ≈ 348, C-N ≈ 308, C-O ≈ 360, C-F ≈ 488, C-Cl ≈ 328. Bond strength generally increases with bond polarity (greater ΔEN) and shorter bond length. Which single bond is the STRONGEST?
why: C-F has both high polarity (ΔEN = 1.5) and a short bond length (~138 pm) due to F's small radius, giving the highest single-bond dissociation energy (~488 kJ/mol). The bond strength order C-F > C-O > C-C > C-Cl > C-N reflects competing electronegativity, atomic size, and bond length effects.

q: Nitrate ion (NO₃⁻) has three equivalent resonance structures, each containing one N=O double bond and two N-O single bonds. Bond order is calculated as (total bonds shared) / (number of equivalent bonds). What is the average N-O bond order in NO₃⁻?
why: Total π and σ bond character distributed over 3 equivalent N-O positions: each O has bond order (1+1+2)/3 = 4/3 ≈ 1.33. All three N-O bonds in NO₃⁻ are equivalent in length and strength because of resonance delocalization.

q: Hydrogen fluoride HF (MW = 20, BP = 19.5°C) boils at a much higher temperature than hydrogen chloride HCl (MW = 36.5, BP = -85°C), even though HCl is nearly twice as massive — heavier molecules typically have stronger London forces. What is the dominant explanation?
opts: Strong hydrogen bonding in HF (F is small and highly electronegative); HCl cannot H-bond effectively
HCl is ionic at room temperature
HF is much denser than HCl
why: Hydrogen bonding requires H bonded to N, O, or F. F's small radius and high EN allow strong, focused H-bonds in HF, making it a hydrogen-bond-rich liquid. HCl lacks these conditions; only weaker dipole-dipole and London forces apply, so it remains a gas at RT.

q: Bond dissociation energies for typical carbon-carbon bonds: C-C ≈ 348 kJ/mol, C=C ≈ 614 kJ/mol, C≡C ≈ 839 kJ/mol; for the C-H bond of methane, BDE ≈ 413 kJ/mol. Bond strength rises with bond order. What is the correct bond-strength ranking?
opts: All four bonds are similar in strength
why: Numerically: C-H (413) < C=C (614) < C≡C (839) kJ/mol. A C-H single bond is weaker than the multiply-bonded C=C and C≡C because higher bond orders share more electron density between the carbons. Increasing bond order also shortens the bond and raises BDE.

q: Diatomic fluorine F₂ consists of two fluorine atoms (EN = 4.0 each) sharing one σ bond. Apply ΔEN = 4.0 - 4.0 = 0.0 to classify the bond using the rules: ΔEN < 0.4 nonpolar covalent, 0.4 ≤ ΔEN < 1.7 polar, ΔEN ≥ 1.7 ionic.
why: Two identical atoms always have ΔEN = 0, giving a perfectly nonpolar covalent bond. The bonding electrons are shared equally between the two fluorine nuclei. All homonuclear diatomics (H₂, N₂, O₂, F₂, Cl₂, etc.) are nonpolar.

q: Drawing the Lewis structure of water (H₂O) requires the total number of valence electrons. Hydrogen (group 1) contributes 1 valence electron each, and oxygen (group 16) contributes 6. Sum these to find the total valence electron count for H₂O.
why: Total valence e⁻ = 2(1 H) + 6 (O) = 8. These eight electrons make up the two O-H bonding pairs (4 e⁻) plus the two lone pairs on oxygen (4 e⁻), giving a complete octet on O.

q: Methane (CH₄) is the simplest alkane with one carbon bonded to four hydrogens. Carbon (group 14) has 4 valence electrons; each hydrogen (group 1) has 1. What is the total number of valence electrons used to draw the Lewis structure of CH₄?
why: Total valence e⁻ = 4 (C) + 4(1 H) = 8 electrons. All 8 electrons are used as four C-H bonding pairs. Carbon achieves an octet, and each H satisfies the duet rule.

q: Phosphorus trichloride (PCl₃) has a trigonal pyramidal molecular geometry similar to NH₃, with P-Cl bonds at angles near 100°. Phosphorus (group 15) contributes 5 valence electrons, and three Cl atoms each form one bond. After drawing the structure, how many lone pairs reside on the central P?
why: P has 5 valence e⁻; using 3 of them in three P-Cl σ bonds leaves 2 electrons (one lone pair) on phosphorus. Steric number = 3 bonds + 1 lone pair = 4 (sp³, tetrahedral electron geometry, trigonal pyramidal molecular geometry).

q: In the most common Lewis structure of sulfate (SO₄²⁻), sulfur is the central atom bonded to four oxygens, with two of the bonds drawn as S=O and two as S-O⁻ (single bonds with formal -1 on those O atoms). Using FC = (valence e⁻) - (lone pair e⁻) - ½(bonding e⁻), calculate the formal charge on sulfur.
why: Sulfur has 6 valence e⁻, 0 lone pair e⁻, and shares 12 bonding e⁻ (2 double bonds = 4 + 2 single bonds = 4, total = 8 around S, but bonding electrons = 12). Wait: bonds = 2(S=O, 4e⁻) + 2(S-O, 2e⁻ each) = 8 + 4 = 12 bonding e⁻. FC = 6 - 0 - ½(12) = 6 - 6 = 0.

q: In a typical organic compound such as methane CH₄ or any alkyl group, a carbon with four single bonds and no lone pairs (saturated, sp³) has the standard organic 'normal' valence. Apply the formula FC = (valence e⁻) − (lone-pair e⁻) − ½(bonding e⁻) to compute the formal charge of this C.
why: Carbon has 4 valence e⁻; with 4 bonds and 0 lone pairs, lone-pair e⁻ = 0 and bonding e⁻ = 8. FC = 4 - 0 - ½(8) = 4 - 4 = 0. This is the canonical neutral organic carbon (4 bonds, no lone pairs).

q: Phosphate (PO₄³⁻) is a key biochemical anion found in DNA, ATP, and bones. Phosphorus contributes 5 valence electrons, each of the four oxygens contributes 6, and the 3- charge adds 3 more electrons. Calculate the total valence electrons for drawing PO₄³⁻.
why: Total valence e⁻ = 5 (P) + 4(6 O) + 3 (charge) = 5 + 24 + 3 = 32 electrons. These distribute as four P-O bonds (some drawn as P=O), oxygen lone pairs, and the three formal negative charges.

q: The Lewis structure of water shows oxygen as the central atom bonded to two hydrogens through O-H σ bonds. Oxygen (group 16) brings 6 valence electrons; two are used for the two O-H bonds. How many lone pairs remain on the central oxygen?
why: Oxygen has 6 valence e⁻; using 2 in O-H bonds (1 e⁻ to each bond) leaves 4 nonbonding electrons = 2 lone pairs. Steric number = 2 bonds + 2 LP = 4 (sp³), giving the bent molecular geometry with 104.5° H-O-H angle.

q: Boron trifluoride (BF₃) is a Lewis acid because boron's three valence electrons form three B-F bonds, leaving boron with only 6 electrons in its valence shell rather than the usual octet. How many electrons does the central boron have around it in this structure?
why: B forms 3 B-F bonds (3 × 2 e⁻ = 6 bonding electrons around B) and has 0 lone pairs. Total around B = 6 electrons (sextet, not an octet). The empty p-orbital on B is what allows BF₃ to accept an electron pair from a Lewis base.

q: Carbonate (CO₃²⁻) is trigonal planar with three equivalent C-O bonds of bond order 4/3 in the resonance hybrid. Each Lewis structure has one C=O and two C-O⁻. By placing the double bond at each of the three oxygens in turn, how many equivalent resonance structures does CO₃²⁻ have?
why: There are exactly 3 equivalent resonance structures, one for each oxygen taking the C=O role. Averaging gives bond order (1+1+2)/3 = 4/3 per C-O bond, explaining why all three C-O bonds in CO₃²⁻ are experimentally identical in length.

q: Chlorine trifluoride (ClF₃) is a powerful fluorinating agent with a T-shaped molecular geometry and F-Cl-F angles near 87°. The central Cl has 7 valence electrons, forms 3 Cl-F σ bonds, and has remaining electrons distributed as lone pairs in equatorial positions of a trigonal bipyramid. How many lone pairs are on Cl?
why: Cl contributes 7 e⁻; 3 are used in the three Cl-F σ bonds, leaving 4 e⁻ = 2 lone pairs. Steric number = 3 + 2 = 5 (sp³d, trigonal bipyramidal electron geometry). The two LPs go equatorial, producing the T-shaped molecular geometry.

q: Carbon dioxide (O=C=O) has a central carbon with two double bonds to oxygen and zero lone pairs on C. VSEPR theory predicts geometry by counting electron domains around the central atom (each double bond counts as one domain). What is the molecular shape of CO₂?
why: Steric number on C = 2 bonding domains + 0 lone pairs = 2, which gives linear electron and molecular geometry with 180° bond angle. Despite each C=O being polar, the symmetric linear arrangement makes CO₂ a nonpolar molecule overall.

q: Methane CH₄ has a central carbon with four C-H σ bonds and no lone pairs. VSEPR gives a steric number of 4 with all bonding domains, producing a perfectly tetrahedral molecular geometry. What is the H-C-H bond angle in CH₄?
why: Four equivalent bonding domains around carbon spread out to 109.5° to minimize electron-pair repulsion — this is the ideal tetrahedral angle. Carbon is sp³ hybridized in CH₄.

q: Water (H₂O) has a central oxygen with 2 O-H bonds and 2 lone pairs. The lone pairs occupy more space than bonding pairs and compress the H-O-H angle below the ideal tetrahedral 109.5°. What is the experimentally measured H-O-H bond angle in water?
why: Steric number = 4 (2 bonds + 2 LP), so electron geometry is tetrahedral but molecular shape is bent. The two lone pairs exert greater repulsion than bond pairs, compressing the H-O-H angle from 109.5° to ~104.5°.

q: Sulfur tetrafluoride SF₄ has a central S with 4 σ bonds to F and one lone pair. Steric number = 5, so the electron geometry is trigonal bipyramidal. The lone pair preferentially occupies an equatorial position to minimize 90° interactions. What is the resulting molecular shape?
why: With 4 bonds + 1 LP (sp³d), the LP goes equatorial to minimize close 90° contacts. The remaining 4 F atoms form a 'see-saw' (disphenoidal) shape: two axial F at 180° and two equatorial F at ~120°. Compare ClF₃ (3 bonds + 2 LP = T-shape).

q: Phosphorus pentachloride PCl₅ in the gas phase has a central P bonded to 5 Cl atoms with no lone pairs. The 5 P-Cl bonds spread to form three equatorial bonds at 120° and two axial bonds at 90° to the equatorial plane. What is the molecular geometry?
why: Steric number = 5 (5 bonds + 0 LP), giving sp³d hybridization and trigonal bipyramidal molecular geometry. Three equatorial bonds (120° apart) plus two axial bonds (180° to each other, 90° to equatorial).

q: Among the molecules CO₂ (linear), BF₃ (trigonal planar), CH₂Cl₂ (tetrahedral), and CCl₄ (tetrahedral), each contains polar bonds. Yet only some are net polar molecules. Which of these molecules has individual polar bonds AND a non-zero net dipole moment?
why: Symmetric arrangements (CO₂ linear, BF₃ trig planar, CCl₄ tetrahedral with identical substituents) cause bond dipoles to cancel — net nonpolar. CH₂Cl₂ has two different substituents (2 H and 2 Cl) on a tetrahedral C, so the dipoles do NOT cancel — net polar.

q: Three sp³ molecules — CH₄ (109.5°, 0 LP), NH₃ (~107°, 1 LP), H₂O (~104.5°, 2 LP) — share the same parent tetrahedral electron geometry but differ by lone-pair count. Lone pairs exert stronger repulsion than bonding pairs, compressing the bond angle. Rank the bond angles from smallest to largest.
why: Each lone pair compresses the bond angle. CH₄ (0 LP, 109.5°), NH₃ (1 LP, 107°), H₂O (2 LP, 104.5°). The order from smallest to largest is H₂O < NH₃ < CH₄, i.e., more lone pairs → more compression → smaller angle.

q: Benzene (C₆H₆) is a planar, hexagonal aromatic ring with all C-C bond lengths equal (~140 pm) due to delocalization of 6 π electrons. Each carbon is bonded to two other carbons and one hydrogen, with one π bond's-worth of contribution per carbon. What is the hybridization of carbon in benzene?
why: Each carbon in benzene has 3 σ bonds (2 C-C + 1 C-H) and 0 lone pairs, giving steric number 3 → sp² hybridization. The three sp² hybrids form σ bonds at 120°; the unhybridized p orbital perpendicular to the ring overlaps with the others to form the delocalized π system.

q: In water (H₂O), the central oxygen has 2 O-H σ bonds and 2 lone pairs of electrons. VSEPR predicts a tetrahedral electron geometry with bond angles compressed to ~104.5°. What hybridization at oxygen accommodates 4 electron domains?
why: Steric number on O = 2 σ bonds + 2 lone pairs = 4. This requires sp³ hybridization (one 2s + three 2p = four sp³ orbitals). Two sp³ orbitals form O-H bonds, the other two hold lone pairs.

q: Hydrogen cyanide HCN is a linear, sp-hybridized molecule with structure H-C≡N. The C≡N triple bond consists of one σ + two π bonds, while the H-C bond is a single σ bond. Count and identify the total number of σ and π bonds in HCN.
why: H-C is a single bond (1 σ); C≡N is a triple bond (1 σ + 2 π). Totals: σ = 1 + 1 = 2; π = 0 + 2 = 2. Hence HCN has 2 σ bonds and 2 π bonds. Both C and N are sp hybridized in this linear molecule.

q: For principal quantum number n = 2, the allowed l values are 0 (s) and 1 (p). The 2s subshell has 1 orbital and the 2p subshell has 3 orbitals (m_l = -1, 0, +1). Sum these to find the total number of orbitals in the n = 2 shell.
why: Total orbitals in shell n = n². For n = 2: 2² = 4 orbitals (one 2s + three 2p). Each holds at most 2 electrons (Pauli), so the n = 2 shell can hold up to 8 electrons total.

q: The 4d subshell has principal quantum number n = 4 and angular momentum quantum number l = 2. The number of orbitals in any subshell is (2l + 1), and each orbital holds at most 2 electrons by the Pauli exclusion principle. What is the maximum number of electrons that the 4d subshell can hold?
why: Number of d-orbitals = 2l+1 = 2(2)+1 = 5. Each orbital holds 2 e⁻, so the 4d subshell holds 5 × 2 = 10 electrons maximum. This applies to ALL d-subshells (3d, 4d, 5d, ...).

q: A green photon emitted by a sodium-vapor lamp has frequency ν = 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Using Planck's relation E = hν with Planck's constant h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s, calculate the energy of one photon at this frequency.
why: E = hν = (6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s) × (5.0 × 10¹⁴ s⁻¹) = 3.313 × 10⁻¹⁹ J ≈ 3.31 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. This corresponds to ~600 nm wavelength (yellow-orange light, similar to sodium D-lines).

q: Identifying significant figures: leading zeros (before the first nonzero digit) are NEVER significant; trailing zeros after a decimal point ARE significant. Apply these rules to the measured concentration value 0.0030 mol/L. How many significant figures does this number contain?
why: The leading zeros (0.00...) are placeholders only and do not count. The '3' is significant, and the trailing '0' after the decimal IS significant. Total = 2 significant figures. In scientific notation: 3.0 × 10⁻³.

q: When multiplying or dividing measured values, the result must carry the same number of significant figures as the input with the FEWEST sig figs. Calculate 1.50 × 4.0 (where 1.50 has 3 sf and 4.0 has 2 sf) and express the answer with the correct number of significant figures.
why: Numerical product: 1.50 × 4.0 = 6.00 (raw). Sig-fig limit: minimum of (3 sf, 2 sf) = 2 sf. Therefore the answer must be reported as 6.0 (2 sig figs). Writing '6' alone implies 1 sig fig; '6.00' implies 3.

q: When ADDING measured values, the result must be rounded to the same DECIMAL PLACE as the input with the fewest decimals (not fewest sig figs). Compute 25.34 + 1.2 + 0.123 and report with correct precision.
why: Sum = 26.663. The least precise addend is 1.2 (one decimal place), so the sum must be rounded to one decimal place: 26.663 → 26.7. Addition uses decimal places (not sig figs); multiplication uses sig figs.

q: Solid sodium chloride NaCl(s) has a face-centered cubic lattice in which Na⁺ cations and Cl⁻ anions are held together by strong electrostatic attraction (~787 kJ/mol lattice energy). What type of force describes the attraction between Na⁺ and Cl⁻ in the crystal?
why: Ionic bonding (Coulombic attraction between full + and - charges) holds NaCl together with very high lattice energy. Although called an 'intramolecular' bond in molecular substances, in a salt the ionic attraction is the dominant force between ions in the lattice.

q: Methane CH₄ is a perfectly tetrahedral, nonpolar molecule (all bond dipoles cancel by symmetry). It has no permanent dipole, no acidic H, and is not ionic. Considering two CH₄ molecules in liquid methane at -161°C, what is the dominant intermolecular force between them?
why: Nonpolar molecules can ONLY exhibit London dispersion forces, which arise from instantaneous, induced dipoles in their electron clouds. CH₄'s low boiling point (-161°C) reflects how weak London forces are for a small, light molecule.

q: London dispersion forces increase with the number of electrons (polarizability), which generally tracks atomic mass. For the noble gases He (4 g/mol, BP -269°C), Ar (40 g/mol, BP -186°C), and Xe (131 g/mol, BP -108°C), which has the HIGHEST normal boiling point?
why: Larger noble gases have more electrons and more polarizable electron clouds, leading to stronger London dispersion forces and higher BP. Order: He (-269°C) < Ar (-186°C) < Xe (-108°C). Xe is highest because of its 54 electrons vs 2 in He.

q: The principle 'like dissolves like' states that polar solvents (water) dissolve polar/H-bonding solutes, while nonpolar solvents dissolve nonpolar solutes. Of the following, which is MOST soluble in water at 25°C?
why: Methanol (CH₃OH) has a polar O-H bond that can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds with water; it is fully miscible with water. The alkanes (hexane, octane, diesel, cyclohexane) cannot H-bond and do not have permanent dipoles, so they are essentially insoluble.

q: Vapor pressure varies INVERSELY with intermolecular force strength: weaker IMFs allow molecules to escape into the gas phase more easily. Among water (BP 100°C, H-bond), ethanol (BP 78°C, H-bond), pentane (BP 36°C, London only), and octane (BP 126°C, London only), which has the HIGHEST vapor pressure at 25°C?
why: Lowest BP correlates with highest vapor pressure at room T. Pentane (BP 36°C, only London forces, small molecule) is closest to its boiling point at 25°C and therefore has the highest vapor pressure (~520 mmHg). Octane is heavier, water and ethanol have H-bonding.

q: Water (H₂O, MW = 18) is a liquid at room temperature, while hydrogen sulfide (H₂S, MW = 34) is a gas — even though H₂S is heavier and would seem to have stronger London forces. What is the underlying reason for this anomaly?
opts: H₂O can form strong O-H···O hydrogen bonds; H₂S cannot (S is too large/less electronegative)
H₂S and H₂O have different volumes
H₂O is a metal but H₂S is not
H₂S has more electrons so more London force
why: Hydrogen bonding requires H bonded to N, O, or F. Sulfur is below this electronegativity threshold and too large for the focused dipole. H₂O has extensive H-bonding (raising BP to 100°C); H₂S has only weak dipole-dipole forces (BP -60°C, hence a gas at RT).

q: Intermolecular forces vary in strength depending on the charge distribution of the interacting species. Approximate relative strengths (kJ/mol): London (1-10), dipole-dipole (5-25), hydrogen bond (10-40), ion-dipole (40-600). Rank these from WEAKEST to STRONGEST in general.
why: General IMF strength order (weakest → strongest): London < dipole-dipole < hydrogen bond < ion-dipole. Ion-dipole is the strongest IMF (think Na⁺ in water hydration), since it involves a full charge interacting with a partial charge.

q: A small dry-ice fragment has a mass of 22.0 g of solid CO₂ at -78°C. Carbon dioxide has a molar mass MW = 44.0 g/mol (12 + 2×16). Using moles = mass/MW, calculate the number of moles of CO₂ in the fragment.
why: n = m/MW = 22.0 g / 44.0 g/mol = 0.500 mol. A common error is to compute 22/44 = 2 (inverted); always set up the dimensional analysis as g · (1 mol/g) so units work out to mol.

q: A chemist needs exactly 0.250 mol of metallic sodium (Na, atomic mass 23.0 g/mol) for an organic synthesis. Using mass = n × MW, calculate the mass of sodium required.
why: Mass = n × MW = 0.250 mol × 23.0 g/mol = 5.75 g of Na. The other choices represent forgetting the 0.250 multiplier (23 g for 1 mol), doubling errors (11.5, 46.0), or misreading the molar mass.

q: Standard temperature and pressure (STP) is defined as 273.15 K and 1 atm. Under these conditions, the ideal gas law (PV = nRT) gives a universal molar volume V_m = 22.4 L/mol for any ideal gas. What volume does 1.00 mol of O₂ gas occupy at STP?
why: From PV = nRT at STP: V = nRT/P = 1 × 0.0821 × 273 / 1 = 22.4 L. The 22.4 L/mol value applies to ANY ideal gas at STP (O₂, N₂, He, CO₂, etc.) and is independent of identity.

q: A jeweler's gold sample contains 0.500 mol of Au atoms. Avogadro's constant N_A = 6.022 × 10²³ atoms/mol. Use atoms = n × N_A to compute the number of Au atoms in the sample.
why: Atoms = n × N_A = 0.500 × 6.022 × 10²³ = 3.011 × 10²³ atoms. Half of Avogadro's number = 3.011 × 10²³. Memorize: 1 mol = 6.022 × 10²³ particles, regardless of identity.

q: Sodium hydroxide (NaOH) is a strong base used in many neutralization titrations. Atomic masses: Na = 23.0, O = 16.0, H = 1.0 g/mol. Sum these to find the molecular mass (formula weight) of NaOH.
why: MW(NaOH) = 23.0 + 16.0 + 1.0 = 40.0 g/mol. A 1.0 M NaOH stock therefore contains 40 g/L. Skipping the H (giving 39) or doubling the O (giving 56) are common mistakes.

q: A laboratory cylinder contains 14.0 g of pure nitrogen gas (N₂, MW = 28.0 g/mol). Using n = m/MW, determine the number of moles of N₂ molecules in the cylinder.
why: n = 14.0 g / 28.0 g/mol = 0.500 mol. Note: 14.0 g of N₂ contains 1.0 mol of N atoms but only 0.500 mol of N₂ molecules — a common confusion to be aware of when interconverting elemental N and molecular N₂.

q: A balloon contains 4.00 g of helium gas (He, MW = 4.00 g/mol). At STP (273 K, 1 atm), the molar volume of any ideal gas is 22.4 L/mol. What volume does this sample of helium occupy?
why: n = 4.00 g / 4.00 g/mol = 1.00 mol He. V = n × V_m = 1.00 × 22.4 = 22.4 L at STP. He, despite being one of the lightest gases, behaves ideally and occupies the same molar volume at STP as any other ideal gas.

q: Combustion analysis of an unknown organic compound gives the mass percent composition: 40.0% C, 6.7% H, and 53.3% O. Atomic masses: C = 12.0, H = 1.0, O = 16.0. Convert each percentage to moles (assume 100 g sample) and find the simplest whole-number ratio.
why: Per 100 g: 40/12 = 3.33 mol C, 6.7/1 = 6.7 mol H, 53.3/16 = 3.33 mol O. Divide by smallest (3.33): 1 : 2 : 1. Empirical formula = CH₂O. (Glucose's molecular formula C₆H₁₂O₆ is a multiple of this empirical unit.)

q: A 18.0 g sample of pure water (H₂O, MW = 18.0 g/mol) is analyzed. Each H₂O molecule contains 2 hydrogen atoms. Using N_A = 6.022 × 10²³, compute the total number of H atoms present.
why: n_H₂O = 18/18 = 1.00 mol; n_H = 2 × 1.00 = 2.00 mol. Atoms H = 2.00 × 6.022 × 10²³ = 1.20 × 10²⁴. Forgetting the factor of 2 (H per molecule) gives the smaller 6.02 × 10²³ trap.

q: A magnesium ribbon contains 6.02 × 10²² atoms of Mg. Atomic mass of Mg = 24.3 g/mol. First convert to moles using n = atoms/N_A (with N_A = 6.022 × 10²³), then to mass via m = n × MW.
why: n = 6.02 × 10²² / 6.022 × 10²³ = 0.100 mol. m = 0.100 × 24.3 = 2.43 g. The atom count is exactly 1/10 of Avogadro's number, so the answer is 1/10 of one molar mass.

q: A balloon at STP (273 K, 1 atm) contains 5.60 L of pure CO₂. The molar volume of any ideal gas at STP is 22.4 L/mol. Apply n = V / V_m to find the number of moles of CO₂.
why: n = 5.60 L / 22.4 L/mol = 0.250 mol of CO₂. Note that 5.60 L is exactly 1/4 of 22.4 L, so the answer is 1/4 mol. Errors come from confusing molar volume with molar mass.

q: A sample of pure CO₂ is analyzed for elemental carbon content. Atomic mass of C = 12.0 g/mol; molar mass of CO₂ = 44.0 g/mol. The mass percent of an element in a compound is %X = (mass X / mass compound) × 100. Calculate the %w/w of carbon in CO₂.
why: %C = (12.0 / 44.0) × 100 = 27.3%. The remaining 72.7% is oxygen (32 g of O / 44 g total). Useful for back-calculating mass of C from a CO₂ measurement (e.g., 4.4 g CO₂ contains 1.2 g C).

q: An unknown hydrocarbon has the empirical formula CH₂ (empirical formula mass = 12 + 2 = 14 g/mol) and a measured molecular mass MW = 56.0 g/mol. The molecular formula is the empirical formula multiplied by an integer n = MW_actual / MW_empirical. What is the molecular formula?
why: n = 56/14 = 4. Multiply CH₂ by 4 → C₄H₈. This corresponds to butene (or cyclobutane) molecular formula. Checking: 4(12) + 8(1) = 48 + 8 = 56 g/mol ✓.

q: Nitrogen gas (N₂, MW = 28.0 g/mol) is treated as ideal at STP (273 K, 1 atm) where the molar volume V_m = 22.4 L/mol. Density ρ = MW / V_m. Calculate the density of N₂ in g/L at STP.
why: ρ = MW / V_m = 28.0 g/mol / 22.4 L/mol = 1.25 g/L at STP. Compare to air density ≈ 1.29 g/L (mostly N₂), and to denser gases like CO₂ (1.96 g/L) or lighter gases like H₂ (0.090 g/L).

q: A patient receives a 100.0 g infusion of normal saline that contains pure NaCl (MW = 58.5 g/mol; Na = 23, Cl = 35.5). Use n = m/MW to determine how many moles of NaCl are present.
why: n = 100.0 / 58.5 = 1.71 mol of NaCl. The other answers reverse the division (5.85, 17.1) or confuse mass with moles (58.5). Check: 1.71 × 58.5 ≈ 100 g ✓.

q: Ethane combusts in air according to the balanced equation 2 C₂H₆(g) + 7 O₂(g) → 4 CO₂(g) + 6 H₂O(g). Starting with exactly 1.00 mol of C₂H₆, use the mole ratio of O₂ : C₂H₆ from the balanced equation to determine how many moles of O₂ are required.
why: Stoichiometric ratio = 7 mol O₂ / 2 mol C₂H₆ = 3.5. So 1.00 mol C₂H₆ needs 1.00 × 3.5 = 3.5 mol O₂. Forgetting to halve the ratio gives the 7.0 trap; reading 7:2 inverted gives 3.0 or 2.0.

q: A 22.2 g sample of CaCl₂ (MW = 111.0 g/mol; Ca = 40.0, Cl = 35.5 each) is dissolved in water. Each formula unit contains 2 Cl atoms. Use mass% × total mass, OR n_compound × 2 × MW_Cl, to find the total mass of chlorine.
why: Mass fraction of Cl in CaCl₂ = (2 × 35.5) / 111.0 = 71/111 = 0.640. Mass of Cl in 22.2 g CaCl₂ = 0.640 × 22.2 = 14.2 g. Equivalently: n(CaCl₂) = 0.200 mol, so n(Cl) = 0.400 mol → 0.400 × 35.5 = 14.2 g.

q: Glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆, MW = 180.0 g/mol) is the primary blood sugar. A 36.0 g sample contains 12 H atoms per glucose molecule. Use n_H = (m / MW) × 12 to compute the moles of hydrogen.
why: n_glucose = 36/180 = 0.200 mol; n_H = 0.200 × 12 = 2.40 mol. Forgetting the ×12 stoichiometry per molecule gives the 0.20 trap; mistakenly multiplying by 6 (for C₆) gives 1.2.

q: At STP, every gas occupies the same molar volume (22.4 L/mol). Therefore the volume of a fixed mass of gas depends inversely on its molar mass: V = (m / MW) × 22.4. For 1.00 g of each gas at STP, which occupies the GREATEST volume?
why: Volume per gram = 22.4/MW. The lightest gas (smallest MW) has the most moles per gram and therefore the greatest volume. He (MW = 4) has 0.250 mol/g → 5.6 L/g, far more than CO₂ (0.023 mol/g → 0.51 L/g).

q: Consider the balanced reaction A + 2 B → C carried out with 1.0 mol A and 1.0 mol B in a sealed flask. To find the limiting reactant, compute (moles available) / (stoichiometric coefficient) for each reactant — the smallest ratio identifies the limiting reactant.
opts: Both run out at the same time
why: Ratio for A = 1.0/1 = 1.0; ratio for B = 1.0/2 = 0.5. Smallest ratio (0.5) belongs to B, so B is limiting. After reaction, 0.5 mol A would still remain, while B is fully consumed.

q: For the formation of water 2 H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2 H₂O(g), a flask is loaded with 6.0 mol H₂ and 4.0 mol O₂. Find the limiting reactant via mole/coefficient ratios, then use the limiting reactant's stoichiometry to compute the maximum mol H₂O produced.
why: Ratios: H₂ → 6/2 = 3.0; O₂ → 4/1 = 4.0. Smaller is H₂, so H₂ limits. Stoichiometry: 6 mol H₂ × (2 H₂O / 2 H₂) = 6 mol H₂O. (Only 3 mol of the 4 mol O₂ are used; 1 mol O₂ remains.)

q: For 2 H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2 H₂O(g), 4.0 g of H₂ (MW = 2.0 → 2.0 mol) reacts with 32.0 g of O₂ (MW = 32.0 → 1.0 mol). Compute mole/coefficient ratios for each reactant and identify the limiting reactant — or determine if they react stoichiometrically.
why: n(H₂) = 4/2 = 2.0 mol; n(O₂) = 32/32 = 1.0 mol. Ratios: H₂ → 2.0/2 = 1.0; O₂ → 1.0/1 = 1.0. Equal ratios mean both reactants run out simultaneously — perfect stoichiometric match (no excess of either).

q: A laboratory synthesis is calculated to produce a theoretical yield of 5.00 mol of product based on the limiting reactant. The actual isolated yield is 4.20 mol. Apply % yield = (actual / theoretical) × 100 to compute the percent yield.
why: % yield = (4.20 / 5.00) × 100 = 84.0%. Yields above 100% suggest impurity (typically wet/uncrystallized product) and indicate measurement error. Yields below 100% reflect side reactions, incomplete conversion, or losses during workup.

q: For the synthesis 2 Al(s) + 3 Cl₂(g) → 2 AlCl₃(s), 4.0 mol Al and 5.0 mol Cl₂ are placed in a reactor. Compute mole/coefficient ratios (n/coefficient) and identify the limiting reactant.
why: Ratio Al = 4.0/2 = 2.0; ratio Cl₂ = 5.0/3 = 1.67. Smaller ratio = limiting → Cl₂. With Cl₂ limiting, only (5.0)(2/3) = 3.33 mol Al will react, leaving 0.67 mol Al unreacted in excess.

q: A reaction has a theoretical yield of 8.00 g calculated from the limiting reactant, and the chemist achieves a 75.0% yield in practice. Apply actual = (% yield/100) × theoretical to compute the actual mass obtained.
why: Actual = 0.750 × 8.00 = 6.00 g. The 10.7 g distractor results from inverting the formula (8/0.75 = 10.7); the 2.0 g trap from subtracting (8 - 6). Check: % yield = 6/8 × 100 = 75% ✓.

q: For methane combustion CH₄(g) + 2 O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2 H₂O(g), a vessel contains 32.0 g CH₄ (MW = 16 → 2.0 mol) and 64.0 g O₂ (MW = 32 → 2.0 mol). Compute mole/coefficient ratios for each reactant to identify the limiting reactant.
why: Ratios: CH₄ → 2.0/1 = 2.0; O₂ → 2.0/2 = 1.0. Smaller (1.0) is O₂, so O₂ limits. Only 1.0 mol of the 2.0 mol CH₄ will react, leaving 1.0 mol CH₄ in excess.

q: Continuing from the previous problem (CH₄ + 2 O₂ → CO₂ + 2 H₂O with 2.0 mol CH₄ and 2.0 mol O₂, where O₂ is limiting), use the stoichiometry n_CO₂ = n_O₂ × (1 CO₂ / 2 O₂) to find the maximum moles of CO₂ produced.
why: Limiting reactant is O₂ (2.0 mol). n(CO₂) = 2.0 mol O₂ × (1 mol CO₂ / 2 mol O₂) = 1.0 mol CO₂. Forgetting the 1:2 stoichiometric divisor gives the 2.0 mol distractor.

q: The theoretical yield of a Williamson ether synthesis is calculated as 100.0 g, and the chemist isolates 78.0 g of the desired product after recrystallization. Apply % yield = (actual / theoretical) × 100 to find the percent yield.
why: % yield = (78.0 / 100.0) × 100 = 78.0%. The 22% distractor is the COMPLEMENT (loss percentage). Always: % yield uses the actual product mass divided by the theoretical mass times 100.

q: The Haber process N₂(g) + 3 H₂(g) → 2 NH₃(g) is run with 10.0 g N₂ (MW = 28 → 0.357 mol) and 5.00 g H₂ (MW = 2 → 2.50 mol). Compute mole/coefficient ratios to identify the limiting reactant.
why: Ratios: N₂ → 0.357/1 = 0.357; H₂ → 2.50/3 = 0.833. Smaller ratio = N₂ limits. With N₂ limiting, H₂ used = 0.357 × 3 = 1.07 mol, so 2.50 - 1.07 = 1.43 mol H₂ remains in excess.

q: An organic chemist calculates the theoretical yield of an aldol condensation as 50.0 g and isolates 45.0 g of pure aldol product after column chromatography. Use % yield = (actual / theoretical) × 100 to compute the percent yield.
why: % yield = (45.0 / 50.0) × 100 = 90.0%. Most published organic syntheses report yields between 50% and 95%; >100% yields suggest residual solvent or impurities.

q: For Mg(s) + 2 HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g), a strip of magnesium (24.0 g, MW = 24 → 1.00 mol Mg) is added to 36.5 g HCl (MW = 36.5 → 1.00 mol HCl). Compute mole/coefficient ratios to identify the limiting reactant.
why: Ratios: Mg → 1.0/1 = 1.0; HCl → 1.0/2 = 0.5. Smaller ratio = HCl limits. With HCl limiting, only 0.5 mol Mg reacts (consuming 0.5 mol Mg), leaving 0.5 mol Mg unreacted in excess.

q: For a generic 1:1 reaction A + B → products, 4.0 mol of A is mixed with 2.0 mol of B in a sealed reactor. After the reaction goes to completion, identify which reactant remains in excess and how much of it remains.
opts: 2.0 mol of A remains in excess
2.0 mol of B remains in excess
why: B is limiting (smaller amount, equal coefficient). 1:1 stoichiometry means 2.0 mol B consumes 2.0 mol A. Remaining A = 4.0 - 2.0 = 2.0 mol of excess A. All of B is consumed.

q: A student burns 6.0 g of methane in excess O2 at 298 K and 1 atm according to CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O. The theoretical yield of CO2 is 22.0 g, but only 16.0 g is actually collected after drying. What is the percent yield of CO2 for this combustion?
why: Percent yield = (actual / theoretical) x 100%. Plugging in: (16.0 g / 22.0 g) x 100% = 72.7%, which rounds to 73%. Common errors include inverting the ratio or forgetting to multiply by 100.

q: A chemist mixes 0.50 mol N2 with 2.0 mol H2 at 500 K to run N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3. After the reaction goes to completion, 0.50 mol H2 remains in the flask. Which statement best describes the role of H2 in this experiment?
opts: H2 was the limiting reactant because it had the higher mole count
H2 was in excess because some remained after the reaction
H2 had the higher molar mass and therefore controlled the yield
H2 must have been added before N2 to drive the reaction
H2 was at stoichiometric ratio with N2
why: An excess reactant is one that is not fully consumed; some remains after the limiting reactant is exhausted. Here 1.5 mol H2 reacted with 0.50 mol N2 (3:1 stoichiometry), leaving 0.50 mol H2 unreacted, confirming H2 was in excess.

q: A student dissolves 0.20 mol of solid KCl in enough deionized water to make exactly 500. mL of solution at 25 °C in a volumetric flask. Assuming complete dissolution and no volume change beyond the calibration mark, what is the molarity of the resulting KCl solution?
why: Molarity = moles of solute / liters of solution. M = 0.20 mol / 0.500 L = 0.40 M. A common error is dividing by 500 (treating mL as L) or by 250.

q: A pipette is used to transfer 250. mL of a 2.0 M HCl stock solution into a clean beaker at room temperature. Assuming the solution is well mixed and the volume measurement is accurate, how many moles of HCl are contained in this aliquot?
why: moles = M x V(L) = 2.0 mol/L x 0.250 L = 0.50 mol. Forgetting to convert mL to L gives 500, and confusing M with mass gives the wrong dimensional answer.

q: A laboratory technician needs to prepare 1.00 L of 0.25 M NaOH (MW = 40.0 g/mol) for a titration at 25 °C. Solid NaOH pellets are weighed on an analytical balance and quantitatively transferred to a volumetric flask before dilution to the mark. What mass of NaOH must be weighed?
why: mass = M x V x MW = 0.25 mol/L x 1.00 L x 40.0 g/mol = 10.0 g. Forgetting to multiply by MW gives 0.25 g; using 100 mL by mistake gives 1.0 g.

q: A student dissolves 0.50 mol of solid Mg(NO3)2 in enough water to produce 250. mL of solution in a volumetric flask at 25 °C. Considering only the formal molarity of the salt (not the ion concentrations), what is the molarity of Mg(NO3)2 in the resulting solution?
why: M = mol / V(L) = 0.50 mol / 0.250 L = 2.0 M. Doubling for 'two nitrates' (giving 4.0 M) is a common conceptual error since the question asks about the salt, not the ions.

q: A chemist transfers 100. mL of 6.0 M HCl stock into a 1.50 L volumetric flask and dilutes to the mark with deionized water at 25 °C. Assuming volumes are additive and no heat of dilution issues, what is the molarity of HCl in the final diluted solution?
why: Use M1V1 = M2V2: M2 = (6.0 M)(0.100 L) / 1.500 L = 0.40 M. Forgetting unit conversion or using 1.00 L (instead of 1.50 L) gives 0.60 M, a frequent error.

q: A 50.0 mL aliquot of 4.0 M sucrose solution is poured into a graduated cylinder, and water is added to dilute the solution to a final concentration of 2.0 M. Assuming volumes are additive and temperature is constant, what volume of water must be added?
why: M1V1 = M2V2 gives V2 = (4.0)(50.0)/(2.0) = 100. mL final volume. The water added is V2 - V1 = 100 - 50 = 50 mL. Forgetting the subtraction step gives 100 mL.

q: A student prepares a sweetened solution by dissolving 20.0 g of sugar in 80.0 g of water at 25 °C and stirring until homogeneous. The solution is then transferred to a labeled bottle for use in a colligative-properties experiment. What is the percent by mass (% w/w) of sugar in this solution?
why: % w/w = (mass solute / mass solution) x 100 = (20.0 / (20.0 + 80.0)) x 100 = 20%. A common error is dividing solute by solvent only (20/80 = 25%) instead of by total solution mass.

q: A student dissolves 0.10 mol of solid NaCl in 200. g of pure water at 25 °C to prepare a solution for a freezing-point-depression experiment. Assuming the salt fully dissolves and no water evaporates, what is the molality (m) of the resulting NaCl solution?
why: Molality = mol solute / kg solvent = 0.10 mol / 0.200 kg = 0.50 m. Confusing molality with molarity (using volume instead of solvent mass) is the typical pitfall.

q: A 25.0 mL aliquot of 0.40 M KCl solution is pipetted into a clean Erlenmeyer flask at 25 °C as part of a precipitation experiment. Considering only the dissolved KCl (assume complete dissociation but molarity refers to the formula unit), how many moles of KCl are present?
why: moles = M x V(L) = 0.40 mol/L x 0.0250 L = 0.010 mol. Forgetting to convert 25.0 mL to 0.0250 L gives 10 mol, an obviously wrong magnitude.

q: A 5.0% (w/w) NaCl solution has a measured density of 1.04 g/mL at 20 °C, and the molar mass of NaCl is 58.4 g/mol. Assuming the solution is at the same temperature and well mixed, what is the molarity of NaCl in this solution?
why: Per 1.00 L: mass = 1040 g, mass NaCl = 0.050 x 1040 = 52.0 g, mol = 52.0/58.4 = 0.890 mol. Therefore M = 0.89 mol/L. Skipping the density factor gives ~0.86, while doubling gives 1.78.

q: A student prepares an aqueous mixture by dissolving 1.0 mol of NaCl in 9.0 mol of H2O at 25 °C and stirring until uniform. The solution is to be used to verify Raoult's law deviations. What is the mole fraction (X) of NaCl in this solution, treating NaCl as an undissociated molecular formula unit?
why: X(NaCl) = mol NaCl / total mol = 1.0 / (1.0 + 9.0) = 0.10. A common error is dividing by the solvent only (1/9 = 0.11) instead of by total moles.

q: An environmental chemist measures 5.0 mg of dissolved lead in 1.00 L of water at 20 °C. The water has a density of 1.00 g/mL, and ppm is defined as mg solute per kg solution (equivalent here to mg/L). What is the lead concentration in ppm?
why: 1 ppm = 1 mg/L for dilute aqueous solutions because 1 L water has mass ~1 kg. Therefore 5.0 mg/L = 5.0 ppm. Confusing ppm with ppb (1000x) gives 5000.

q: A sealed rigid 2.0 L steel vessel contains a fixed amount of N2 gas at 300 K and 1.0 atm. The vessel is heated in an oil bath until the gas temperature reaches 600 K, while the volume cannot change because the walls are rigid. What happens to the gas pressure?
why: Gay-Lussac's law: P/T = constant at fixed n,V. P2 = P1 x (T2/T1) = 1.0 x (600/300) = 2.0 atm. Doubling T (in K) doubles P. Using °C instead of K gives an incorrect ratio.

q: A student wishes to measure the volume of 0.50 mol of an ideal gas at standard temperature and pressure (STP: 273 K and 1.00 atm), where the molar volume of an ideal gas is 22.4 L/mol. Assuming ideal-gas behavior under these conditions, what volume does the sample occupy?
why: V = n x V_molar = 0.50 mol x 22.4 L/mol = 11.2 L. Forgetting to multiply by n (and reporting 22.4 L) is the most frequent error.

q: A laboratory thermometer reads 27 °C for a sample of an ideal gas inside a sealed flask. To use this temperature in the ideal-gas equation PV = nRT, it must first be converted into the absolute (Kelvin) scale using K = °C + 273. What is the corresponding temperature in Kelvin?
why: K = °C + 273 = 27 + 273 = 300 K. Subtracting (giving 246 K) or adding to 100 instead of 273 are common slips.

q: An ideal gas is sealed in a piston at constant temperature (298 K) and constant amount, with an initial pressure of 2.0 atm and an initial volume of 4.0 L. The piston is allowed to expand isothermally until the volume reaches 8.0 L. What is the new pressure of the gas?
why: Boyle's law (constant n,T): P1V1 = P2V2 -> P2 = (2.0)(4.0)/8.0 = 1.0 atm. Doubling V halves P. Inverting the ratio gives 4.0 atm.

q: A rigid 5.0 L vessel at 298 K contains a mixture of gases with the following partial pressures: P(N2) = 0.60 atm, P(O2) = 0.30 atm, and P(Ar) = 0.10 atm. According to Dalton's law of partial pressures, what is the total pressure in the vessel?
why: Dalton's law: P_total = sum of P_i = 0.60 + 0.30 + 0.10 = 1.0 atm. Adding only two terms (giving 0.90) is a common slip.

q: An ideal gas occupies 11.2 L at a pressure of 1.0 atm and temperature of 273 K (STP), where R = 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K). Using the ideal-gas equation PV = nRT to determine the chemical amount in the sample, how many moles of gas are present?
why: n = PV/RT = (1.0)(11.2)/(0.0821 x 273) = 0.50 mol. Equivalently, 11.2 L at STP = half of 22.4 L (one molar volume), so n = 0.5 mol.

q: A 1.00 mol sample of an ideal gas is held at 0.50 atm and 300. K inside a flexible balloon. Using R = 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K) and assuming ideal behavior throughout, what is the volume of the gas under these conditions?
why: V = nRT/P = (1.00)(0.0821)(300)/0.50 = 49.3 L. Forgetting to divide by P (using P=1) gives 24.6 L; doubling instead of dividing gives 12.3 L.

q: Atmospheric air at sea level has a total pressure of 1.00 atm at 298 K, with O2 contributing a partial pressure of 0.21 atm. Using the relation X_i = P_i/P_total for an ideal-gas mixture, what is the mole fraction of O2 in air?
why: X_O2 = P_O2 / P_total = 0.21 / 1.00 = 0.21. The mole fraction equals the partial pressure ratio for ideal gases. The complement (0.79) is the mole fraction of the rest.

q: A small pinhole is opened in a chamber containing equal partial pressures of H2 (MW = 2.0 g/mol) and O2 (MW = 32 g/mol) at 298 K. Graham's law states that the rate of effusion is inversely proportional to the square root of molar mass. What is the ratio of effusion rates rate(H2)/rate(O2)?
why: rate(H2)/rate(O2) = sqrt(MW_O2/MW_H2) = sqrt(32/2) = sqrt(16) = 4.0. Forgetting the square root gives 16; inverting molar masses gives 0.25.

q: A 1.00 mol sample of CO2 is held at 0.50 atm and 273 K in a sealed flexible container. Using R = 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K) and treating CO2 as ideal under these conditions, what volume does the gas occupy?
why: V = nRT/P. At STP one mole of ideal gas is 22.4 L; halving the pressure to 0.50 atm doubles the volume to 44.8 L. Confusing P direction gives 11.2 L.

q: A fixed sample of ideal gas initially has P1 = 2.0 atm, V1 = 10. L, and T1 = 300. K. The gas is then warmed and allowed to expand to a final volume V2 = 20. L at a final temperature T2 = 600. K. Using the combined gas law, what is the final pressure P2?
why: Combined gas law: P1V1/T1 = P2V2/T2, so P2 = P1 x (V1/V2) x (T2/T1) = 2.0 x (10/20) x (600/300) = 2.0 atm. The volume doubles (halving P) but T doubles (doubling P), so P stays the same.

q: A rigid steel cylinder at 298 K contains a binary mixture in which N2 contributes a partial pressure of 0.50 atm and O2 contributes 1.50 atm, with no other gases present. According to Dalton's law and the relation X_i = P_i/P_total, what is the mole fraction of N2?
why: P_total = 0.50 + 1.50 = 2.00 atm. X_N2 = 0.50/2.00 = 0.25. Confusing X_N2 with the smaller-of-two ratio (0.50/1.50 = 0.33) is the most common error.

q: An ideal gas of CO2 (MW = 44.0 g/mol) is held at standard temperature and pressure (273 K, 1.00 atm), where the molar volume of an ideal gas is 22.4 L/mol. Using density = MW/V_molar, what is the density of CO2 in g/L under these conditions?
why: Density = MW / V_molar = 44.0 g/mol / 22.4 L/mol = 1.96 g/L. Inverting (22.4/44 = 0.51) is a frequent slip; reporting V_molar itself (22.4) confuses units.

q: A balloon contains 5.00 L of pure N2 (MW = 28.0 g/mol) at standard temperature and pressure (273 K, 1.00 atm), where the molar volume of an ideal gas is 22.4 L/mol. Using ideal-gas behavior, what mass of N2 is contained in the balloon?
why: n = V/V_molar = 5.00 / 22.4 = 0.223 mol; mass = n x MW = 0.223 x 28.0 = 6.25 g. Forgetting to convert to moles (and using V x MW directly) gives 140 g.

q: Real gases obey the ideal-gas equation PV = nRT poorly when intermolecular attractions and finite molecular volume become significant. Considering the conditions under which N2 deviates most strongly from ideal behavior, in which regime does an ideal gas approximation FAIL most severely?
why: Real gases deviate most at low T (slow molecules feel attractions strongly) and high P (molecules are close, finite size matters). Hence low T + high P is least ideal; high T + low P is most ideal.

q: When 1.00 mol of CH4 burns in excess O2 at 25 °C and 1 atm to give CO2 and H2O(l), the system releases 890 kJ of heat to the surroundings, and the bath water temperature rises measurably. Considering this is a classic combustion calorimetry result, what is the sign of ΔH for this reaction?
why: Exothermic reactions release heat, so the system loses enthalpy and ΔH < 0 (negative). The convention assigns heat outflow from the system as a negative ΔH.

q: A reference table lists standard enthalpies of formation (ΔHf°) at 25 °C and 1 atm for various species, including O2(g), N2(g), C(graphite), and Fe(s) in their standard states. Based on the formal definition of standard enthalpy of formation for a pure element in its reference state, what is ΔHf° for O2(g) at 25 °C?
opts: Equal to the bond energy of O=O
why: ΔHf° of any element in its standard state (reference form, 25 °C, 1 atm) is defined as exactly 0 kJ/mol. This convention makes ΔHf° tables internally consistent with Hess's law.

q: A 50.0 g sample of an unknown solid with specific heat c = 2.0 J/(g·°C) is heated from 20.0 °C to 30.0 °C inside a well-insulated calorimeter. Assuming all heat is absorbed by the solid and using q = m·c·ΔT, how much heat (q) was supplied to the sample?
why: q = m·c·ΔT = 50.0 g x 2.0 J/(g·°C) x 10.0 °C = 1000 J. Forgetting to multiply by mass gives 20 J, while doubling ΔT gives 2000 J.

q: For the forward reaction A -> B at 25 °C and 1 atm, the standard enthalpy change is ΔH_forward = +50 kJ. The reverse reaction (B -> A) is run under the same conditions in a separate calorimeter. According to the property that enthalpy is a state function, what is ΔH for the reverse reaction?
why: Reversing a reaction reverses the sign of ΔH while preserving its magnitude. Therefore ΔH(B->A) = −(+50) = −50 kJ. This follows from H being a state function.

q: Two separate experiments at 25 °C give ΔH(A -> B) = +30 kJ and ΔH(B -> C) = −10 kJ for stoichiometrically connected steps. Using Hess's law to combine these into the overall transformation A -> C, what is ΔH(A -> C)?
why: Hess's law: ΔH(overall) = sum of step ΔH = +30 + (−10) = +20 kJ. Sign mistakes (subtracting magnitudes only) give +40 or −40.

q: For the gas-phase reaction H2(g) + Cl2(g) -> 2 HCl(g), use bond energies (kJ/mol): D(H–H) = 436, D(Cl–Cl) = 243, D(H–Cl) = 431. The bond-energy approximation gives ΔH = sum(bonds broken) − sum(bonds formed). What is ΔH for this reaction?
why: Bonds broken: 436 + 243 = 679 kJ. Bonds formed: 2 x 431 = 862 kJ. ΔH = 679 − 862 = −183 kJ. Forgetting to multiply H–Cl by 2 gives +248; reversing the formula gives +183.

q: Given ΔHf° (kJ/mol): CO2(g) = −394, H2O(g) = −242, CH3OH(l) = −239, and O2(g) = 0, calculate the standard enthalpy of combustion for CH3OH(l) + 1.5 O2(g) -> CO2(g) + 2 H2O(g) at 25 °C.
why: ΔH_rxn = sum(ΔHf° products) − sum(ΔHf° reactants) = [−394 + 2(−242)] − [−239 + 1.5(0)] = −878 − (−239) = −639 kJ. Sign errors on reactants give −1117 or +639.

q: A coffee-cup calorimeter contains 25.0 g of pure water at 20.0 °C, and a small electric heater raises the water temperature to 30.0 °C with negligible heat loss to the surroundings. Using c(water) = 4.18 J/(g·°C) and q = m·c·ΔT, how much heat was delivered to the water?
why: q = m·c·ΔT = 25.0 g x 4.18 J/(g·°C) x 10.0 °C = 1045 J. Forgetting the mass term gives 41.8 J; doubling ΔT (mistaking final T for ΔT) gives ~3135 J.

q: Inside a well-insulated coffee-cup calorimeter, 50.0 g of hot water at 90.0 °C is mixed with 50.0 g of cold water at 10.0 °C, and the mixture is allowed to reach thermal equilibrium. Assuming no heat loss and equal specific heats, what is the final equilibrium temperature?
why: Energy balance: m·c·(Tf − 90) + m·c·(Tf − 10) = 0. With equal masses, Tf is the simple average: (90 + 10)/2 = 50 °C. Unequal masses would weight the average.

q: Solid CO2 (dry ice) at −78.5 °C and 1.00 atm sublimes directly to gaseous CO2 in an open container, dramatically increasing the number of accessible microstates of the system. Considering the change in molecular disorder for the phase transition CO2(s) -> CO2(g), what is the sign of ΔS_system?
why: Going from a highly ordered solid to a gas dramatically increases the number of microstates, so ΔS > 0. Solid -> gas (sublimation) always has positive ΔS.

q: Consider the gas-phase dimerization 2 A(g) -> A2(g) at 298 K and 1 atm, where two moles of gas combine into one mole of gas. Using the rule that gas-phase moles dominate ΔS_system, what is the sign of ΔS_system for this reaction?
why: Δn(gas) = 1 − 2 = −1, so the number of gas-phase microstates decreases. Therefore ΔS_system < 0 (negative). Combining gas particles into fewer particles always lowers entropy.

q: A chemist compares standard molar entropies (S°) at 298 K and 1 atm for ice, liquid water, and steam. Although the temperature is hypothetical for some phases (e.g., ice above 0 °C is metastable), entropy generally increases with translational and rotational freedom. Which phase has the LARGEST molar entropy?
why: Gas phase has the most accessible microstates (free translation, rotation, vibration), so steam has the largest S°. Generally S°(g) >> S°(l) > S°(s) for the same substance.

q: Consider the gas-phase reaction 2 NO2(g) + 0.5 O2(g) -> N2O5(g) at 298 K and 1 atm. The number of moles of gas decreases substantially as the reactants combine into a single gaseous product. Based on Δn(gas), what is the sign of ΔS_system for this reaction?
opts: Cannot be determined without S° values
why: Δn(g) = 1 − (2 + 0.5) = −1.5. Fewer gas-phase particles means fewer microstates, so ΔS_system < 0 (negative). Δn(gas) is the dominant factor when phase counts change.

q: At 298 K and 1 atm, a chemical reaction has a calculated standard Gibbs free-energy change of ΔG = −10.0 kJ/mol under the reaction conditions. Using the criterion that ΔG predicts spontaneity at constant T and P, what is the spontaneity of this process?
why: ΔG < 0 at constant T,P means the reaction is spontaneous in the forward direction. ΔG > 0 is non-spontaneous; ΔG = 0 is at equilibrium.

q: A reaction at 1 atm has both ΔH > 0 (endothermic) and ΔS > 0 (positive entropy change). Using the equation ΔG = ΔH − T·ΔS, the spontaneity depends on temperature. Under what temperature regime is the reaction spontaneous (ΔG < 0)?
why: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. With ΔH > 0 and ΔS > 0, raising T makes the −TΔS term dominate negatively. Spontaneity (ΔG < 0) requires T > ΔH/ΔS.

q: A reaction has reached equilibrium at 298 K and 1 atm in a sealed container, with no net change in concentrations of reactants or products. Considering the relation between ΔG and the position of equilibrium under reaction conditions, what is the value of ΔG (not ΔG°) at equilibrium?
why: At equilibrium, the driving force vanishes, so ΔG = 0 (under reaction conditions). Note: ΔG° (standard) need not be zero; only ΔG = ΔG° + RT·ln(Q) becomes 0 when Q = K.

q: At 300. K, a reaction has ΔH = +20.0 kJ/mol and ΔS = +50.0 J/(mol·K). Using ΔG = ΔH − T·ΔS and being careful with units, what is ΔG in kJ/mol under these conditions?
why: Convert ΔS to kJ: 50.0 J/(K·mol) = 0.0500 kJ/(K·mol). ΔG = 20.0 − (300)(0.0500) = 20.0 − 15.0 = +5.0 kJ/mol. Forgetting unit conversion gives ΔG = 20 − 15000 (absurd).

q: A reaction has ΔH = +40.0 kJ/mol and ΔS = +100. J/(mol·K), with both values approximately temperature-independent. Setting ΔG = ΔH − T·ΔS = 0 to find the crossover temperature above which the reaction becomes spontaneous, what is T_cross?
why: Set ΔG = 0: T = ΔH/ΔS = 40.0 kJ / 0.100 kJ/K = 400 K. Above 400 K the reaction is spontaneous. Forgetting J->kJ conversion (using 100 directly) gives 0.4 K.

q: A reaction at 1 atm has both ΔH < 0 (exothermic) and ΔS < 0 (decrease in disorder), placing it in the (−,−) quadrant of the spontaneity table. Using ΔG = ΔH − T·ΔS, the sign of ΔG depends on whether |ΔH| or |T·ΔS| dominates. Under what temperature regime is the reaction spontaneous?
why: With ΔH < 0 and ΔS < 0, the −TΔS term is positive. At low T, |ΔH| > |TΔS|, so ΔG < 0 (spontaneous). At high T, the TΔS penalty dominates and ΔG > 0.

q: A kinetics experiment for the reaction A -> products at 298 K determines the empirical rate law to be rate = k[A]^2, with k = 0.10 M^(-1)·s^(-1) and [A]_0 = 1.0 M. Considering only the dependence on [A] in the rate expression, what is the order of the reaction with respect to A?
why: The exponent on [A] in the rate law is 2, so the reaction is second order in A. The units of k (M^(-1)·s^(-1)) confirm second-order kinetics.

q: A first-order reaction A -> products at 298 K has [A]_0 = 2.0 M and rate constant k = 0.10 s^(-1). Using the first-order half-life formula t_(1/2) = 0.693/k (which is independent of [A]_0), how long does it take for [A] to reach 1.0 M?
why: t_(1/2) = ln(2)/k = 0.693/0.10 s^(-1) = 6.93 s. First-order half-life is independent of [A]_0. Confusing 1/k with the formula gives 10 s.

q: Initial-rate data for A -> products at 298 K: Trial 1, [A] = 0.10 M, rate = 0.010 M/s; Trial 2, [A] = 0.20 M, rate = 0.040 M/s. Doubling [A] increases the rate by a factor of 4. What is the order of the reaction with respect to A?
why: Rate ratio = (0.040/0.010) = 4 when [A] ratio = 2. Since 2^n = 4, n = 2. The reaction is second order in A.

q: For a zero-order reaction A -> products at 298 K, the rate law is rate = k (independent of [A]) with rate having units of M/s. Using the relation rate = k·[A]^0 and dimensional analysis, what are the SI-style units of the rate constant k for a zero-order reaction?
why: Rate (M/s) = k·[A]^0 = k. Therefore k has units of M·s^(-1) (M/s). First-order k has s^(-1); second-order k has M^(-1)·s^(-1).

q: A zero-order reaction A -> products at 298 K has rate constant k = 0.050 M/s and initial concentration [A]_0 = 1.00 M. Using the zero-order half-life formula t_(1/2) = [A]_0 / (2k), how long does it take for [A] to fall to 0.50 M?
why: t_(1/2) = [A]_0 / (2k) = 1.00 / (2 x 0.050) = 10. s. Note that for zero order, t_(1/2) depends on [A]_0; using [A]_0/k (without the 2) gives 20 s.

q: A reaction A -> products at 298 K is studied with several different starting concentrations [A]_0, and the measured half-life is found to be CONSTANT (independent of [A]_0) for all trials. Using the integrated rate-law dependence of t_(1/2) on [A]_0, what is the order of the reaction with respect to A?
why: Only first-order reactions have a half-life t_(1/2) = ln(2)/k that is independent of [A]_0. Zero-order t_(1/2) is proportional to [A]_0; second-order t_(1/2) is inversely proportional to [A]_0.

q: A platinum catalyst is added to the gas-phase decomposition 2 H2O2(aq) -> 2 H2O(l) + O2(g) at 298 K, dramatically speeding up the reaction without being consumed. Considering the Arrhenius equation k = A·exp(−Ea/RT), which thermodynamic/kinetic parameter does a catalyst directly affect?
why: A catalyst lowers E_a by providing an alternative reaction path with a lower transition-state barrier. ΔH, ΔG, ΔS, and K_eq are state functions and are unchanged by a catalyst.

q: An Arrhenius experiment varies the temperature of a first-order reaction from 300 K to 350 K while holding the activation energy constant at E_a = 75 kJ/mol. According to k = A·exp(−E_a/RT), how does the rate constant k change as T increases?
opts: k stays the same regardless of T
why: As T increases, −E_a/(RT) becomes less negative, so exp(−E_a/RT) increases. Therefore k increases with temperature for any positive E_a.

q: Two reactions A and B share the same pre-exponential factor A and are studied at the same temperature 298 K, but reaction A has E_a = 50 kJ/mol while reaction B has E_a = 100 kJ/mol. Using k = A·exp(−E_a/RT), how does k for reaction B compare with k for reaction A?
why: Higher E_a makes −E_a/(RT) more negative, so exp(−E_a/RT) is much smaller. Therefore k_B (higher E_a) is smaller than k_A at the same temperature.

q: A catalyst lowers the activation energy of a reaction from E_a = 75 kJ/mol to E_a' = 50 kJ/mol while leaving the Arrhenius pre-factor A unchanged at T = 300 K (R = 8.314 J/(mol·K)). Using k_new/k_old = exp((E_a − E_a')/RT), estimate the rate-enhancement factor.
why: ΔE_a = 25,000 J/mol; (E_a − E_a')/(RT) = 25000/(8.314 x 300) ≈ 10.0. exp(10.0) ≈ 2.2 x 10^4, near 5 x 10^4. Forgetting J vs kJ gives a hugely different (and wrong) answer.

q: An empirical kinetics rule of thumb for reactions with typical activation energies (~50 kJ/mol) near room temperature states that the rate constant k approximately doubles per a fixed temperature rise. Based on Arrhenius behavior at ~300 K with E_a ≈ 50 kJ/mol, what is the approximate temperature rise (in K) required to double k?
why: For E_a ~ 50 kJ/mol near 300 K, k roughly doubles for every ~10 K rise (the classic 'Q10 ≈ 2' biochemical rule). This stems from exp(E_a·ΔT/(R·T^2)) ≈ 2 when ΔT ≈ 10 K.

q: For the reversible reaction A(g) ⇌ B(g) at 298 K in a 1.0 L container, equilibrium concentrations are measured as [A] = 2.0 M and [B] = 4.0 M. Using the equilibrium-constant expression Kc = [B]/[A] for this 1:1 stoichiometry, what is the value of Kc?
why: Kc = [B]/[A] = 4.0/2.0 = 2.0. A common error is inverting the ratio (giving 0.5) or multiplying instead of dividing (giving 8).

q: Consider the heterogeneous reaction A(s) + B(g) ⇌ C(g) at 298 K, in which species A is a pure solid and B and C are gases at 1 atm. By the convention that pure solids and pure liquids have unit activity (and are thus omitted from K), what is the correct equilibrium-constant expression?
why: Pure solids and liquids have activity 1 and are omitted from K. Therefore K = [C]/[B], with [A(s)] left out. Including A(s) in the denominator is the most common error.

q: For the reaction 2 A(g) ⇌ B(g) at 298 K and 1 atm, the reaction quotient is Q = [B]/[A]^2. At a given instant the concentrations are measured as [A] = 1.0 M and [B] = 4.0 M, before equilibrium is reached. What is the value of Q at this instant?
why: Q = [B]/[A]^2 = 4.0 / (1.0)^2 = 4.0. Forgetting to square [A] gives 4.0 (correct here only by coincidence with [A]=1); using [A] = 0.5 would expose the squaring error.

q: A chemist measures Q = 0.10 for a gas-phase reaction at 298 K, while the literature equilibrium constant is K = 1.0 at the same temperature. Comparing Q to K determines the direction of net reaction needed to reach equilibrium. Which way will the reaction shift?
why: When Q < K, [products]/[reactants] is too low, so the reaction must proceed forward (toward products) until Q = K. When Q > K, it shifts reverse.

q: For the gas-phase reaction A(g) ⇌ B(g) at 298 K, the equilibrium constant is K_forward = 5.0. A chemist now writes the reverse reaction B(g) ⇌ A(g) at the same temperature. Using the rule that reversing a reaction inverts K, what is K_reverse?
why: Reversing a reaction gives K_reverse = 1/K_forward = 1/5.0 = 0.20. Squaring K (giving 25) corresponds to doubling stoichiometry, not reversing.

q: Consider the gas-phase reaction 2 NO(g) + O2(g) ⇌ 2 NO2(g) at 298 K and 1 atm, with all species in the gas phase. The change in moles of gas, Δn(g), is used to relate Kp and Kc and to predict pressure-shift behavior. What is Δn(g) for this reaction as written?
why: Δn(g) = mol products(g) − mol reactants(g) = 2 − (2 + 1) = −1. The total gas moles decrease by 1 from reactants to products.

q: For the gas-phase reaction A(g) ⇌ B(g) at 298 K, the equilibrium constant is K_1 = 5.0. The chemist now multiplies all stoichiometric coefficients by 2 to write 2A(g) ⇌ 2B(g) at the same temperature. What is the new equilibrium constant K_2?
why: Multiplying coefficients by n raises K to the n-th power: K_new = K_old^n. Here n = 2, so K_2 = (5.0)^2 = 25. Doubling K (giving 10) is the most common error.

q: An equilibrium mixture of N2(g) + 3 H2(g) ⇌ 2 NH3(g) at 500 K and 200 atm is disturbed by injecting additional N2 gas while keeping the total volume constant. According to Le Chatelier's principle, the system reacts to partially counteract the imposed change. Which way does the equilibrium shift?
why: Adding a reactant raises Q below K, so the system shifts forward (toward products) to consume some of the added reactant and restore Q = K.

q: An endothermic gas-phase equilibrium A(g) + heat ⇌ B(g) is held at 400 K, and the temperature is then lowered to 300 K while the volume is held constant. According to Le Chatelier (treating heat as a reactant for endothermic reactions), how does the equilibrium shift?
why: Endothermic forward reaction has heat as a reactant. Removing heat (lowering T) shifts the equilibrium reverse to replace the lost heat. Equivalently, K decreases for endothermic reactions as T falls.

q: An exothermic gas-phase equilibrium A(g) ⇌ B(g) + heat is held at 300 K, and the temperature is then raised to 400 K while pressure is constant. Treating heat as a product for exothermic reactions and applying Le Chatelier's principle, how does the equilibrium shift?
why: Exothermic forward reaction has heat as a product. Adding heat (raising T) shifts the system reverse to absorb the added heat. K decreases for exothermic reactions as T rises.

q: Consider the gas-phase equilibrium H2(g) + I2(g) ⇌ 2 HI(g) at 700 K, in which the moles of gas are equal on both sides (Δn(gas) = 0). The system is compressed isothermally to half its original volume, doubling the total pressure. How does the equilibrium position shift?
why: Pressure shifts only matter when Δn(g) ≠ 0. Here Δn(g) = 2 − 2 = 0, so changing P (or V) does not shift the equilibrium position. Q and K both change identically.

q: A student sets up an ICE table for the reaction A(g) ⇌ B(g) at 298 K, with rows labeled I, C, and E representing the three stages tracked during equilibrium calculations. Considering the standard ICE-table convention used in equilibrium problems, what does the C row represent?
why: ICE = Initial, Change, Equilibrium. The C row tracks the change in each species' concentration as the reaction proceeds (e.g., −x for a reactant, +x for a product), based on stoichiometry.

q: A student writes an ICE table for the gas-phase reaction 2 A(g) ⇌ B(g) at 298 K, beginning with [A]_0 = 1.0 M and [B]_0 = 0. If the change row for A is set as −2x (i.e., 2x of A reacts), what is the corresponding change in [B] based on stoichiometry?
why: Stoichiometry says 2 A produces 1 B. If 2x mol/L of A is consumed, only x mol/L of B forms. Equivalently, if the change in A is set as −x (with x small), B's change is +x/2.

q: A student uses the small-x approximation in an ICE-table calculation for a weak acid HA, assuming [HA]_eq ≈ [HA]_0 because x is small relative to [HA]_0. The standard rule of thumb is that the approximation must be checked at the end. Under what condition does the small-x approximation FAIL?
why: Standard chemistry convention: the small-x approximation fails when x > 5% of [A]_0, because then [A]_0 − x cannot be approximated as [A]_0. This typically corresponds to small [A]_0 or large K.

q: For the gas-phase reaction A(g) ⇌ B(g) at 298 K with Kc = 4.0, a 1.0 L flask is initially loaded with [A]_0 = 1.0 M and [B]_0 = 0. Setting up an ICE table with change −x for A and +x for B, solve for the equilibrium concentration [B]_eq.

A weak acid HA dissociates as HA(aq) ⇌ H+(aq) + A-(aq) at 25 °C, with Ka = 1.0x10^(-4) and [HA]_0 = 0.05 M, [H+]_0 ≈ 0, [A-]_0 = 0. Using the small-x approximation in an ICE table, calculate the equilibrium [H+].

A student dissolves enough HCl(g) in water at 25 °C to make a 0.010 M HCl solution, which dissociates completely into H+ and Cl- because HCl is a strong acid. Using pH = -log[H+] for this strong-acid solution, what is the pH of the resulting solution?
why: [H+] = 0.010 M = 1.0x10^(-2) M because HCl fully dissociates. pH = -log(1.0x10^(-2)) = 2.0. Confusing the exponent magnitude (giving 1 or 3) is a common slip.

q: A beaker holds pure deionized water at 25 °C and 1 atm with no dissolved acids or bases. Water self-ionizes as 2 H2O ⇌ H3O+ + OH- with Kw = 1.0x10^(-14), so [H+] = [OH-] = 1.0x10^(-7) M. Using pH = -log[H+], what is the pH of pure water?
why: [H+] = 1.0x10^(-7) M, so pH = -log(10^(-7)) = 7.0. Note that pH = 7 is neutral only at 25 °C; at higher T, Kw is larger and neutral pH is below 7.

q: A pH electrode placed in an aqueous solution at 25 °C reports the hydrogen-ion activity, and a separate measurement determines [H+] = 1.0x10^(-5) M. Using pH = -log[H+] (treating activity as concentration for dilute solutions), what is the pH of the solution?
why: pH = -log(1.0x10^(-5)) = 5.0. Forgetting the negative sign gives -5; flipping to pOH (=14 - pH = 9) is a common confusion.

q: A solution at 25 °C has pH = 3.0 as measured by a calibrated pH meter, and the relation pH + pOH = 14 holds because Kw = 1.0x10^(-14) at this temperature. Using this water-autoionization relation, what is the pOH of this solution?
why: At 25 °C, pH + pOH = 14, so pOH = 14 - 3.0 = 11. This relation depends on T because Kw is T-dependent; at higher T, the sum is less than 14.

q: A 0.0010 M aqueous NaOH solution is prepared at 25 °C, and the strong base fully dissociates to give [OH-] = 1.0x10^(-3) M. Using pOH = -log[OH-] and pH + pOH = 14, what is the pH of this solution?
why: [OH-] = 1.0x10^(-3) M -> pOH = 3.0. Therefore pH = 14 - 3.0 = 11. Confusing pH with pOH gives 3; forgetting the conversion gives 13.

q: A buffer at 25 °C has pH = 9.0 as measured by a calibrated pH meter. Using Kw = 1.0x10^(-14) and the relation [H+][OH-] = Kw at this temperature, what is the hydroxide concentration [OH-] in the solution?

Consider the conjugate acid-base pair HA / A- in water at 25 °C, with the acid having Ka and the conjugate base having Kb. Using the equations HA ⇌ H+ + A- and A- + H2O ⇌ HA + OH-, the relation between Ka and Kb at this temperature is determined by water's self-ionization. What does Ka × Kb equal?
why: Multiplying the two equilibrium expressions gives Ka·Kb = [H+][OH-] = Kw = 1.0x10^(-14) at 25 °C. Equivalently, pKa + pKb = pKw = 14.

q: A 0.10 M HCl solution is prepared in a volumetric flask at 25 °C, where HCl fully dissociates to give [H+] = 0.10 M. Using pH = -log[H+] for this strong-acid solution and ignoring water's contribution, what is the pH?
why: [H+] = 0.10 = 10^(-1) M, so pH = -log(10^(-1)) = 1.0. Confusing log scales (giving 2) or sign (giving -1) is the typical pitfall.

q: A water sample at 25 °C is measured with a calibrated pH meter and gives pH = 6.5. Using the convention that at 25 °C, neutral water has pH = 7.0 (because [H+] = [OH-] = 10^(-7)), classify this solution as acidic, basic, or neutral.
why: At 25 °C, pH < 7 means [H+] > 10^(-7) > [OH-], so the solution is acidic. pH = 6.5 corresponds to [H+] ≈ 3.2x10^(-7) M, slightly above neutral.

q: A 0.010 M Ba(OH)2 solution is prepared in water at 25 °C, where Ba(OH)2 dissociates completely to give 1 Ba(2+) and 2 OH- per formula unit. Therefore [OH-] = 0.020 M. Using pOH = -log[OH-] and pH + pOH = 14, what is the pH?
why: [OH-] = 2 x 0.010 = 0.020 M; pOH = -log(0.020) = 1.70. Therefore pH = 14 - 1.70 = 12.30. Forgetting the factor of 2 (using 0.010 M) gives pH = 12.0.

q: At 25 °C, 50.0 mL of 0.10 M HCl is mixed with 50.0 mL of 0.10 M NaOH in a beaker, producing 100.0 mL of solution containing only NaCl and water. Considering that HCl + NaOH -> NaCl + H2O fully neutralizes (equimolar strong acid + strong base), what is the final pH?
why: Equal moles of strong acid and strong base produce a salt of a strong acid and strong base (NaCl), which is pH-neutral. The resulting solution is pure NaCl(aq) at pH = 7.0 at 25 °C.

q: A student tests four 0.10 M acid solutions at 25 °C: HF, HCl, H2CO3, and CH3COOH. Using a conductivity meter, one solution shows complete dissociation (very high conductivity) while the others are weakly conductive. Which of these acids is classified as a STRONG acid?
why: HCl is one of the seven strong acids (HCl, HBr, HI, HNO3, H2SO4, HClO4, HClO3) that dissociate fully in water. HF, H2CO3, and CH3COOH are weak (Ka << 1).

q: Four bases are dissolved in water at 25 °C to form 0.10 M solutions: NH3, Mg(OH)2, NaOH, and HCO3-. A pH meter shows one solution near pH 13 while the others are mildly basic or only sparingly soluble. Which is classified as a STRONG base?
why: NaOH is a Group 1 hydroxide that fully dissociates in water — a strong base. NH3 and HCO3- are weak bases; Mg(OH)2 is a strong base in solution but barely soluble (limited [OH-]).

q: A 1.0 M aqueous HF solution is prepared at 25 °C, with Ka = 6.6x10^(-4) for HF ⇌ H+ + F-. Using the small-x approximation [H+] ≈ sqrt(Ka·[HF]_0) for a weak monoprotic acid, what is the approximate pH of this solution?
why: x = [H+] ≈ sqrt((6.6x10^(-4))(1.0)) = sqrt(6.6x10^(-4)) ≈ 2.57x10^(-2) M. pH = -log(2.57x10^(-2)) ≈ 1.59 ≈ 1.6. Treating HF as a strong acid would give pH = 0.

q: Compare the conjugate bases of the four acids HCl, HF, HI, and HBr at 25 °C, all at 0.10 M. Three of these are strong acids whose conjugate bases are extremely weak (negligible basicity), while one is a weak acid whose conjugate base is measurably basic. Which conjugate base is the STRONGEST?
why: Stronger acids -> weaker conjugate bases. HCl, HBr, HI are strong acids, so Cl-, Br-, I- are negligibly basic. HF is weak (Ka = 6.6x10^(-4)), so F- is measurably basic — the strongest of the four.

q: A 0.010 M aqueous acetic acid (CH3COOH) solution at 25 °C has Ka = 1.8x10^(-5) for CH3COOH ⇌ H+ + CH3COO-. Using [H+] ≈ sqrt(Ka·[HA]_0) (small-x approximation), what is the approximate pH?

Four 0.10 M aqueous acid solutions at 25 °C are tested: HCl (strong), HF (Ka = 6.6x10^(-4)), HCN (Ka = 4.9x10^(-10)), and CH3COOH (Ka = 1.8x10^(-5)). Considering that pH depends on the extent of dissociation, which solution has the LOWEST pH?
why: HCl is the only strong acid here; it fully dissociates to give [H+] = 0.10 M and pH = 1.0. The weak acids dissociate only partially, giving higher pH (HF ~ 2.1, CH3COOH ~ 3.4, HCN ~ 5.2).

q: A dilute 0.10 M aqueous H2SO4 solution at 25 °C is prepared. The first ionization (H2SO4 -> H+ + HSO4-) is essentially complete (strong), while the second (HSO4- ⇌ H+ + SO4^(2-), Ka2 ≈ 1.2x10^(-2)) is moderate but not fully dissociated. How many H+ does H2SO4 effectively donate per molecule?
why: H2SO4 is diprotic; the first H+ ionizes completely, but the second has Ka2 ≈ 1.2x10^(-2), so it is only partially dissociated in dilute solution. The effective [H+] per H2SO4 is between 1 and 2.

q: Two weak acids at 25 °C are compared: HF with pKa = 3.18 and CH3COOH with pKa = 4.74. The stronger acid has the LARGER Ka and therefore the SMALLER pKa. Which of these two acids is the stronger acid?
opts: CH3COOH because it has more atoms
why: Smaller pKa means larger Ka, hence stronger acid. HF (pKa 3.18) ionizes more than CH3COOH (pKa 4.74), making HF the stronger acid by a factor of ~36 in Ka.

q: A biochemist needs to prepare an aqueous buffer at 25 °C with target pH = 7.0 and uses the rule that the best buffer has pKa within ±1 of the target pH. The available buffer systems and their pKa values are: acetate (4.74), phosphate (7.21), ammonia (9.25), and carbonate (10.3). Which buffer is BEST suited for pH = 7.0?
why: A buffer is most effective when pKa is within ±1 of the target pH. |7.21 − 7.00| = 0.21 (best); other systems are too far. Phosphate is the standard physiological buffer near pH 7.

q: The Henderson–Hasselbalch equation for a buffer of weak acid HA and conjugate base A- at 25 °C is pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]). At a particular concentration ratio, the buffer's pH equals exactly its pKa. What is the value of the ratio [A-]/[HA] under that condition?
why: When [A-] = [HA], the ratio is 1, log(1) = 0, and pH = pKa + 0 = pKa. This is the half-equivalence (mid-titration) point of a weak-acid titration.

q: A buffer at 25 °C contains 0.10 M weak acid HA and 0.50 M conjugate base A-, where the weak acid has pKa = 5.00. Using the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]) and the given concentrations, what is the pH of this buffer?
why: log([A-]/[HA]) = log(0.50/0.10) = log(5) ≈ 0.70. pH = 5.00 + 0.70 = 5.70. Inverting the ratio gives 4.30, a common error.

q: A buffer chemist is selecting a weak-acid system to control pH near a target value. According to the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]), the buffer is most effective when [A-]/[HA] is between 0.1 and 10. Within how many pH units of pKa should the target pH lie for an effective buffer?
why: log(10) = 1 and log(0.1) = -1, so the ratio range 0.1–10 corresponds to pH = pKa ± 1. Outside this range, one component is too dilute to neutralize added acid or base effectively.

q: A chemist prepares an NH4+/NH3 buffer at 25 °C with pKa(NH4+) = 9.25 and target pH = 10.00. Using the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation pH = pKa + log([NH3]/[NH4+]), what ratio [NH3]/[NH4+] is required to reach the target pH?
why: log([NH3]/[NH4+]) = pH − pKa = 10.00 − 9.25 = 0.75. [NH3]/[NH4+] = 10^0.75 ≈ 5.6. Inverting gives 0.18; using base-e instead of base-10 gives ~2.1.

q: A 100. mL buffer at 25 °C contains 0.010 mol HA and 0.010 mol A- (pKa = 4.74). 0.005 mol HCl is added (no volume change assumed). HCl converts A- -> HA: new mol HA = 0.015, new mol A- = 0.005. Using pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]), what is the new pH?
why: log(0.005/0.015) = log(1/3) ≈ -0.477. pH = 4.74 + (-0.48) = 4.26. Forgetting the sign of log gives 5.22; ignoring the shift gives 4.74.

q: A 100. mL buffer at 25 °C contains 0.010 mol HA and 0.010 mol A- (pKa = 4.74). 0.001 mol NaOH is added with no volume change. NaOH converts HA -> A-: new mol HA = 0.009, new mol A- = 0.011. Using pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]), what is the new pH?
why: log(0.011/0.009) = log(1.222) ≈ 0.087. pH = 4.74 + 0.09 = 4.83. Forgetting the small adjustment leaves 4.74; flipping the ratio gives 4.65.

q: A 0.10 M HA / 0.10 M A- buffer at 25 °C is treated with small additions of strong acid or strong base, and the pH changes only slightly compared to an equivalent unbuffered solution. Considering the chemical species available in the buffer to react with added acid/base, why does the buffer resist large pH changes?
opts: HA neutralizes added base; A- neutralizes added acid
Buffers are very dilute and hence robust
Buffers raise the temperature, suppressing dissociation
why: Added OH- is consumed by HA (HA + OH- -> A- + H2O); added H+ is consumed by A- (A- + H+ -> HA). Both reactions shift the [A-]/[HA] ratio only slightly, so pH changes minimally per Henderson–Hasselbalch.

q: In a strong-acid–strong-base titration, 25.0 mL of 0.10 M HCl is titrated with 0.10 M NaOH at 25 °C. At the equivalence point, all HCl has reacted with NaOH to give NaCl + H2O, and the solution contains only the spectator ions Na+ and Cl-. What is the pH at the equivalence point?
why: At the SA + SB equivalence point, the resulting salt (NaCl) is the conjugate of a strong acid and strong base — neither hydrolyzes. The solution is pure salt water at pH = 7 (at 25 °C).

q: A chemist titrates 25.0 mL of 0.10 M HCl with 0.10 M NaOH at 25 °C, reaching the equivalence point at pH = 7.0. The pH jumps very steeply across this point (from ~3 to ~11). Which acid–base indicator's color-change range is best centered on the equivalence-point pH?
why: Bromothymol blue (6.0–7.6) brackets pH 7, exactly the SA+SB equivalence-point pH. Although phenolphthalein is also acceptable for SA+SB titrations because of the steep jump, BTB is the best-centered choice.
