q: A 25.0 mL sample of monoprotic 0.10 M HCl is titrated with 0.10 M NaOH at 25 °C, and a pH curve is recorded versus titrant volume. Considering that HCl donates only one proton and that the curve has a single steep jump in pH, how many equivalence points does this titration exhibit?
why: HCl is monoprotic and donates only one H+, so it has exactly one equivalence point. Diprotic acids (e.g., H2SO4 in concentrated form, H2CO3) can show 2; triprotic (e.g., H3PO4) can show 3.

q: At 25 °C, 25.0 mL of 0.20 M acetic acid (Ka = 1.8x10^(-5)) is titrated with 25.0 mL of 0.20 M NaOH, exactly reaching the equivalence point. The product is 0.10 M sodium acetate (CH3COO-) in 50.0 mL solution. Using Kb = Kw/Ka and [OH-] ≈ sqrt(Kb·[A-]), what is the equivalence-point pH?
why: Kb = 1x10^(-14)/1.8x10^(-5) = 5.56x10^(-10). [OH-] ≈ sqrt(5.56x10^(-10) x 0.10) ≈ 7.45x10^(-6) M. pOH ≈ 5.13, so pH ≈ 8.87 (closest answer: 8.72; the slightly different number reflects rounding). At a WA + SB equivalence point, pH > 7.

q: Solid AgBr is sparingly soluble in water at 25 °C and dissociates as AgBr(s) ⇌ Ag+(aq) + Br-(aq). Using the convention that pure solids have unit activity (and are omitted from K), what is the correct Ksp expression for AgBr?
why: Ksp is the product of dissolved-ion molarities raised to their stoichiometric powers, with the pure-solid activity equal to 1. For AgBr (1:1), Ksp = [Ag+][Br-].

q: CaSO4 is sparingly soluble in water at 25 °C and dissociates as CaSO4(s) ⇌ Ca^(2+) + SO4^(2-) with Ksp = 4.9x10^(-5). Defining molar solubility s such that [Ca^(2+)] = [SO4^(2-)] = s, then Ksp = s^2. What is the molar solubility s of CaSO4?
why: Ksp = s·s = s^2 = 4.9x10^(-5). s = sqrt(4.9x10^(-5)) ≈ 7.0x10^(-3) M. Forgetting the square root (using Ksp directly) gives 4.9x10^(-5) M.

q: A chemist mixes two aqueous solutions at 25 °C and computes the reaction quotient Q for a possible precipitation product. The measured Q is found to be smaller than the literature Ksp for that salt. Using the Q vs Ksp criterion for precipitation, will a precipitate form?
opts: Yes, but only at low T
why: If Q < Ksp, the solution is unsaturated and no precipitate forms; more solid would need to dissolve to reach saturation. Q > Ksp causes precipitation; Q = Ksp is saturated.

q: At 25 °C, Ksp(PbCl2) = 1.6x10^(-5) for PbCl2(s) ⇌ Pb^(2+) + 2 Cl-. A solution is prepared with [Pb^(2+)] = 0.010 M and [Cl-] = 0.010 M. Calculate Q = [Pb^(2+)][Cl-]^2 and compare to Ksp to predict whether a precipitate forms.
why: Q = (0.010)(0.010)^2 = 1.0x10^(-6). Compare to Ksp = 1.6x10^(-5): Q < Ksp, so the solution is unsaturated and no precipitate forms. Forgetting the square on [Cl-] gives Q = 10^(-4) (wrongly predicting ppt).

q: A galvanic cell at 25 °C is constructed with a Zn electrode in 1.0 M ZnSO4 and a Cu electrode in 1.0 M CuSO4, connected by a salt bridge. Considering the standard convention that the electrode where electrons are released is named for the half-reaction occurring there, what redox process happens at the anode?
why: By definition, the anode is the site of oxidation (loss of electrons) in any electrochemical cell. The cathode is the site of reduction. Mnemonic: An Ox / Red Cat.

q: A standard galvanic (voltaic) cell at 25 °C is built and the standard cell potential E°_cell is computed from tabulated half-cell reduction potentials. Using the relation ΔG° = -nFE°_cell, the cell operates spontaneously if ΔG° < 0. What sign of E°_cell does this require?
why: ΔG° = -nFE°_cell; for ΔG° < 0 (spontaneous), we need E°_cell > 0. A positive cell potential drives current flow from anode to cathode through the external circuit.

q: A galvanic cell at 25 °C is constructed with copper (E°(Cu^(2+)/Cu) = +0.34 V) and zinc (E°(Zn^(2+)/Zn) = -0.76 V) half-cells in 1.0 M solutions, connected by a salt bridge. Using E°_cell = E°_cathode - E°_anode (cathode is the more positive E°), what is the standard cell potential?
why: Cu^(2+)/Cu is the cathode (more positive); Zn^(2+)/Zn is the anode. E°_cell = +0.34 - (-0.76) = +1.10 V. Adding magnitudes (giving 0.42) is a common sign error.

q: In an operating galvanic cell at 25 °C, electrons flow externally from anode to cathode, while ions flow through the salt bridge to maintain electrical neutrality in each half-cell. Cations from the salt-bridge electrolyte (e.g., K+) migrate to balance charge buildup. In which direction do these cations move?
why: At the cathode, reduction consumes positive ions (e.g., Cu^(2+) -> Cu), creating a buildup of negative charge. Cations from the salt bridge flow toward the cathode to neutralize this; anions flow to the anode.

q: A reference table at 25 °C lists standard reduction potentials: F2/F- = +2.87 V, Cl2/Cl- = +1.36 V, I2/I- = +0.54 V, and Li+/Li = -3.04 V. The species with the LARGEST E°_red has the strongest tendency to gain electrons. Which is the strongest oxidizing agent (strongest oxidizer)?
why: Higher E°_red means a greater tendency to be reduced — i.e., to oxidize something else. F2 (E° = +2.87 V) has the largest E°_red of common reagents, making it the strongest oxidizer.

q: A reference table at 25 °C lists standard reduction potentials: F2/F- = +2.87 V, Cu^(2+)/Cu = +0.34 V, Au^(3+)/Au = +1.50 V, and Li+/Li = -3.04 V. The species with the most NEGATIVE E°_red has the strongest tendency to lose electrons. Which is the strongest REDUCING AGENT?
why: Most negative E°_red means the reverse (oxidation) is most favorable; that species (or its metal form) is the best reducing agent. Li+/Li at -3.04 V is the most negative, so Li metal is the strongest reducer of these options.

q: At 25 °C, a strip of Zn metal is placed in 1.0 M Cu^(2+) solution. The standard reduction potentials are E°(Zn^(2+)/Zn) = -0.76 V and E°(Cu^(2+)/Cu) = +0.34 V. Calculating E°_cell = E°_cathode - E°_anode for Zn(s) + Cu^(2+) -> Zn^(2+) + Cu(s) and applying the spontaneity criterion E°_cell > 0, will Zn reduce Cu^(2+)?
why: E°_cell = +0.34 - (-0.76) = +1.10 V > 0, so the reaction is spontaneous. Zn is below Cu in the activity series, so Zn reduces Cu^(2+) to Cu metal.

q: A piece of Fe metal at 25 °C (E°(Fe^(2+)/Fe) = -0.44 V) is placed in four separate 1.0 M solutions of metal ions: Mg^(2+) (-2.37 V), Cu^(2+) (+0.34 V), Li+ (-3.04 V), and Na+ (-2.71 V). Iron is oxidized only by ions whose E°_red is MORE POSITIVE than Fe's. Which ion can oxidize Fe?
why: For Fe to be oxidized, the oxidizing ion must have E°_red > E°(Fe^(2+)/Fe) = -0.44 V. Only Cu^(2+) (+0.34) qualifies; the others are more negative and cannot oxidize Fe.

q: At 25 °C, the cell reaction is 2 Ag+(aq) + Cu(s) -> 2 Ag(s) + Cu^(2+)(aq), with E°(Ag+/Ag) = +0.80 V and E°(Cu^(2+)/Cu) = +0.34 V. Using E°_cell = E°_cathode - E°_anode (potentials are intensive, NOT multiplied by stoichiometric coefficients), what is E°_cell?
why: Cathode (reduction): Ag+ + e- -> Ag, E° = +0.80 V. Anode (oxidation): Cu -> Cu^(2+), E°_red = +0.34 V. E°_cell = 0.80 - 0.34 = +0.46 V. NOT multiplied by 2, since potentials are intensive.

q: The Nernst equation at 25 °C reads E = E° - (0.0592/n)·log Q for an electrochemical cell with reaction quotient Q. At equilibrium, the cell is no longer producing useful work and the voltage drops to zero. What does Q equal at equilibrium?
why: At equilibrium, Q = K and E = 0. Substituting into Nernst: 0 = E° - (0.0592/n) log K, giving log K = nE°/0.0592 (the link between E° and K).

q: A galvanic cell at 25 °C has E°_cell = 1.00 V with n = 2 electrons transferred. Under non-standard conditions where Q = 10, calculate the actual cell voltage E using the Nernst equation E = E° - (0.0592/n)·log Q.
why: (0.0592/2)·log(10) = 0.0296 x 1 = 0.0296. E = 1.00 - 0.030 = 0.97 V. With Q > 1 (more products than equilibrium), E is below E°. Forgetting the negative sign gives 1.03 V.

q: A galvanic cell at 25 °C operates under non-standard conditions described by the Nernst equation E = E° - (0.0592/n)·log Q. The chemist measures E to be MORE POSITIVE than E°, indicating greater driving force than at standard state. What is required of Q?
why: For E > E°, the second term must be negative: -(0.0592/n)·log Q < 0 means log Q < 0, i.e., Q < 1. More reactants than products gives a stronger driving force toward products, raising E.

q: A concentration cell at 25 °C consists of two Cu electrodes immersed in Cu^(2+) solutions of different concentrations (0.001 M and 1.0 M), connected by a salt bridge. Because both half-cells use the SAME redox couple, the standard potentials of the two halves are identical. What is E° for the overall concentration cell?
why: Both halves have the same E° (Cu^(2+)/Cu), so E°_cell = E°_cath - E°_an = 0. The voltage arises entirely from the concentration difference via the Nernst term -(0.0592/n)·log Q.

q: At 25 °C, a galvanic cell has E°_cell = 0.50 V and n = 2 electrons transferred per cell reaction. Using the relation between E° and K: log K = nE°/0.0592, calculate the equilibrium constant K for the cell reaction.
why: log K = nE°/0.0592 = (2)(0.50)/0.0592 = 16.9 ≈ 17. Therefore K ≈ 10^17. Forgetting n (using just E°/0.0592) gives ~10^8.5; sign errors give 10^(-17).

q: A hydrogen electrode operating at 25°C (298 K) is immersed in a solution buffered to pH 4.00 with H2 gas bubbling at 1.00 atm above the platinum surface. Given the half-reaction 2H+ + 2e- -> H2 with E° = 0.000 V and n = 2, what is the electrode potential E predicted by the Nernst equation?
why: Apply E = E° - (0.0592/n)log Q with Q = P(H2)/[H+]^2 = 1/(10^-4)^2 = 10^8. So E = 0 - (0.0592/2)(8) = -0.2368 V, which rounds to -0.24 V. The negative sign reflects that low [H+] makes reduction less favorable.

q: A 32.0 mg sample of iodine-131 (t1/2 = 8.02 days) is stored in a lead-shielded vial at room temperature for exactly 16.04 days, allowing two complete half-lives to elapse. What fraction of the original I-131 atoms remain undecayed at the end of this storage period?
why: The fraction remaining after n half-lives is N/N0 = (1/2)^n. With n = 2, the fraction is (1/2)^2 = 1/4, so 8.0 mg of I-131 remain. Each half-life independently halves the surviving population.

q: A 1.00 g sample of radium-226 (Z = 88), used historically in luminous paints, undergoes alpha decay by emitting a 4He nucleus from each parent atom. Writing the balanced nuclear equation 226-88 Ra -> X + 4-2 He, identify the daughter nuclide X produced in this single decay step.
why: Alpha emission reduces mass number A by 4 and atomic number Z by 2. From 226-88 Ra: A = 226 - 4 = 222 and Z = 88 - 2 = 86, giving radon-222. Conservation of A and Z drives every nuclear decay equation.

q: Carbon-14 produced naturally in the upper atmosphere undergoes beta-minus (electron) emission with a half-life of 5730 years, the basis of radiocarbon dating. In the nuclear equation 14-6 C -> X + 0-1 e + antineutrino, what is the daughter nuclide X formed when a neutron in the C-14 nucleus converts into a proton?
why: In beta-minus decay a neutron becomes a proton plus an emitted electron, so A is unchanged and Z increases by 1. From 14-6 C, the daughter has A = 14 and Z = 7, which is nitrogen-14. Mass and charge are conserved across the equation.

q: Solid CO2 (dry ice) has a triple point at 5.11 atm and 216.6 K, so its solid-liquid-gas point lies above 1 atm. If gaseous CO2 at 1.00 atm is cooled isobarically from 25°C down through 195 K, which phase transition occurs first as the temperature line crosses a phase boundary?
opts: Gas deposits directly to solid (sublimation line)
Gas condenses to liquid at the boiling line
why: Because 1 atm lies below the 5.11 atm triple-point pressure of CO2, the liquid phase is not stable at this pressure. Cooling the gas at 1 atm therefore crosses only the gas-solid boundary, depositing CO2 directly as dry ice. The reverse process is the familiar sublimation observed at room conditions.

q: A 25.0 mL aliquot of 0.100 M phosphoric acid (H3PO4; pKa1 = 2.15, pKa2 = 7.20, pKa3 = 12.35) is titrated with 0.100 M NaOH while monitoring pH with a calibrated electrode. Considering the three sequential acid dissociations, how many distinct equivalence-point inflections appear in the resulting titration curve (the third is often poorly resolved but theoretically present)?
why: A polyprotic acid with n acidic protons gives n equivalence points, one per stepwise neutralization. H3PO4 has three acidic protons, so three equivalence points exist at moles NaOH = 1, 2, and 3 times moles H3PO4. The third is faint because pKa3 is near pKw, but it is still a true equivalence point.

q: A blood-buffer model solution of 0.0500 M carbonic acid (H2CO3; pKa1 = 6.35, pKa2 = 10.33) is titrated at 25°C with 0.0500 M NaOH. At the SECOND half-equivalence point, where exactly half of the bicarbonate (HCO3-) has been converted to carbonate (CO3^2-), what pH does a properly calibrated meter report?
why: By Henderson-Hasselbalch, pH = pKa + log([base]/[acid]); at the half-equivalence point [base] = [acid], so pH = pKa. For the second deprotonation [HCO3-] = [CO3^2-], so pH = pKa2 = 10.33.

q: A chemistry student dissolves four reagents separately in dry, aprotic dichloromethane at 25°C: HCl, BF3, NH3, and OH-. They then test each for the ability to accept an electron pair (Lewis acid) versus the ability to donate a proton (Bronsted acid). Which species behaves as a Lewis acid yet has NO ionizable proton to donate, making it Bronsted-inactive?
why: BF3 has an empty 2p orbital on boron and accepts an electron pair, fulfilling the Lewis-acid definition. It has no H to release, so it cannot be a Bronsted acid. HCl is both a Bronsted and Lewis acid, while NH3 and OH- are bases.

q: When equimolar amounts of NH3 and BF3 are combined in dry hexane at 0°C, they react instantly to form the adduct H3N-BF3, in which a B-N coordinate covalent bond is established. In this single-step Lewis acid-base reaction, how should NH3 be classified based on the role of its lone pair?
why: A Lewis base donates an electron pair; a Lewis acid accepts one. NH3 donates the lone pair on nitrogen into boron's empty orbital, so NH3 is the Lewis base. No proton transfer occurs, so the Bronsted classification does not apply.

q: Consider HCl ionizing in water (Bronsted) and BF3 accepting NH3's lone pair to form H3N-BF3 (Lewis). Comparing the two definitions: a Bronsted acid donates a proton (which has an empty 1s orbital), while a Lewis acid accepts an electron pair. Which statement correctly describes the relationship between Bronsted and Lewis acid categories?
opts: Every Bronsted acid is also a Lewis acid
Every Lewis acid is also a Bronsted acid
The two categories are mutually exclusive
Only Bronsted theory applies in water
Only Lewis theory applies to organic solvents
why: Donating an H+ is equivalent to having a proton accept an electron pair from the base, so all Bronsted acids meet the Lewis criterion. The reverse fails: Lewis acids like BF3 or AlCl3 contain no proton to donate. Lewis is the broader category and includes Bronsted as a subset.

q: A 25.0 mL sample of 0.100 M acetic acid (pKa = 4.74) is titrated with 0.100 M NaOH at 25°C, giving an equivalence-point pH near 8.7 because the conjugate base CH3COO- hydrolyzes. Choosing an indicator whose color change brackets that equivalence pH, which of the following is the BEST choice?
why: An indicator works best when its pKa lies within ~1 pH unit of the equivalence-point pH, since color changes occur around its pKa. The weak acid/strong base equivalence pH (~8.7) is closest to phenolphthalein's pKa ~9.0. Methyl orange and methyl red would change too early on the buffer plateau.

q: A 25.00 mL Class A volumetric pipet stamped 'TD 20°C' is used to deliver acetic acid solution into a flask. After the meniscus drains under gravity, a small droplet remains in the tip. According to standard pipetting technique, how should this final drop be handled to deliver the calibrated 25.00 mL?
opts: Blow it out forcefully into the flask
Leave it in the tip; calibration accounts for it
Tilt the pipet sideways to add it
Add a drop of distilled water to chase it
Tap the pipet against the flask to dislodge it
why: TD ('to deliver') pipets are calibrated assuming the residual tip drop remains; blowing it out adds an extra ~0.02-0.05 mL beyond the stated volume. TC ('to contain') pipets are different and do require rinsing or blow-out. Always touch the tip to glass to release the hanging drop, then stop.

q: An analyst weighs a sample of NaCl on an analytical balance and records the mass as 0.00450 g for use in a standardization calculation. Counting digits according to the convention that leading zeros are placeholders but trailing zeros after a decimal are significant, how many significant figures does this measurement contain?
why: Leading zeros (0.00) are not significant; the digits 4, 5, and the trailing 0 after the decimal are. So 0.00450 has 3 sig figs. In scientific notation it is 4.50 x 10^-3, which makes the count obvious.

q: A spectrophotometer manual reports the molar absorptivity of a dye at 1.200 x 10^3 L/(mol·cm). Because scientific notation removes ambiguity about trailing zeros, every digit shown in the coefficient is significant. How many significant figures does 1.200 x 10^3 contain?
why: In scientific notation a x 10^b, all digits in the coefficient a are significant. The coefficient 1.200 has four significant digits because the two trailing zeros after the decimal are meaningful. So 1.200 x 10^3 has 4 sig figs.

q: A student adds two volumes of acid measured with different glassware, recording 12.34 mL (buret) and 5.6 mL (graduated cylinder), and writes 12.34 + 5.6 = 17.94 mL on her datasheet. Applying the addition/subtraction rule that the answer keeps the fewest decimal places, what is the correctly rounded result?
why: For addition, the result has the smallest number of decimal places among the inputs. 12.34 has 2 decimals and 5.6 has 1 decimal, so the sum keeps 1 decimal place. 17.94 rounds to 17.9.

q: A reaction stoichiometry problem requires the product 4.56 x 1.4 (concentration in M times path length in cm). The calculator displays 6.384, but proper sig-fig rules for multiplication state the answer keeps the smallest number of significant figures among the factors. What is the correctly reported result?
why: Multiplication retains the smallest sig-fig count of the factors. 4.56 has 3 sig figs and 1.4 has 2, so the product keeps 2. 6.384 rounds to 6.4.

q: A microbalance reading reports a sample mass of 0.030 g, which the analyst records exactly as displayed. Using the convention that the last significant digit conveys the precision (uncertainty in the last decimal place), how many sig figs does this measurement carry, and what is the implied uncertainty?
why: Leading zeros are placeholders, but the trailing zero after the decimal is significant. The digits 3 and 0 give 2 sig figs, with implied uncertainty in the last decimal place of ±0.001 g. Writing 3 x 10^-2 would imply only 1 sig fig and a larger uncertainty.

q: A transition-metal cation has an unpaired electron occupying a 3d orbital, characterized by principal quantum number n = 3 and angular momentum quantum number l = 2. Magnetic quantum number m_l ranges from -l to +l in integer steps. How many distinct m_l values (and therefore degenerate orbitals at the same energy) does the 3d subshell contain?
why: The number of m_l values per subshell equals 2l + 1, so the d subshell (l = 2) has 2(2) + 1 = 5 orbitals. These five orbitals are degenerate in a free atom and split in a ligand field.

q: A laser emits a photon of wavelength 400 nm (4.00 x 10^-7 m), used to excite a molecule's pi-pi* transition. Given Planck's constant h = 6.63 x 10^-34 J·s and c = 3.00 x 10^8 m/s, calculate the energy carried by a single 400 nm photon using E = hc/lambda.
why: Using E = hc/lambda = (6.63e-34)(3.0e8)/(4.0e-7) = (1.989e-25)/(4.0e-7) = 4.97 x 10^-19 J ~ 5.0 x 10^-19 J. Doubling the wavelength would halve the photon energy.

q: Liquid water at 25°C and 1 atm has an unusually high boiling point of 100°C, surface tension of 72 mN/m, and heat of vaporization of 40.7 kJ/mol compared with similar-mass molecules. These anomalies are dominated by one intermolecular force. Which IMF is strongest in pure liquid water?
why: Hydrogen bonds form when H is bonded to N, O, or F and interacts with another N/O/F lone pair. Each H2O has two donors and two acceptors, giving an extensive H-bond network worth ~20 kJ/mol per bond. This far outweighs ordinary dipole-dipole or London forces.

q: Four substances of comparable molar mass are at 1 atm: CH4 (MW 16), Ne (MW 20), HF (MW 20), and H2O (MW 18). Their boiling points reflect their dominant intermolecular forces (London only for nonpolar species, H-bonding for HF and H2O, with H2O having more H-bonds per molecule). Rank their normal boiling points from LOWEST to HIGHEST.
why: Among nonpolar species London force tracks polarizability/MW, so Ne (bp 27 K) < CH4 (bp 112 K). HF (bp 293 K) and H2O (bp 373 K) both H-bond, but each H2O can form ~2 H-bonds versus 1 for HF. Order: Ne < CH4 < HF < H2O.

q: Two C5H12 isomers (MW 72.15) are compared at 1 atm: linear n-pentane (bp 36°C) and spherical neopentane (2,2-dimethylpropane, bp 9.5°C). Both are nonpolar, so London dispersion governs. Considering how molecular shape affects surface contact area between molecules, which isomer has the HIGHER boiling point?
opts: Both equal because MWs are identical
why: London forces scale with surface contact area: linear molecules pack tightly along their length, while branched/spherical shapes minimize contact. n-Pentane has greater contact area than neopentane, giving stronger total London attraction and a higher bp (36°C vs 9.5°C).

q: A 200. g sample of distilled water in an open beaker on a hot plate is heated from 25.0°C to 75.0°C. Using the specific heat capacity of water c = 4.18 J/(g·K) and the relation q = m·c·ΔT, how much heat (in kJ) is absorbed by the water?
why: q = m·c·ΔT = (200 g)(4.18 J/g·K)(50 K) = 41,800 J = 41.8 kJ. ΔT in K is identical to ΔT in °C, so no conversion is needed for the temperature difference.

q: A 50.0 g iron block (c = 0.45 J/g·K) heated to 100.0°C is dropped into a coffee-cup calorimeter holding 200.0 g water (c = 4.18 J/g·K) at 20.0°C. Assuming negligible heat loss to surroundings, which equation correctly relates the heat exchanged between iron and water at thermal equilibrium?
opts: q_iron = -q_water (heat lost by iron = heat gained by water)
why: Conservation of energy in an isolated calorimeter requires q_iron + q_water = 0, i.e. q_iron = -q_water. Heat lost by the hot metal equals heat gained by the cool water, with the sign flip indicating direction of flow.

q: A general-chemistry lab measures ΔH of neutralization by mixing 50 mL of 1.0 M HCl with 50 mL of 1.0 M NaOH inside a nested polystyrene-foam (Styrofoam) cup with a cardboard lid. Compared to using a metal beaker or thin glass cup, why is the polystyrene cup the preferred calorimeter material?
opts: Excellent thermal insulator that minimizes heat loss to surroundings
Conducts heat faster, reaching equilibrium quicker
Reacts with acids to absorb extra heat
why: Polystyrene foam has low thermal conductivity (~0.03 W/m·K), so very little heat escapes during the experiment. This keeps the calorimeter approximately adiabatic, validating q_rxn = -q_solution. Metal would conduct heat away rapidly and ruin the measurement.

q: An electroplating cell contains 0.50 M CuSO4(aq) and runs at a constant current of 1.00 A for 1.00 hour at 25°C. The cathode half-reaction is Cu^2+ + 2e- -> Cu(s). Using F = 96485 C/mol e- and M(Cu) = 63.5 g/mol, calculate the mass of copper deposited on the cathode.
why: Charge Q = It = (1.00 A)(3600 s) = 3600 C. Moles of e- = 3600/96485 = 0.0373 mol; moles of Cu = 0.0373/2 = 0.01866 mol; mass = 0.01866 x 63.5 ~ 1.18 g. Forgetting to divide by n = 2 gives the doubled distractor 2.37 g.

q: A silver-plating bath uses Ag+ + e- -> Ag(s) at a constant current of 0.50 A. To deposit exactly 1.00 g of silver (M = 108 g/mol) on a piece of jewelry, how many minutes must the cell run? Use F = 96,485 C/mol and t = nFm/(IM).
why: Moles Ag = 1.00/108 = 0.00926 mol; moles e- = 0.00926; charge Q = 0.00926 x 96485 = 893 C. Time t = Q/I = 893/0.50 = 1787 s ~ 30 min. n = 1 because Ag+ accepts a single electron.

q: In the Hall-Heroult process, molten Al2O3 is electrolyzed at ~960°C to deposit aluminum at the cathode via Al^3+ + 3e- -> Al(s). To produce exactly 1.00 mol of aluminum metal (27 g), how many moles of electrons must flow through the cell?
why: Stoichiometry of the cathode half-reaction shows 3 mol of electrons reduce 1 mol of Al^3+ to Al. So 1 mol Al requires 3 mol e- = 3 x 96485 ~ 2.9 x 10^5 C. The factor n equals the change in oxidation state.

q: Two electrolytic cells are wired in SERIES so the same current passes through both: cell 1 deposits Cu (Cu^2+ + 2e- -> Cu, M = 63.5), cell 2 deposits Ag (Ag+ + e- -> Ag, M = 108). For every 1.00 g of Cu plated in cell 1, what mass of Ag is plated in cell 2?
why: Same charge, so moles e- equal: moles Cu x 2 = moles Ag x 1. Moles Cu = 1.00/63.5 = 0.01575 mol, moles Ag = 0.0315 mol, mass Ag = 0.0315 x 108 = 3.40 g. Forgetting the n-factor mismatch yields the trap 1.7 g.

q: A heating curve for 1.00 mol of pure water is recorded at 1.00 atm by adding heat at a steady 100 W and plotting temperature versus time. The curve shows a long horizontal plateau at 100°C lasting until all liquid is gone. What does this flat segment physically represent?
opts: Vaporization (l -> g phase change at constant T)
why: During a phase change at 1 atm, added heat goes entirely into breaking IMFs (PE up) without raising kinetic energy/T. So T is constant while heat = n·ΔHvap is absorbed, producing the plateau at the boiling point.

q: On a complete heating curve from -10°C ice to 110°C steam at 1 atm, four energy demands per gram apply: heating ice (c_ice = 2.09 J/g·K), fusion (ΔHf = 334 J/g), heating liquid (c_liq = 4.18 J/g·K, 0->100°C), and vaporization (ΔHv = 2260 J/g). Which segment requires the MOST energy per gram?
why: Per gram: heating ice ~21 J, fusion 334 J, heating liquid 418 J, vaporization 2260 J. ΔHvap dominates because complete IMF disruption (gas formation) requires far more energy than mere lattice loosening. This is why steam burns are so severe.

q: Both 100°C steam and 100°C boiling water reach skin at the same starting temperature, yet a steam burn is far more severe than a boiling-water burn. The skin captures all heat released as the fluid cools to body temperature. Which physical quantity primarily explains the extra damage from steam?
opts: Steam is hotter than boiling water
Condensing steam releases ΔHvap (~2260 J/g) before any cooling occurs
Steam moves faster and impacts harder
Steam has a larger specific heat than liquid water
Skin reflects liquid water but absorbs steam
why: When steam condenses on skin it deposits ~2260 J/g in latent heat before any sensible cooling, on top of any q = mcΔT. Boiling water releases only the smaller mcΔT term. Latent heat of vaporization is the dominant energy contribution.

q: For the standard Daniell-style cell Zn(s) + Cu^2+(aq) -> Zn^2+(aq) + Cu(s) at 25°C, n = 2 and E°cell = +1.10 V. Setting E = 0 in the Nernst equation E = E° - (0.0592/n)·log Q corresponds to the reaction reaching equilibrium (Q = K). Solve for the value of Q at which E = 0.
why: Set E = 0: 0 = 1.10 - (0.0592/2)·log Q, so log Q = 1.10·2/0.0592 = 37.16, giving Q = 10^37. At equilibrium Q = K, confirming the reaction goes essentially to completion.

q: A galvanic cell at 25°C is assembled with reactants and products at non-standard concentrations and the measured EMF is found to be LESS than its E° value. Using the Nernst equation E = E° - (0.0592/n)·log Q, what does this observation indicate about the reaction quotient Q?
why: If E < E°, then -(0.0592/n)·log Q is negative, requiring log Q > 0, i.e. Q > 1. The cell has accumulated products (or depleted reactants), so EMF has fallen toward zero as it approaches equilibrium.

q: A buret reading of 2.36 mL is added to a graduated-cylinder reading of 0.011 mL, then the sum is multiplied by a measured concentration factor of 1.20. Apply addition rules first (smallest decimal places), THEN multiplication rules (smallest sig figs) to determine the correct value of (2.36 + 0.011) x 1.20.
why: Add: 2.36 + 0.011 = 2.371; rounded to 2 decimal places (the addition rule) gives 2.37 (3 sig figs). Multiply: 2.37 x 1.20 = 2.844, with both factors having 3 sig figs, so report 2.84.

q: A trace-metal analysis report gives the lead concentration in a water sample as 0.00050300 g/L exactly as printed on the data sheet. Counting all non-leading-zero digits including trailing zeros after the last nonzero digit, how many significant figures does this value carry?
why: Leading zeros (0.000) are placeholders. The digits 5, 0, 3, 0, 0 are significant: the first 5 starts the count, and trailing zeros after a decimal are significant. Total = 5 sig figs (or 5.0300 x 10^-4).

q: A 350 nm UV photon strikes a sodium photocathode whose work function is phi = 2.28 eV. Using the photoelectric relation KE = E_photon - phi and the convenient formula E_photon (eV) ~ 1240/lambda(nm), calculate the maximum kinetic energy of the ejected photoelectron.
why: E_photon = 1240/350 = 3.54 eV. KE = 3.54 - 2.28 = 1.26 eV. Because E_photon > phi, ejection occurs; the leftover energy becomes kinetic energy of the photoelectron.

q: Four solids at 1 atm have the following melting points to be matched: NaCl (801°C), H2O (0°C), CH4 (-182°C), KBr (734°C). Their dominant intermolecular/lattice forces are ionic for the salts, H-bonding for water, and London dispersion for methane. Which solid has the LOWEST melting point?
why: Methane is nonpolar with only weak London forces (~1 kJ/mol), making it the easiest to melt. Ionic lattices (NaCl 787 kJ/mol lattice energy) and H-bonded water are dramatically harder to disrupt, so CH4 melts at only -182°C.

q: Carbon-11 is a positron emitter (t1/2 = 20.4 min) used in PET imaging. A proton in the C-11 nucleus converts into a neutron with the emission of a positron (and a neutrino), via 11-6 C -> X + 0+1 e + neutrino. Identify the daughter nuclide X.
why: Positron emission converts a proton to a neutron, so A is unchanged and Z decreases by 1. From 11-6 C, the daughter is 11-5 B (boron-11). Mass and charge are conserved across the equation.

q: On a single-component P-T phase diagram, the three coexistence curves (sublimation, fusion, vaporization) intersect at one unique combination of pressure and temperature called the triple point. For water this point lies at 0.006 atm and 273.16 K. Which statement is TRUE at the triple point?
opts: Solid, liquid, and gas coexist in stable equilibrium
Liquid and gas become indistinguishable (critical condition)
why: The triple point is the unique P,T at which the three two-phase coexistence lines meet, so all three phases (s, l, g) coexist simultaneously. Above the critical point, l and g merge; that is a different feature of the diagram.

q: On the CO2 phase diagram, the triple point lies at 5.11 atm and 216.6 K, while the critical point is at 73 atm and 304 K. A sample of CO2 is held at 1.00 atm and 25°C (298 K), conditions that fall well below the triple-point pressure but above its temperature. What phase is the CO2 in?
why: At 1 atm (below 5.11 atm triple-point pressure) liquid CO2 is unstable, so the diagram shows only solid below the sublimation curve and gas above. At 298 K and 1 atm we are above the sublimation curve, so CO2 exists as a gas.

q: Four solids are examined for their internal bonding character: NaCl, HCl(g), NH4Cl, and CO2. NH4Cl crystallizes as a salt with NH4+ and Cl- ions, but the cation itself contains four N-H covalent bonds (with a fifth coordinate covalent bond when forming from NH3 + H+). Which compound contains BOTH ionic AND covalent bonding?
why: NaCl is purely ionic; HCl, CO2, and H2O are purely covalent molecules. NH4Cl contains an ionic bond between NH4+ and Cl- AND four polar covalent N-H bonds inside the cation, satisfying both bond types simultaneously.

q: Molecular nitrogen (N2, MW 28, bond length 1.10 A, bond energy 945 kJ/mol) has 10 valence electrons. Filling the MO diagram (sigma_2s, sigma*_2s, pi_2p_x, pi_2p_y, sigma_2p_z) gives 8 bonding and 2 antibonding electrons. Compute its bond order using BO = (n_bonding - n_antibonding)/2.
why: Bond order = (8 - 2)/2 = 3, consistent with the Lewis structure :N#N: showing a triple bond. The very high bond energy (945 kJ/mol) and short length (1.10 A) corroborate BO = 3.

q: A thermochemistry experiment determines ΔH of HCl/NaOH neutralization in a coffee-cup calorimeter built from two nested polystyrene foam cups with a cardboard lid. The student questions why polystyrene rather than glass or metal is used. Which feature of polystyrene foam most directly justifies its choice?
opts: Excellent thermal insulator that minimizes heat lost to surroundings
Reacts less with hot acidic solutions
why: Polystyrene foam's low thermal conductivity (~0.03 W/m·K) keeps the calorimeter approximately adiabatic, so q_rxn ~ -q_solution. Metal would conduct heat to the surroundings rapidly and bias measured ΔH toward zero.

q: Iron rusts in air according to the equation 4 Fe(s) + 3 O2(g) -> 2 Fe2O3(s) at 25°C. Three moles of gaseous O2 disappear and only solid product remains. Using the rule that gases dominate entropy and Δn_gas controls ΔS for reactions with mixed phases, predict the sign and approximate magnitude of ΔS_rxn.
why: Δn_gas = 0 - 3 = -3, so 3 mol of gas disappears into a more ordered solid lattice. This collapse in microstates makes ΔS strongly negative (~-550 J/K typical for this reaction). Gases overwhelmingly dominate the entropy change.

q: A platinum catalyst is added to a slow gas-phase reaction 2 SO2 + O2 -> 2 SO3 (ΔH = -198 kJ, K_eq = 4 x 10^24 at 298 K). The catalyst lowers Ea for both the forward and reverse paths by the same amount. Which quantity is UNCHANGED by the catalyst?
why: Catalysts lower Ea symmetrically for forward and reverse, so both rate constants increase but their ratio (K_eq) is fixed. ΔH is determined by reactant/product enthalpies, which are unchanged. The system reaches the same equilibrium faster, but the position is identical.

q: An equilibrium mixture of N2(g) + 3 H2(g) ⇌ 2 NH3(g) sits in a sealed 5.00 L vessel at 500 K. A chemist injects 1.0 mol of inert argon while keeping the volume constant at 5.00 L. Considering that K_p depends only on partial pressures of N2, H2, and NH3 (not on Ar), which way does the equilibrium shift?
why: Adding inert gas at constant V does not change the partial pressures or molar concentrations of N2, H2, or NH3, so Q is unchanged and Q = K still holds. Le Chatelier's principle predicts no shift. (At constant pressure, dilution would shift toward more moles of gas.)

q: The contact-process equilibrium 2 SO2(g) + O2(g) ⇌ 2 SO3(g) is exothermic (ΔH = -198 kJ) and decreases moles of gas from 3 to 2. To MAXIMIZE the equilibrium yield of SO3 (while ignoring kinetic considerations), which combination of changes should be applied?
opts: Add inert gas at constant V
why: Exothermic forward direction is favored by lowering T (Le Chatelier removes heat). Δn_gas = -1, so increasing P pushes the system toward fewer moles of gas (forward). Combined: low T + high P maximizes SO3 yield (industrially limited by kinetics, hence the V2O5 catalyst at ~700 K).

q: When solving the ICE table for HA ⇌ H+ + A- with initial [HA]0 and Ka, the small-x approximation assumes [HA]0 - x ~ [HA]0. Practitioners use the 5% rule: the approximation is acceptable only when x/[HA]0 < 0.05. In which scenario does the approximation FAIL?
opts: When Ka is very small relative to [HA]0
It never fails for monoprotic acids
why: x ~ sqrt(Ka·[HA]0), so x/[HA]0 ~ sqrt(Ka/[HA]0). Failure occurs when Ka/[HA]0 exceeds ~10^-3 (giving x/[HA]0 > 5%). In that case solve the full quadratic instead of the simplified expression.

q: A galvanic-cell laboratory provides four standard reduction potentials at 25°C: Li+/Li = -3.04 V, Mg^2+/Mg = -2.37 V, Zn^2+/Zn = -0.76 V, Cu^2+/Cu = +0.34 V. Recall that the species with the most NEGATIVE reduction potential is the strongest reducing agent (most easily oxidized). Which metal is the STRONGEST reducing agent?
why: More negative E° (red) means the species prefers to be oxidized, releasing electrons easily; that is the textbook definition of a strong reducing agent. Li (-3.04 V) is by far the most negative, making lithium the strongest reducer of the four.

q: Two sparingly soluble salts at 25°C are compared: AgCl (Ksp = 1.8 x 10^-10, dissolves as Ag+ + Cl-) and PbI2 (Ksp = 9.8 x 10^-9, dissolves as Pb^2+ + 2 I-). Note the different stoichiometries: s for AgCl satisfies Ksp = s^2, while s for PbI2 satisfies Ksp = 4s^3. Which salt is MORE soluble in pure water?
opts: Equal because Ksp values are similar
Cannot determine without comparing s values
why: AgCl: s = sqrt(1.8e-10) = 1.3 x 10^-5 M. PbI2: s = (9.8e-9/4)^(1/3) = 1.34 x 10^-3 M. PbI2 is ~100x more soluble, even though Ksp values look 'close' on a log scale. Ksp alone cannot rank solubility when stoichiometries differ.

q: Four monoprotic acids are dissolved separately in water at 0.10 M and 25°C: HCl, HF (Ka = 6.6 x 10^-4), HClO4, and HBr. Three are strong (essentially fully dissociated), one is weak. Recall the inverse rule: weaker acid has a STRONGER conjugate base. Which acid has the STRONGEST conjugate base?
why: Strong acids (HCl, HBr, HClO4) produce essentially non-basic conjugate bases. HF is weak (Ka = 6.6 x 10^-4), so F- is the only conjugate base in this list with measurable basicity (Kb ~ 1.5 x 10^-11). Stronger acid -> weaker conjugate base.

q: A biochemist mixes solid sodium acetate into a 0.10 M acetic acid stock (pKa = 4.74) at 25°C, aiming for a final buffer pH of 5.04. Using Henderson-Hasselbalch, pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]), what ratio [acetate]/[acetic acid] is required?
why: 5.04 - 4.74 = 0.30 = log([A-]/[HA]), so [A-]/[HA] = 10^0.30 ~ 2. The ratio acetate:acid is 2:1. A 1:1 ratio would give pH = pKa = 4.74, not 5.04.

q: A physiology buffer contains 0.10 M HA and 0.20 M A- in 1.0 L of solution (pKa = 4.74). The buffer capacity for added strong acid is limited by the moles of A- available before all conjugate base is converted back to HA. Approximately how many mol/L of strong acid (H+) can be added before the buffer is exhausted?
why: Each mole of added H+ converts one mole of A- to HA. Buffering ends when [A-] reaches zero, so the maximum H+ that can be neutralized equals the initial moles of A-, ~0.20 mol/L. Beyond that, pH crashes.

q: For the dimerization 2 NO2(g) ⇌ N2O4(g) at 100°C, Kc = 4.6. A 1.00 L flask currently contains [NO2] = 0.10 M and [N2O4] = 0.020 M. Compute Q = [N2O4]/[NO2]^2 and compare with Kc to predict the direction of net reaction.
why: Q = 0.020/(0.10)^2 = 0.020/0.010 = 2.0 < Kc = 4.6, so the system has too few products. To reach equilibrium it must shift forward (consume NO2, generate N2O4) until Q rises to 4.6.

q: Four ground-state species are examined for paramagnetism (presence of unpaired electrons): Ar ([Ne]3s^2 3p^6), Mg^2+ ([Ne]), Fe^2+ ([Ar]3d^6), and Zn^2+ ([Ar]3d^10). Hund's rule applied to the d^6 configuration of Fe^2+ leaves four unpaired electrons. Which species is paramagnetic?
why: Ar (3p^6) and Mg^2+ ([Ne]) are closed-shell. Zn^2+ has 3d^10, fully filled and diamagnetic. Fe^2+ has 3d^6: filling t2g/eg (or just five degenerate d orbitals in a free ion) by Hund's rule leaves 4 unpaired e- and so is paramagnetic.

q: Four main-group elements are compared for atomic radius using x-ray covalent radii: Si (118 pm), P (110 pm), Ge (122 pm), Sn (140 pm). Atomic radius increases down a group (more shells) and decreases across a period (higher Z_eff). Which element is the LARGEST?
why: Sn lies lowest in group 14, so it has the most occupied principal shells (5p valence) and the largest radius. Going down trumps going across: Sn > Ge > Si and Si > P (same row).

q: An unknown main-group element shows successive ionization energies (kJ/mol) of 786, 1577, 3232, 4356, 16,091, 19,805, ... A huge gap appears between IE4 and IE5. The size of this jump signals that the 5th electron is being removed from a much more tightly bound (core) shell. To which group does the element belong?
why: A 'huge jump' between IE_n and IE_(n+1) reveals n valence electrons; the (n+1)-th comes from a noble-gas core. Here n = 4, so the element has 4 valence electrons - Group 14 (silicon's IE pattern, in fact).

q: Bond dissociation energies (kJ/mol) for the C-X bonds at 25°C are roughly: C-F 485, C-Cl 327, C-Br 285, C-I 213. Bond strength tracks orbital overlap, which is best for compact atoms with similar size to carbon. Rank C-X strength from strongest to weakest.
why: Bond strength generally decreases as halogen size increases because of poorer overlap with carbon's 2p orbital. So C-F (485) > C-Cl (327) > C-Br (285) > C-I (213) kJ/mol.

q: The chlorate ion ClO3- is drawn for a Lewis structure exercise. Cl contributes 7 valence electrons, each O contributes 6, and the -1 charge adds 1 more electron. How many total valence electrons must appear in the completed structure?
why: Total valence e- = 7 (Cl) + 3 x 6 (O) + 1 (charge) = 7 + 18 + 1 = 26. Distribute these as bonds and lone pairs to satisfy octets (with formal-charge minimization on Cl).

q: The nitrite ion NO2- has 18 valence electrons, a bent (V-shaped) geometry, and a bond order of 1.5 (one N-O single, one N=O double in any single resonance form). How many equivalent resonance structures must be drawn to represent the delocalized pi system correctly?
why: The double bond can be placed on either oxygen, giving 2 equivalent resonance contributors. The actual structure is the average, with each N-O bond having BO = 1.5. Three forms would only apply to a trigonal-planar species like NO3-.

q: Sulfur tetrafluoride (SF4) has a see-saw geometry with 4 S-F bonds and 1 lone pair on the central sulfur (10 electrons around S, expanded octet). Using formal charge = (valence e-) - (non-bonded e-) - (1/2)(bonded e-), what is the formal charge on the central S atom?
why: S has 6 valence electrons. In SF4: non-bonded e- = 2 (one LP); bonded e- = 8 (four bonds). FC = 6 - 2 - (8/2) = 6 - 2 - 4 = 0. Sulfur's expanded octet is allowed because of accessible 3d orbitals in some treatments.

q: The triiodide-like dichloroiodate ICl2- has 22 valence electrons around the central iodine: 2 bonding pairs to Cl and 3 equatorial lone pairs (AX2E3 by VSEPR). With the lone pairs occupying the equatorial positions of a trigonal bipyramid, what is the Cl-I-Cl bond angle?
why: AX2E3 places three lone pairs in the equatorial plane (minimizing LP-LP repulsion at 120° apart), and the two Cl ligands occupy the two axial positions opposite each other. The axial-axial Cl-I-Cl angle is therefore 180° (linear).

q: Four molecules with central atoms of differing geometries are compared: CH4 (109.5°), NH3 (107°), H2O (104.5°), and BF3 (120°). Lone-pair to bonding-pair repulsions reduce the ideal geometry's bond angles in NH3 and H2O. Which molecule has the LARGEST X-Y-X bond angle?
why: BF3 is AX3 (trigonal planar, no lone pairs on B), so F-B-F = 120°, the largest among these. CH4 (tetrahedral) is 109.5°, while NH3 (107°) and H2O (104.5°) are compressed by lone pairs.

q: Phosphorus pentachloride PCl5 in the gas phase has a trigonal-bipyramidal geometry with three equatorial P-Cl bonds at 120° and two axial bonds at 90°. The central P forms 5 sigma bonds with no lone pairs (steric number = 5). Which hybridization scheme correctly accommodates these 5 bonding orbitals?
why: Steric number 5 demands 5 hybrid orbitals: one s + three p + one d = sp^3 d. (sp^3 d^2 would be 6 hybrids for octahedral SF6.) The mixing of 3d orbitals with s and p enables the expanded octet around P.

q: A baker measures out 36.0 g of pure glucose (C6H12O6, MW 180.0 g/mol) for a fermentation experiment. Each glucose molecule contains 6 oxygen atoms. Using N_A = 6.022 x 10^23, how many oxygen atoms are present in this 36.0 g sample?
why: Moles glucose = 36.0/180 = 0.200 mol; molecules = 0.200 x 6.022e23 = 1.20e23. Each has 6 O atoms, so N(O) = 1.20e23 x 6 = 7.2 x 10^23 oxygen atoms.

q: A combustion analysis shows a hydrocarbon is 80.0% carbon and 20.0% hydrogen by mass. Assume a 100.0 g sample, then convert each mass to moles using M(C) = 12 g/mol and M(H) = 1 g/mol. After dividing both by the smaller number, what is the empirical formula?
why: Moles C = 80/12 = 6.67; moles H = 20/1 = 20. Divide both by 6.67: C = 1, H = 3. Empirical formula = CH3 (the molecular formula could be C2H6 ethane, but the question asks for empirical).

q: Propane combusts in air per C3H8 + 5 O2 -> 3 CO2 + 4 H2O. A camp stove burns 11.0 g propane (MW 44) with 32.0 g O2 (MW 32). Convert each to moles, then compare the mole ratio supplied to the stoichiometric requirement. Which reagent runs out first?
why: Moles C3H8 = 11/44 = 0.25; moles O2 = 32/32 = 1.0. Required O2 for 0.25 mol propane = 0.25 x 5 = 1.25 mol; only 1.0 mol available, so O2 is limiting. Propane is in excess.

q: Continuing the C3H8 + 5 O2 -> 3 CO2 + 4 H2O combustion with 0.25 mol propane and 1.00 mol O2 (O2 is limiting), use the stoichiometric ratio between the limiting reagent and CO2 to compute the maximum theoretical moles of CO2 produced.
why: Use the limiting reagent: 1.00 mol O2 x (3 mol CO2)/(5 mol O2) = 0.60 mol CO2. (If propane had been limiting: 0.25 x 3 = 0.75 mol — that is the trap distractor.)

q: From the same combustion (theoretical yield = 0.60 mol CO2 = 26.4 g, MW 44), a student measures an actual yield of 22.0 g CO2 trapped on lime water. Using % yield = (actual/theoretical) x 100%, calculate the percent yield.
why: Theoretical mass CO2 = 0.60 x 44 = 26.4 g. % yield = (22.0/26.4) x 100% ~ 83.3%. Reasons for less than 100% include incomplete combustion or product loss to the atmosphere.

q: A student dissolves 5.85 g of NaCl (MW 58.5 g/mol) in distilled water and dilutes the solution to a final volume of exactly 250.0 mL in a volumetric flask at 20°C. Using M = mol/L, calculate the molarity of the resulting saline solution.
why: Moles NaCl = 5.85/58.5 = 0.100 mol. Volume = 0.250 L. M = 0.100/0.250 = 0.40 M. Watch the unit conversion from mL to L.

q: A stockroom 12.0 M concentrated HCl is to be diluted into 500.0 mL of 0.100 M HCl for a titration prep. Using the dilution relation M1V1 = M2V2 (assuming volumes are additive at low concentration), what volume of stock HCl is required?
why: V1 = M2V2/M1 = (0.100)(500)/12.0 = 50/12 = 4.17 mL ~ 4.2 mL. Pipet 4.2 mL of stock into a 500 mL flask, then dilute (always add acid to water).

q: Pure water at 25°C has vapor pressure P° = 23.8 torr. A NaCl solution is prepared so the mole fraction of solvent water is chi_solvent = 0.90 (treating NaCl as a non-volatile, non-dissociating solute for this calculation). Apply Raoult's law P_solution = chi_solvent · P° to find the new vapor pressure.
why: P_solution = 0.90 x 23.8 = 21.42 torr ~ 21.4 torr. The 2.4 torr drop is the colligative vapor-pressure lowering. (A real NaCl solution would dissociate into 2 ions per formula unit, doubling the apparent solute fraction.)

q: Surface tensions at 25°C (mN/m): hexane 17.9, acetone 23.7, water 72.0, pentane 16.0. Surface tension scales with the strength of cohesive intermolecular forces. Hydrogen bonding produces unusually large cohesion. Which liquid has the HIGHEST surface tension?
why: Water's extensive H-bond network (~20 kJ/mol per bond, 2 H-bonds per molecule) produces strong cohesive forces, giving the largest surface tension (72 mN/m). Hexane and pentane have only London forces (~17 mN/m); acetone is dipolar but cannot H-bond donate strongly.

q: At 25°C and 1 atm, Br2 (MW 159.8, 70 electrons) is a dark-red liquid (bp 59°C) while Cl2 (MW 70.9, 34 electrons) is a yellow-green gas (bp -34°C). Both are nonpolar diatomics with no permanent dipole. Which IMF property explains why Br2 is liquid while Cl2 is gas?
opts: Br2 has more lone pairs than Cl2
Br2 has more electrons, giving stronger London dispersion (greater polarizability)
Br is more electronegative than Cl
why: London dispersion strength scales with polarizability, which increases with the number of electrons and atomic size. Br2 has roughly twice the electrons of Cl2, so its instantaneous dipoles are larger and the resulting attraction stronger, raising the boiling point above 25°C.

q: An electron is described by quantum numbers n = 4 and l = 2 (a 4d orbital), with m_l ranging from -2 to +2 and m_s = ±1/2. Using the formula for maximum electrons in a subshell, max e- = 2(2l + 1), how many electrons can occupy the 4d subshell at most?
why: For l = 2 (d), there are 2l + 1 = 5 orbitals; with 2 electrons each (Pauli), the max is 10. So the 4d subshell holds up to 10 electrons (transition-metal first-row d-block has 10 elements).

q: Hydrogen energy levels follow E_n = -13.6/n^2 eV. Photon energy emitted on a transition from n_high to n_low is ΔE = 13.6(1/n_low^2 - 1/n_high^2). The longest wavelength corresponds to the SMALLEST ΔE. Among the four transitions n=4->1, n=2->1, n=4->2, n=4->3, which emits the LONGEST wavelength photon?
why: Compute ΔE: 4->1 = 12.75 eV; 2->1 = 10.2 eV; 4->2 = 2.55 eV; 4->3 = 0.66 eV. Smallest ΔE = 4->3 (Paschen series, infrared, ~1875 nm). Long lambda = small E by E = hc/lambda.

q: An electron in a multi-electron atom has principal quantum number n = 3 and angular-momentum quantum number l = 1. The letter labels for l (s = 0, p = 1, d = 2, f = 3) determine the subshell name. In which subshell does this electron reside?
why: n = 3 specifies the third shell; l = 1 corresponds to the p subshell. The electron is therefore in 3p, with m_l ranging over -1, 0, +1 (three orbitals).

q: A laboratory report adds three independently measured volumes: 1.234 mL (4 sig figs), 5.6 mL (2 sig figs), and 12.34 mL (4 sig figs). The calculator returns 19.174. Apply the addition rule (smallest decimal places) to round the sum to its proper precision.
why: Decimal places: 1.234 (3), 5.6 (1), 12.34 (2). The sum keeps the smallest = 1 decimal place. 19.174 rounds to 19.2.

q: A textbook lists a town's population as 100,000 with no decimal point shown. Without a decimal point or scientific notation, trailing zeros may or may not be significant. How many significant figures should this value be reported as having?
why: Without a decimal point or scientific notation, trailing zeros in 100,000 are ambiguous: it could be 1, 2, ..., 6 sig figs depending on context. Reporting as 1.00 x 10^5 (3 sig figs) or 1.0 x 10^5 (2 sig figs) removes ambiguity.

q: A multistep calculation reports (12.0 x 0.30)/6.00. The calculator output is 0.6. Apply the multiplication/division rule: the answer keeps the smallest number of significant figures among the values used. Which value should be reported?
why: Sig figs: 12.0 has 3, 0.30 has 2, 6.00 has 3. The minimum is 2, so the result keeps 2 sig figs. (12.0 x 0.30)/6.00 = 0.60.

q: Two rigid 5.00 L flasks at 298 K hold the same number of moles of gas: Flask A contains 1.00 mol He (MW 4) and Flask B contains 1.00 mol N2 (MW 28). Apply PV = nRT, which depends only on n, V, T (not molar mass), to compare the two flask pressures.
opts: Depends on which gas leaks faster
why: Ideal-gas pressure P = nRT/V is independent of molar mass when n, V, and T are equal. With n = 1, V = 5 L, T = 298 K, P = (1)(0.0821)(298)/5 ~ 4.89 atm for both flasks. He's lower mass affects KE distribution, not P.

q: A balloon of helium initially has V1 = 2.0 L at P1 = 1.0 atm and T1 = 300 K. It is moved to a new condition where P2 = 2.0 atm and T2 = 600 K (no gas added or lost). Apply the combined gas law P1V1/T1 = P2V2/T2 and solve for V2.
why: V2 = V1 (P1/P2)(T2/T1) = 2.0 x (1.0/2.0) x (600/300) = 2.0 x 0.5 x 2 = 2.0 L. Doubling P and doubling T cancel out exactly.

q: The catalytic Ostwald oxidation of ammonia is 4 NH3 + 5 O2 -> 4 NO + 6 H2O(g). Standard enthalpies of formation (kJ/mol): NH3 = -46, NO = +90, H2O(g) = -242, O2 = 0. Use ΔH_rxn = sum(n·ΔH_f,products) - sum(n·ΔH_f,reactants) to compute ΔH_rxn for one mole of equation.
why: Products: 4(+90) + 6(-242) = 360 - 1452 = -1092. Reactants: 4(-46) + 5(0) = -184. ΔH = -1092 - (-184) = -908 kJ. The reaction is highly exothermic.

q: Two related reactions are tabulated at 298 K: (1) A -> B with ΔH1 = -50 kJ; (2) 2 B -> C with ΔH2 = +30 kJ. Apply Hess's law (multiply step 1 by 2 to match B stoichiometry, then add to step 2) to compute ΔH for the combined reaction 2 A -> C.

A 250.0 g aluminum block (specific heat c = 0.90 J/(g·K)) is removed from a 100.0°C bath and allowed to cool to 25.0°C in a calorimeter. Apply q = m·c·ΔT (using ΔT = T_final - T_initial) to determine the heat lost by the aluminum.
why: ΔT = 25 - 100 = -75 K. q = m·c·ΔT = 250 x 0.90 x (-75) = -16,875 J ~ -16.9 kJ. The aluminum loses 16.9 kJ; the magnitude (without sign) is 16.9 kJ.

q: A bomb calorimeter with a calorimeter constant of C_cal = 7.5 kJ/°C burns a 0.500 g sample of an unknown sugar, raising the bomb's temperature by 4.00°C. Using q = C_cal · ΔT (mass cancels), calculate the energy released per gram of sample.
why: Total q = 7.5 x 4.00 = 30.0 kJ. Per gram = 30.0/0.500 = 60 kJ/g. Bomb calorimeters use a known C_cal, not m·c, because the system has multiple heat-absorbing components.

q: Standard molar entropies S° at 298 K (J/(mol·K)) for several substances are: diamond C(s) 2.4, H2O(l) 70, H2O(g) 189, NaCl(s) 72. Entropy generally increases s < l < g and with greater molecular complexity/disorder. Which of the following has the HIGHEST molar entropy at 298 K?
why: Gases have far more accessible microstates than liquids or solids because of free translation and large volumes available. Diamond has unusually low entropy (rigid covalent network, S° = 2.4 J/(mol·K)). H2O(g) at 189 J/(mol·K) is the largest.

q: Limestone calcination is CaCO3(s) -> CaO(s) + CO2(g) at ~825°C. The reaction converts a single solid into a solid + 1 mol of gas. Using the principle that gas-producing reactions strongly increase disorder, predict the sign of ΔS_rxn.
why: Δn_gas = +1 (zero gas reactant; 1 mol gas product), and CO2 has S° ~ 214 J/(mol·K) far above the solids. ΔS° ~ +160 J/(mol·K) for this reaction. Reactions that liberate gas always carry strongly positive ΔS.

q: A reaction has ΔH = -120 kJ/mol and ΔS = -150 J/(K·mol). Spontaneity requires ΔG = ΔH - T·ΔS < 0. Set ΔG = 0 to find the crossover temperature, then state the temperature range over which the reaction is spontaneous.
why: Set ΔG = 0: T = ΔH/ΔS = (-120,000 J)/(-150 J/K) = 800 K. Below 800 K, the favorable enthalpy dominates the unfavorable entropy. Above 800 K, T·|ΔS| exceeds |ΔH| and the reaction becomes nonspontaneous.

q: For a 2nd-order reaction A -> products, the half-life is t1/2 = 1/(k·[A]0), so it depends inversely on initial concentration. A reaction begins with [A]0 = 0.10 M and is repeated with [A]0 = 0.20 M (same k, same T). What happens to the half-life when [A]0 is doubled?
why: Because t1/2 = 1/(k[A]0) for second order, doubling [A]0 cuts t1/2 in half. (For 1st order, t1/2 = ln2/k is independent of concentration; for zero order, t1/2 = [A]0/(2k) increases with concentration.)

q: Three initial-rate experiments at 25°C give: trial 1 [A]=1.0, [B]=1.0, rate = 0.10 M/s; trial 2 [A]=2.0, [B]=1.0, rate = 0.40 M/s; trial 3 [A]=1.0, [B]=2.0, rate = 0.10 M/s. Compare ratios to deduce the orders, then write the rate law.
why: Trials 1 vs 2 ([A] doubles, rate x4) give order 2 in A. Trials 1 vs 3 ([B] doubles, rate unchanged) give order 0 in B. So rate = k[A]^2.

q: A first-order decomposition has rate constant k = 0.0100 s^-1 at 25°C. A reactor begins with [A]0 = 1.00 M; we want to know how long until [A] drops to 0.125 M (1/8 of initial). Use ln([A]0/[A]) = kt or recognize three half-lives, then solve for t.
why: 1/8 = (1/2)^3 means three half-lives have passed. t1/2 = ln2/k = 0.693/0.010 = 69.3 s, so t = 3 x 69.3 = 208 s ~ 210 s. Equivalently ln(1/0.125)/0.01 = 208 s.

q: The Arrhenius equation k = A·exp(-Ea/RT) governs how a rate constant depends on temperature, with activation energy Ea > 0. As temperature T increases (e.g. from 300 K to 350 K) at fixed Ea and pre-exponential factor A, what happens to k?
opts: Depends on the sign of Ea (which is always positive)
why: Higher T makes the exponent -Ea/RT less negative, so exp(-Ea/RT) increases and k rises. A common rule-of-thumb is that k roughly doubles for every 10 K rise near room T. Reactions speed up with heat.

q: A catalyst lowers the activation energy of a reaction from Ea = 75 kJ/mol to 50 kJ/mol at T = 300 K. Using the Arrhenius ratio k_cat/k_uncat = exp[(Ea - Ea_cat)/(RT)] with R = 8.314 J/(mol·K), estimate the rate enhancement.
why: ΔEa = 25,000 J/mol; RT = 8.314 x 300 = 2494 J/mol; ΔEa/RT = 25,000/2494 = 10.02. exp(10.02) ~ 2.25 x 10^4 ~ 10,000x. Each ~5.7 kJ/mol drop in Ea at 300 K multiplies k by ~10.

q: For the reaction A(g) ⇌ B(g) at 500 K, the equilibrium constant is K = 100. The equation is rewritten as 2 A(g) ⇌ 2 B(g) (multiplying coefficients by 2). The new equilibrium constant equals the old one raised to the multiplier. What is the new K?
why: If a balanced equation is multiplied by factor n, K_new = K^n. Here n = 2, so K_new = 100^2 = 10,000. The original equilibrium position is unchanged - just the way K is written.

q: The Haber-Bosch synthesis N2(g) + 3 H2(g) ⇌ 2 NH3(g) is exothermic (ΔH = -92 kJ) with Δn_gas = 2 - 4 = -2 (moles of gas decrease). Le Chatelier favors the exothermic direction at low T and the side with fewer gas moles at high P. Which conditions MAXIMIZE NH3 yield?
opts: Add inert gas at constant V
why: Forward reaction is exothermic and produces fewer moles of gas, so the equilibrium shifts toward NH3 when T is lowered and P is raised. Industrially, Haber uses ~200-300 atm and ~700 K (a kinetic compromise) with an Fe-K2O catalyst.

q: The water-gas shift CO(g) + H2O(g) ⇌ CO2(g) + H2(g) has Δn_gas = 0 (2 moles gas on each side) and ΔH ~ -41 kJ. Compressing the system to half its original volume affects partial pressures equally for reactants and products. Which change has NO effect on the equilibrium position?
why: Because Δn_gas = 0, Q = (Pco2 Ph2)/(Pco Ph2o) is unchanged when all partial pressures scale by the same factor (volume change). So Q remains equal to K and the position is unaffected. Concentration changes and T changes still shift the equilibrium.

q: An ICE-table calculation for HA ⇌ H+ + A- with [HA]0 = 0.10 M solves the small-x approximation and obtains x = 0.080 M. Apply the 5% rule (x/[HA]0 should be < 5%) to evaluate whether the approximation is justified.
why: x/[HA]0 = 0.080/0.10 = 0.80 = 80% >> 5%, so the small-x approximation fails. Solve the full quadratic equation x^2 = Ka(0.10 - x) to obtain a self-consistent x and a correct equilibrium pH.

q: Phosphorus pentachloride decomposes per PCl5(g) ⇌ PCl3(g) + Cl2(g) with K_c = 1.0 at 525 K. A 1.00 L flask is charged with [PCl5]0 = 1.00 M (no PCl3 or Cl2 present). Set up the ICE table with x = [PCl3]_eq, then solve x^2/(1 - x) = 1 for [PCl3] at equilibrium.
why: x^2 = 1·(1 - x) gives x^2 + x - 1 = 0, so x = (-1 + sqrt(5))/2 ~ 0.618 M. The small-x approximation fails here (K is comparable to [PCl5]0), so the quadratic is necessary.

q: An aqueous solution at 25°C is measured with a calibrated pH electrode and reads pH = 4.00. The autoionization equilibrium of water requires [H+]·[OH-] = Kw = 1.0 x 10^-14 at this temperature. Use [H+] = 10^-4 M to compute [OH-].
why: [OH-] = Kw/[H+] = 10^-14/10^-4 = 10^-10 M. Equivalently pOH = 14 - pH = 10, so [OH-] = 10^-10 M. Both forms come from the water autoionization expression.

q: An amphiprotic species can both donate AND accept a proton (a Bronsted acid AND a Bronsted base). A test set includes NH4+ (only acid), HCO3- (intermediate of polyprotic), H3O+ (only acid), and OH- (only base). Which species in the list is amphiprotic?
why: HCO3- can donate a proton to give CO3^2- (acid behavior) or accept one to give H2CO3 (base behavior), so it is amphiprotic. Intermediate ions of polyprotic acids generally are. NH4+ donates only; OH- and H3O+ are essentially terminal in the proton-transfer chain in water.

q: Four 0.10 M solutions are prepared at 25°C: HF (Ka = 6.6 x 10^-4, weak), HCl (strong, fully ionized), CH3COOH (Ka = 1.8 x 10^-5, weak), and pure water. Strong acids dissociate completely so [H+] = formal acid concentration; weak acids give [H+] = sqrt(Ka·C). Which solution has the LOWEST pH?
why: 0.10 M HCl gives [H+] = 0.10 M, pH = 1.0 (strong, complete ionization). HF: [H+] = sqrt(6.6e-4 x 0.10) ~ 0.0081, pH ~ 2.1. CH3COOH: pH ~ 2.9. Water: pH ~ 7. HCl is by far the most acidic.

q: A 1.00 L acetate buffer at pH 4.74 (equimolar 0.10 M CH3COOH and 0.10 M CH3COO-, pKa = 4.74) is treated with a small addition of 0.005 mol NaOH. The OH- converts a small amount of CH3COOH to CH3COO-. What happens to the pH?
why: Strong base reacts 1:1 with HA, slightly increasing the [A-]/[HA] ratio. Henderson-Hasselbalch: pH = 4.74 + log(0.105/0.095) = 4.74 + 0.043 ~ 4.78, a small rise. The buffer absorbs the added OH-, preventing a dramatic change.

q: A biochemist needs a buffer at pH = 9.0 for an enzymatic assay. The best buffer has pKa within ±1 of the target pH so that the [A-]/[HA] ratio remains close to 1. Available pairs: acetic/acetate (pKa 4.74), phosphate (pKa2 7.21), NH4+/NH3 (pKa 9.25), bicarbonate/carbonate (pKa2 10.33). Which is best?
why: Buffer capacity is maximal when |pH - pKa| < 1. Distances from pH 9.0: acetate 4.26, phosphate 1.79, ammonia 0.25, bicarbonate 1.33. NH4+/NH3 (pKa 9.25) is closest to 9.0 and gives the best buffering.

q: A 1.00 L buffer of 0.10 M HA and 0.10 M A- (pKa 5.00) receives a 0.05 mol bolus of HCl, which converts 0.05 mol of A- into HA. New concentrations: [HA] = 0.15 M, [A-] = 0.05 M. Using Henderson-Hasselbalch, find the resulting pH.
why: pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]) = 5.00 + log(0.05/0.15) = 5.00 + log(0.333) = 5.00 - 0.477 = 4.52. The buffer absorbed the proton and pH dropped only ~0.5 unit instead of crashing to ~1.

q: A 25.0 mL aliquot of 0.100 M acetic acid (pKa = 4.74, weak acid) is titrated with 0.100 M NaOH (strong base). At the equivalence point all acetic acid has been converted to acetate (CH3COO-), which hydrolyzes to give a basic solution. What pH range applies at the equivalence point?
why: Conjugate base CH3COO- accepts H+ from water (Kb = Kw/Ka = 5.6 x 10^-10), generating OH-. pH at equivalence is therefore basic (~8.7 for this system). Only strong-acid + strong-base titrations give pH = 7 at equivalence.

q: A 25.0 mL sample of 0.100 M ammonia (pKb = 4.74) is titrated with 0.100 M HCl. At equivalence, all NH3 has been converted to NH4+, which hydrolyzes to give an acidic solution near pH 5.3. Choose the indicator whose pKa is closest to the equivalence pH.
why: Weak base titrated with strong acid gives acidic equivalence pH ~5.3. Methyl red (pKa ~5.0) brackets this region with a sharp color change. Phenolphthalein would change too late (basic side) and miss the equivalence inflection.

q: Magnesium hydroxide Mg(OH)2 dissolves per Mg(OH)2(s) ⇌ Mg^2+ + 2 OH- with Ksp = 5.6 x 10^-12 at 25°C. Define molar solubility s such that [Mg^2+] = s and [OH-] = 2s, then substitute to get Ksp = s·(2s)^2 = 4s^3. Solve for s in pure water.
why: s = (Ksp/4)^(1/3) = (5.6e-12/4)^(1/3) = (1.4e-12)^(1/3) = 1.12 x 10^-4 M ~ 1.1 x 10^-4 M. Forgetting the (2s)^2 factor and using sqrt(Ksp) gives the trap 2.4 x 10^-6, while using 4 x in the wrong place gives the 5.6e-6 distractor.

q: In a Daniell galvanic cell (Zn(s) | Zn^2+(aq) || Cu^2+(aq) | Cu(s)) at 25°C, electrons flow externally from anode to cathode while the salt bridge (e.g., KNO3 in agar) connects the two half-cells internally. Without the salt bridge, the cell stops working immediately. What is its primary role?
opts: Provides additional electrons to the circuit
Maintains charge balance via internal ion flow
why: As Zn^2+ accumulates in the anode compartment and Cu^2+ depletes in the cathode compartment, charge imbalance builds and stops electron flow. The salt bridge supplies anions (NO3-) to the anode side and cations (K+) to the cathode side, keeping each compartment electrically neutral.

q: Four chemical species are listed: Fe^3+, Cu^2+, Cu(s) (metallic copper), and Cl2(g). 'Most reduced form' means the species with the lowest possible oxidation state given the element's available redox states. Which species is ALREADY in its most reduced form?
why: Cu(s) has oxidation state 0, the lowest accessible state for copper (Cu^- is unstable). Fe^3+ can be reduced to Fe^2+ or Fe^0; Cu^2+ to Cu^+ or Cu^0; Cl2 to Cl^-. Only Cu(s) is at zero oxidation state already.

q: A copper strip is placed in 1.0 M HCl(aq) at 25°C. The activity series ranks Cu BELOW H2 (Cu^2+/Cu E° = +0.34 V vs 2H+/H2 E° = 0). For Cu to displace H2 the cell potential must be positive. Predict whether Cu(s) reacts with HCl(aq) to liberate H2 gas.
opts: No — Cu sits below H2 in the activity series, so reaction is not spontaneous
Yes — but only at high T
Yes — but only with a Pt catalyst
Yes — only in the presence of light
why: E°cell = E°cathode - E°anode = 0 - 0.34 = -0.34 V (negative), so Cu + 2 H+ -> Cu^2+ + H2 is non-spontaneous. Cu does not bubble in non-oxidizing acids like HCl. (Hot concentrated HNO3 attacks Cu via NO3- reduction, a different mechanism.)

q: A copper electrode is dipped into 1.00 x 10^-3 M Cu^2+ at 25°C and connected to a standard reference. For the half-reaction Cu^2+ + 2 e- -> Cu(s), E° = +0.34 V and n = 2. Apply E = E° - (0.0592/n)·log(1/[Cu^2+]) to compute the actual electrode potential E.

A concentration cell at 25°C uses Cu electrodes in two Cu^2+ solutions: [Cu^2+] = 0.10 M (left) and 1.0 M (right). Both half-cells share E° = 0 (same reaction) so E_cell is determined entirely by the concentration difference via E = -(0.0592/n) log([dilute]/[concentrated]) with n = 2. Find E_cell.
why: E_cell = (0.0592/2) log(1.0/0.10) = 0.0296 x 1 = 0.0296 V ~ 0.030 V. Concentration cells extract free energy from a concentration gradient until the two cells equalize.

q: An electrochemical cell is assembled at standard state: all dissolved species at 1.00 M, all gases at 1.00 atm, and T = 25°C (298 K). Under these conditions Q = 1 in the Nernst equation E = E° - (0.0592/n)·log Q. What does E reduce to?
why: log(1) = 0, so the correction term vanishes and E = E°. Standard state is defined precisely so that the Nernst correction drops out and E equals the tabulated E°.

q: Molten Al2O3 (cryolite-dissolved) is electrolyzed in a Hall-Heroult cell. The cathode reaction is Al^3+ + 3 e- -> Al(s), with M(Al) = 27 g/mol and F = 96485 C/mol. A total charge of 9650 C passes through the cell. Calculate the mass of aluminum deposited.
why: Moles e- = 9650/96485 = 0.100 mol. Moles Al = 0.100/3 = 0.0333 mol. Mass = 0.0333 x 27 = 0.90 g. Forgetting to divide by n = 3 gives the trap value 2.7 g.

q: An aqueous Na2SO4 cell is set up to electrolyze water; the overall reaction is 2 H2O -> 2 H2 + O2. Anode (oxidation): 2 H2O -> O2 + 4 H+ + 4 e-; cathode (reduction): 2 H2O + 2 e- -> H2 + 2 OH-. Which gas appears at the ANODE?
why: Oxidation occurs at the anode; water loses electrons to form O2 (and H+). Reduction at the cathode produces H2. The overall stoichiometry yields a 2:1 ratio of H2:O2 by volume.

q: An electroplating bath of CuSO4 deposits Cu via Cu^2+ + 2 e- -> Cu(s) at a constant current of 0.50 A. To deposit exactly 1.0 g of Cu (M = 63.5 g/mol) using F = 96485 C/mol, compute the time required from t = nFm/(IM) and convert to minutes.

A 64.0 mg sample of phosphorus-32 (t1/2 = 14.3 days) is sealed in a vial and stored for exactly 4 half-lives (~57.2 days) before use. Each half-life independently halves the surviving population. Using N/N0 = (1/2)^n, what fraction of the original P-32 atoms remains?
why: After n = 4 half-lives, fraction = (1/2)^4 = 1/16, so 4.0 mg of the original 64 mg remains. Decay is exponential, not linear, so the fraction does not scale arithmetically.

q: Carbon-14, used in radiocarbon dating, undergoes beta-minus emission per 14-6 C -> X + 0-1 e + antineutrino. Beta-minus converts a neutron to a proton, leaving A unchanged but raising Z by 1. Identify the daughter nuclide X.
why: A is conserved (14) and Z increases by 1 (6 -> 7). The daughter is nitrogen-14. This single transmutation is the basis of natural N-14 production from atmospheric C-14.

q: On a P-T phase diagram, the liquid-gas coexistence curve begins at the triple point (where solid, liquid, and gas meet) and ascends to higher T and P. Beyond a specific (P_c, T_c), the curve abruptly stops. What is the special point at which the liquid-gas line terminates?
why: The liquid-gas line ends at the critical point (P_c, T_c). Above it, liquid and vapor merge into a single supercritical fluid with no meniscus. Water's critical point is at 374°C and 218 atm.

q: A sample of pure water at -10°C and 1.00 atm is heated isobarically (constant pressure) at a steady rate of 100 W/kg until it reaches 110°C. Because 1 atm is well above the triple-point pressure (0.006 atm), all three phases are accessible by crossing the s-l and l-g boundaries. Which phase sequence is observed?
why: At 1 atm we cross the ice-liquid boundary at 0°C and the liquid-gas boundary at 100°C. So heating gives ice -> liquid -> gas. Sublimation directly to vapor would require P below the 0.006 atm triple-point pressure of water.

q: On a P-T phase diagram, the triple point is where the three two-phase coexistence curves (sublimation, fusion, vaporization) intersect at one unique combination of pressure and temperature. For water this occurs at 273.16 K and 0.00604 atm. What is true at this point?
opts: Solid, liquid, and gas all coexist in stable equilibrium
Liquid and gas become indistinguishable (critical condition)
why: By definition the triple point is the unique P,T where solid, liquid, and gas coexist simultaneously. All three two-phase boundaries meet here. Above the critical point l and g merge - that is a different feature of the diagram.

q:
The reaction A + 2B → C was studied at 25°C with the following initial rate data:
Trial[A] (M)[B] (M)Initial rate (M/s)
10.100.102.0×10−4
20.200.104.0×10−4
30.100.208.0×10−4
What is the rate law for this reaction?
why: Doubling [A] (T1→T2) doubles rate → 1st order in A. Doubling [B] (T1→T3) quadruples rate → 2nd order in B. rate = k[A][B]².

q: For the reaction N2(g) + 3 H2(g) ⇌ 2 NH3(g), ΔH = −92 kJ/mol. A reaction vessel at equilibrium contains all three gases. The temperature is then increased while the volume is kept constant. According to Le Chatelier's principle, which change correctly describes the new equilibrium position?
opts: Shifts right; more NH3 is produced because the system absorbs heat
Shifts left; the equilibrium favors reactants because the forward reaction is exothermic
No shift; temperature does not affect equilibrium position
Shifts right; Kp increases with temperature for all reactions
Shifts left; the increase in pressure compensates for added heat
why: Forward reaction is exothermic. Adding heat is like adding "product heat"; equilibrium shifts left (toward reactants) to consume the added heat.

q: A 25.0 mL sample of 0.100 M acetic acid (Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵) is titrated with 0.100 M NaOH. What is the pH at the half-equivalence point?
why: At half-equivalence, [HA] = [A⁻] in the buffer, so pH = pKa = −log(1.8×10⁻⁵) = 4.74. This is the classic Henderson-Hasselbalch result.

q: A galvanic cell is constructed with a Zn electrode in 1.0 M Zn(NO3)2 and a Cu electrode in 1.0 M Cu(NO3)2 at 25°C. The standard reduction potentials are: E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V, E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = −0.76 V. If the [Cu²⁺] is then increased to 2.0 M while [Zn²⁺] stays at 1.0 M, the new cell potential will:
opts: Decrease, because the cathode half-cell is now more dilute relative to the anode
Increase, because Q decreases and the Nernst equation gives Ecell = E°cell − (0.0592/n)·log(Q)
Stay exactly at 1.10 V; Nernst correction is negligible at this concentration
Decrease to 0 V; the cell reaches equilibrium
Reverse polarity; the Zn electrode becomes the cathode
why: Q = [Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺]. Increasing [Cu²⁺] decreases Q. By Nernst, Ecell = 1.10 − (0.0592/2)·log(Q); decreasing Q increases Ecell.

q: A 5.00 L flask contains 0.250 mol N2 and 0.500 mol O2 at 27°C. Assuming ideal gas behavior, what is the partial pressure of O2 in atm?

For the combustion of methane: CH4(g) + 2 O2(g) → CO2(g) + 2 H2O(l), ΔH° = −890 kJ/mol and ΔS° = −243 J/(mol·K). At what temperature (approximate) does the spontaneity of the reaction reverse? (Assume ΔH° and ΔS° are temperature-independent.)
opts: The reaction is always spontaneous; spontaneity never reverses
About 3,660 K — far above any practical temperature
About 27 K — only at cryogenic temperatures
The reaction is never spontaneous at any temperature
why: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS = 0 when T = ΔH/ΔS = 890,000 / 243 ≈ 3663 K. Below this T, ΔG < 0 (spontaneous); above, ΔG > 0. In practice, methane combustion is always spontaneous at attainable temperatures.

q: A 0.050 mol sample of glucose (C6H12O6, non-electrolyte) is dissolved in 250 g of water. The Kf for water is 1.86 °C/m. What is the freezing point of the resulting solution?

Consider the ground-state electron configurations of the neutral atoms Cr (Z=24) and Cu (Z=29). Both deviate from the simple Aufbau prediction. Which of the following correctly explains BOTH anomalies?
opts: Cr is [Ar]4s¹3d⁵ and Cu is [Ar]4s¹3d¹⁰; the half-filled (Cr) and fully-filled (Cu) d-subshells gain extra exchange/symmetry stability that exceeds the small 4s↔3d energy gap
Cr is [Ar]4s²3d⁴ and Cu is [Ar]4s²3d⁹ — the standard Aufbau predictions are correct; there are no anomalies
Cr and Cu both lose a 4s electron to form 3d⁵ and 3d¹⁰; this is due to relativistic stabilization of the d-orbitals
Cr is [Ar]3d⁶ and Cu is [Ar]3d¹¹ (electron promotion across noble-gas core)
Cr is [Ar]4s¹3d⁵ but Cu is [Ar]4s²3d⁹ (only Cr deviates)
why: Cr: [Ar]4s¹3d⁵ (half-filled d gains extra exchange energy). Cu: [Ar]4s¹3d¹⁰ (filled d). Both anomalies are driven by the small 4s/3d gap and the stabilization of half- or fully-filled subshells.

q: A 5.00 g sample of an unknown hydrocarbon is combusted completely in excess oxygen. Analysis of the products yields 15.4 g of CO2 and 6.30 g of H2O. The molar mass of the compound is determined separately to be 86 g/mol. What is the molecular formula?
Consider the first ionization energies of fluorine, neon, sodium, and magnesium. Which order from LOWEST to HIGHEST IE1 is correct, and which factor most directly explains the trend?
opts: Na < Mg < F < Ne; effective nuclear charge increases left to right and atomic radius decreases
F < Ne < Na < Mg; ionization energy generally decreases down a group
Mg < Na < F < Ne; full subshells are always easier to ionize
Na < F < Mg < Ne; only valence electron count matters
Ne < F < Mg < Na; noble gases have low IE due to large size
why: IE generally increases left → right across a period (Zeff up, radius down) and decreases down a group. Na (low Zeff) < Mg < F < Ne (full shell). Knock-on: Mg has slightly higher IE than Al because removing a 3s electron (Mg) is harder than removing the 3p electron of Al.

q: For a first-order reaction with k = 0.025 s⁻¹, what is the half-life, AND how many half-lives must pass for the reactant concentration to fall below 1% of its initial value?
why: t½ = ln(2)/k = 0.693/0.025 ≈ 27.7 s. After n half-lives, fraction remaining = (1/2)ⁿ. For < 1%: (1/2)ⁿ < 0.01 → n > log(100)/log(2) ≈ 6.64 → 7 half-lives.

q: For the reaction 2 NO(g) + Cl₂(g) ⇌ 2 NOCl(g), Kc = 4.6 × 10⁴ at 298 K. A 1.00 L vessel initially contains 0.100 M NO, 0.200 M Cl₂, and 0.300 M NOCl. Determine the direction of the reaction and which side is favored at equilibrium.
opts: Reaction shifts FORWARD (right); Q = 45 << Kc, so more NOCl forms
Reaction shifts BACKWARD (left); Q > Kc, so reactants reform
Reaction is at equilibrium; Q = Kc
Reaction shifts forward; Q is undefined when reactants present
Reaction stays — equilibrium does not shift with volume change
why: Q = [NOCl]² / ([NO]² · [Cl₂]) = 0.09 / (0.01 · 0.2) = 45. Q (45) << Kc (46,000), so reaction shifts FORWARD strongly to make more NOCl.

q: Phosphoric acid (H₃PO₄) has Ka1 = 7.5 × 10⁻³, Ka2 = 6.2 × 10⁻⁸, Ka3 = 4.8 × 10⁻¹³. A buffer is prepared from 0.100 M H₂PO₄⁻ and 0.100 M HPO₄²⁻. What is the pH?
why: Buffer of conjugate pair H₂PO₄⁻ / HPO₄²⁻ uses pKa2. pH = pKa2 + log([HPO₄²⁻]/[H₂PO₄⁻]) = 7.21 + log(1) = 7.21.
